## contact

- `contact.check.note`: Our own check, used on this contact page only. In the browser it records pointer positions with times and key timings (never which keys), in memory. Pointer: the trace is cut into strokes at pauses and each stroke is measured for straightness, a rise-and-fall speed profile, smooth speed changes, speed spread, sharp turns, hand tremor, the walk exponent (1 for a random walk, exactly 2 for a ruler line, a hand is neither), sample timing, pauses and slowing before clicks. Keyboard: spread of the gaps between keys, key hold times, corrections and Tab moves, so a keyboard or screen-reader user passes without a mouse. Each measure maps to 0..1 and a weighted mean gives the score; the larger of the two paths counts. A hidden field and a minimum time before sending are cheap extras. Only the score and these reasons are sent; the trace is dropped when the page closes.
- `contact.chip.check`: our own human check
- `contact.chip.cookie`: no cookies
- `contact.chip.local`: runs in your browser
- `contact.chip.path`: your pointer path is never sent
- `contact.copied`: copied

- `contact.email`: email
- `contact.endpoint.none`: This copy of the site has no server behind the form, so nothing can be sent from here.

- `contact.endpoint.probing`: Asking the server whether it can send mail.
- `contact.endpoint.ready`: This server sends: a message goes to our inbox.

- `contact.h1`: Contact
- `contact.how.label`: THE HUMAN CHECK
- `contact.how.p1`: A hand moves in strokes: it speeds up, slows down near what it aims at, shakes a little, and stops to read. A script draws straight lines at one speed, or wanders like a random walk, on a clock that never varies. The page measures those differences while you are here and sends the result with your message.
- `contact.how.p3`: A score of 0.6 or more sends the message. A lower score does not end anything: a small puzzle opens, you slide a loose piece until it fits its cut-out, and then the message goes. The server draws the puzzle and keeps its answer. It also turns a message away when the hidden field is filled and the score is under 0.2.
- `contact.how.title`: How the page tells a hand from a script
- `contact.lede`: Write to us here. Each letter you type settles into place, and the page says plainly whether this copy of the site can send it.
- `contact.letter.empty`: Your message appears here as you type.
- `contact.letter.from`: from
- `contact.letter.kicker`: THE LETTER, SETTLING
- `contact.letter.reply`: reply to
- `contact.lines.label`: WHERE
- `contact.lines.title`: The address, the handle, the code
- `contact.privacy.label`: PRIVACY
- `contact.privacy.p1`: The pointer check runs in your browser. It keeps pointer positions with their times, and the time of each key press with its kind (a character, a correction, Tab), never which key.
- `contact.privacy.p2`: Sending the form sends your name, your email, your message, the check score, its verdict and its reason lines. It does not send the pointer path or the key timings.
- `contact.privacy.p3`: Nothing else is stored. The page sets no cookie and writes nothing to your browser storage, and the recorded movement is gone when you leave the page.
- `contact.privacy.p4`: The message goes by email to our inbox. The server keeps only the times of recent messages from each network address, in memory, to limit how many arrive in ten minutes.
- `contact.privacy.p5`: If the puzzle opens, the page sends the slider position you chose and nothing else about it. The server keeps a used puzzle and a count of missed tries, in memory, for a few minutes.
- `contact.privacy.short`: The human check runs in your browser. We receive its score and its reasons with your message, not your pointer path.
- `contact.privacy.title`: What this page keeps and what it sends

- `data.descend.2abd50f6`: c, the bias
- `data.descend.4743368b`: a real fit (logistic loss of 20 points)
- `data.descend.4767ff0d`: E = (x^2 - 1)^2 - 0.35 x + y^2: a shallow well on the left, a deeper one on the right, a hill of about 1 between. Started on the left, gradient descent stays left; heat carries walkers over the hill; cooling slowly leaves most of them in the deeper well.
- `data.descend.4a44986f`: the banana (a curved valley)
- `data.descend.69a6c057`: the bowl (the springs above)
- `data.descend.82b474d9`: two wells (a hill between)
- `data.descend.9efb254a`: w, the slope
- `data.descend.e81a2566`: E = (1 - x)^2 + 4 (y - x^2)^2: a long curved valley floor. Gradient descent zigzags down the steep walls, then crawls along the floor to (1, 1).
- `data.descend.ec38f461`: E = x.A.x/2 - b.x with A = [[3, 1], [1, 2]], b = [1, 1]: the NUMBERS springs. One valley, so gradient descent finds it, and the hot cloud is a Gaussian with covariance T A^-1.
- `data.descend.effcbeee`: E(w, c) = sum over 20 examples of [log(1 + e^z) - y z], z = w x + c, plus (w^2 + c^2)/18: logistic regression with a prior of sd 3. At T = 1 the cloud is the Bayesian posterior over the slope w and the bias c.

- `data.glossary.0a4bff89`: The word stored and read back. In SETTLE's autoassociative memories the data word is the pattern itself.
- `data.glossary.2ded83e4`: Sampling: re-tossing one thing at a time so that each arrangement turns up with probability proportional to exp(-energy / temperature).
- `data.glossary.3a0d6bae`: The Model Context Protocol: a client such as Claude Code starts a server and calls the tools it registers.
- `data.glossary.3f90fdc4`: The number of bit positions in which two words differ.
- `data.glossary.41a3462a`: How far a read-address can be from a stored word and still converge to it under iterated reads.
- `data.glossary.5645a572`: What one run block holds: the held things, the samples drawn and the counts that show and ask report.
- `data.glossary.59655103`: A thing's own preference, a real number h. leans: :yes, by: b adds +b to it.
- `data.glossary.5fc7f6b2`: The address you read at. SETTLE says read because the statement is s.read.
- `data.glossary.68156c98`: One yes or no value for every thing of a model at once.
- `data.glossary.7c9ed491`: The integer counters each hard location keeps, one per bit of the data word. A write adds +1 or -1 to each.
- `data.glossary.7faf967d`: How settle-mcp talks to its client: messages on the process’s input and output, no network port.
- `data.glossary.86325b04`: The Hamming distance within which a hard location is activated by an address.
- `data.glossary.8926dd78`: A named yes/no variable of a model. In any arrangement its value is yes (+1) or no (-1).
- `data.glossary.8a00a85f`: The address a word is stored at.
- `data.glossary.8b181fb5`: The hard locations within the activation radius of an address.
- `data.glossary.9f70dfe7`: The memory locations that are built, each with a fixed random address.
- `data.glossary.a3fa9249`: A probabilistic bit: a coin that comes up +1 or -1 with a chance set by the push on it.
- `data.glossary.a9db0913`: The fraction of the read-address's bits flipped at random before the read. address-noise: 0.2 flips a fifth of them.
- `data.glossary.c8235994`: A number J between two things. A positive pull makes them agree, a negative pull (a push) makes them disagree.
- `data.glossary.d1f23b3d`: The most times a read uses its own result as the next read-address. The read stops early when the result stops changing.
- `data.glossary.d8d64d9c`: Pentti Kanerva's memory (1988): long binary words are written to the many hard locations near their address and read back by a vote of the locations near a read-address.
- `data.glossary.db06198c`: How much the samples ignore the energy. Hot: nearly random. Cold: nearly always the calmest arrangement.
- `data.glossary.e6526c96`: The number of bits in an address and in a data word. SETTLE uses one length for both.
- `data.glossary.ea4ece08`: Settling while the temperature steps down, so the arrangement ends near the lowest energy.
- `data.glossary.f66590dc`: A setup call that runs nothing and returns every command with a plan id; the second call must repeat that id.
- `data.glossary.f6eac7c7`: The fraction of hard locations one address activates. SETTLE derives the activation radius from it.
- `data.glossary.fe37f969`: A number for each arrangement: minus the leans times the values, minus the pulls times the paired values. Low energy is likely.

- `data.herocontrols.9a8a9a34`: Everything keeps one beat. The light, the sound, the picture's 500 ms frames and the music's bar lines all count from the page's one master clock. The light draws a frame bright or dark by where that frame falls on the master beat, drops a frame the screen missed rather than catching up, and never flashes twice in one cycle. The sound starts on a master tick, so a 40 Hz binaural beat and the light cross their starts together.

- `data.herocontrols.b419b998`: A 60 Hz screen cannot show 40 Hz at all: a cycle there is a whole number of frames, so the rates it draws exactly are 30 Hz (one frame lit, one dark), 15 Hz, 10 Hz and slower. Asked for 40 Hz, it draws an uneven pattern the eye reads mostly as 20 Hz. So on a display below 100 frames a second the light runs the nearest exact rate and says so: 30 Hz at 60, 36 at 72, 37.5 at 75, 45 at 90.

- `data.kanerva.16a69249`: The memory can say "I never stored that"
- `data.kanerva.1e932ea1`: A soft edge turns SDM into attention
- `data.kanerva.21e866df`: Kanerva's own critical distance, rebuilt at a million hard locations
- `data.kanerva.3706471f`: At Kanerva's 1988 operating point (1,000-bit words, a million hard locations, ten thousand stored patterns) the critical distance, the farthest a read-address can start and still come back to its pattern, measured 204.3 bits: above Kanerva's figure of 188 and above our own signal-to-noise estimate of 165.
- `data.kanerva.5117afe7`: At equal memory, SDM holds far more than a Hopfield net
- `data.kanerva.5f4cabcc`: With a read-address that has 10% of its bits wrong, the number of patterns the memory recalls in 90% of reads rises almost in proportion to the number of hard locations, from 2,000 hard locations to a million.
- `data.kanerva.819e340b`: With the memory of a million 256-bit hard locations, a Hopfield net of the same size recalls 100 patterns at 10% address-noise; SDM read by address recalls 20,000, and SDM read by content (the top-k rows that match the read-address) 70,000.
- `data.kanerva.8e6633b3`: Capacity grows with the number of hard locations
- `data.kanerva.aba349fa`: A read that moves a random read-address a long way is refused (rule R: travel above a threshold set by how many patterns are stored); where random read-addresses settle onto stored patterns, this refusal matches a memory that sees every pattern, at no cost to recall up to 30% address-noise.
- `data.kanerva.c540b8fd`: Built from p-bits with a soft cut-off, the memory reads like a softmax attention over its stored patterns, agreeing on 93 to 96% of reads where recall works, but holding fewer patterns than the ideal kernel or softmax.

- `data.mcp.03ae1a06`: Verify: the built `settle` runs a tested core example and a tested sdm example from its own `docs/examples/`, and each output must match the stored `.out` byte for byte. Then the folder and binary path are written to `~/.settle-mcp/state.json` (or `SETTLE_MCP_STATE`).

- `data.mcp.07270e1d`: Add it to Claude Code

- `data.mcp.168e350c`: Install Node
- `data.mcp.19ff8220`: For a project, put this in `.mcp.json` at the project root. For Claude Desktop, put the same `mcpServers` block in `claude_desktop_config.json` (on macOS in `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/`, on Windows in `%APPDATA%\Claude\`) and restart it. Any client that speaks MCP over stdio takes the same command and arguments.
- `data.mcp.1b1bfc9b`: Call `sdm_store_recall` with a few names, one of them holding a short text, and read that one back from a noisy read-address:
- `data.mcp.24714246`: `noise` is the share of the read-address bits flipped before the read. A small noise comes back; near 0.4 the read stops finding the pattern, because the basins are narrow. `size` (bits, default 256) and `locations` (hard locations, default 2000) shape the memory.
- `data.mcp.2483d037`: `setup` waits up to `wait_seconds` (default 50) and then returns while the build goes on; `setup_status` reports each step as it finishes.
- `data.mcp.24aa10bf`: Run a first program
- `data.mcp.29fa459e`: `git`, only to fetch from a git URL. Node 18 or newer, to run settle-mcp itself.
- `data.mcp.2b1be8d7`: Store three memories, read one from a noisy read-address
- `data.mcp.2c342e60`: Show one tested example: its program and the exact output (or error) the interpreter is tested to produce.
- `data.mcp.2e0d0489`: Start from a tested example
- `data.mcp.2e8247c8`: Check the machine, then fetch, build and verify SETTLE and KANERVA in a folder you choose.
- `data.mcp.30002d68`: Run a tested example
- `data.mcp.304f6686`: Explain SETTLE, KANERVA and this server. With a topic, look the word up in the glossary built from the site and its docs; "glossary" lists every name.
- `data.mcp.310bb9b5`: Run KANERVA on its own
- `data.mcp.3da7a7dd`: `check_system` runs `rustc --version`, `cargo --version` and `git --version` and reports each one. It runs nothing else.
- `data.mcp.4043c10d`: Run a SETTLE program, from a .settle file or from program text, and return what it printed, its errors and its exit code.
- `data.mcp.45a01767`: settle-mcp has no default source and never guesses one. Give it a local folder (a clone of SETTLE, or a folder that holds the `settle-rs` crate) or a git URL you were given access to, such as `https://github.com/triplesparkle/SETTLE`. KANERVA is found where `settle-rs/Cargo.toml` names it by path (`../kanerva`); SETTLE's own repository names KANERVA by its git URL instead, so with it pass `kanerva_source` as well (`https://github.com/triplesparkle/KANERVA`).
- `data.mcp.479a980f`: The second call repeats the arguments with `dry_run` false and `confirm` set to the plan id. Any changed argument changes the id, so the commands that run are the commands you read.
- `data.mcp.4fa3b099`: Write named patterns (or short texts) into a sparse distributed memory, then read one back from a noisy read-address. Shows the SETTLE program it ran.
- `data.mcp.509add18`: `help` with a `topic` searches a glossary built from the site and its docs: statements, families, tokens, the words the docs define in bold, KANERVA modules, the site vocabulary, and KANERVA's terms file when it exists. The same list is the resource `settle-mcp://glossary`.
- `data.mcp.52dd08c3`: Check `rustc` and `cargo` (and `git` for a git source). Make the folder. Copy each crate without `target/` and `.git/`, or clone it. Run `cargo build --release` in `settle-rs` and `cargo build --release --example quickstart` in `kanerva`.
- `data.mcp.5387a366`: Call `list_examples`, pick one, and call `run_program` with its path, or pass program text as `source`:
- `data.mcp.538caaeb`: What it never does
- `data.mcp.55206771`: Call `check_system`, then `setup` with a `folder` and a `settle_source`: the local folder holding `settle-rs`, or a git URL you were given. The first call is a dry run that lists every command and returns a plan id. Read it, then call `setup` again with `dry_run` false and `confirm` set to that id.
- `data.mcp.5564a303`: Read one SETTLE, KANERVA or site document by name (for example "03-syntax", "sdm", "kanerva://readme", "what"); with no name, list them.
- `data.mcp.564e32ca`: The statement words it writes are read from the installed interpreter's `settle --help`, so the program always matches the SETTLE you built.
- `data.mcp.5a54f20e`: Store and recall a memory
- `data.mcp.6258955c`: Get the package
- `data.mcp.65766897`: Set `SETTLE_BIN` to a built `settle` binary, or `SETTLE_MCP_HOME` to a folder holding a built `settle-rs/` and `kanerva/`. Every usage tool also takes the paths directly.
- `data.mcp.68955352`: List the tested example programs from the SETTLE docs, each with its first comment line. Filter by family or by kind (ok or error).
- `data.mcp.6bbb40ff`: Where the code comes from
- `data.mcp.6f85bd8d`: Clone its repository, `github.com/triplesparkle/settle-mcp`. The repository is private for now, so a clone needs access; once it is public anyone can clone it or download its zip. Then install its two dependencies (the MCP SDK and zod):
- `data.mcp.71e11804`: Ask for help
- `data.mcp.735ab112`: `run_program` takes a `path` to a `.settle` file or the program text as `source`, and returns what it printed, its errors and its exit code. Text runs in a fresh temporary folder.
- `data.mcp.74893632`: Check the machine (version commands only)
- `data.mcp.76e9af67`: The two calls
- `data.mcp.7d1bc5a0`: Look a word up
- `data.mcp.80c6e26b`: Ask for help with nothing installed
- `data.mcp.84da61e0`: Look up an SDM word
- `data.mcp.9038cc22`: A git source is cloned with `git clone --depth 1`. A private repository asks for your credentials at that step, and the step reports git's own words if access is refused.
- `data.mcp.9710e49f`: Set SETTLE up
- `data.mcp.98418a55`: Ask the assistant to call `help`. It works with nothing installed: the three parts, every tool, and a glossary of every SETTLE and KANERVA name. Try `help` with the topic `lean`, `radius` or `glossary`.
- `data.mcp.a1d89ef2`: Run the KANERVA crate's own quickstart example: build a memory, write 300 patterns, read one back, predict capacity, refuse, a keyed note and the soft machine.
- `data.mcp.a3a22c1d`: Or add it to a project, Claude Desktop, or any MCP client
- `data.mcp.a6dcf259`: The website is the source of truth. These docs are generated from the SETTLE site (its pages, its English strings, the SETTLE docs and the KANERVA README it shows) by `tools/build_mcp_docs.mjs`. Never edit a generated file by hand; change the site and rebuild.
- `data.mcp.aeaa2523`: Store and recall with a sparse distributed memory
- `data.mcp.b20f96b9`: Run KANERVA's own quickstart
- `data.mcp.b4beb3ef`: The steps
- `data.mcp.b613b6d9`: Run a program
- `data.mcp.b9bd4a46`: An MCP server that explains SETTLE and KANERVA, sets them up on your machine, and runs them.
- `data.mcp.c35d9f90`: One command adds it for your user:
- `data.mcp.c4af44a7`: Explain a SETTLE error message: the documented cause, where it is documented, and a tested program that produces it.
- `data.mcp.c5be50a5`: It never uses `sudo` or another privileged command; the command runner refuses one. It never runs an installer, never edits a shell profile, and writes only inside your folder and its one state file. It never invents a public URL.
- `data.mcp.cdb2e93d`: `rustc` and `cargo`, to build SETTLE and KANERVA. Install Rust from rustup.rs; settle-mcp never runs an installer.
- `data.mcp.cfdd1096`: Explain an error message
- `data.mcp.d05b2427`: A failing program exits with status 2 and prints `settle: line N: `. Hand that line to `explain_error`, with the program as `source` to see the line it names.
- `data.mcp.d265821c`: Plan the setup: a dry run, nothing runs
- `data.mcp.d3c9a740`: `sdm_store_recall` writes named patterns, or short texts, into a sparse distributed memory and reads one back from a noisy read-address. It writes a short SETTLE program with the `sdm` statements, which call the KANERVA crate, and shows that program in its reply.
- `data.mcp.d536db9e`: Fetch, build and verify SETTLE and KANERVA in a folder. Dry run by default: returns every command and a plan id. Run it with dry_run false and confirm set to that id.
- `data.mcp.dc1fe21e`: Run exactly that plan, by its id
- `data.mcp.e28c7769`: settle-mcp runs on Node 18 or newer. Check with `node --version`; if it is missing, install it from nodejs.org.
- `data.mcp.e3c936d2`: `kanerva_quickstart` runs the crate's own example, `cargo run --release --example quickstart`, in the kanerva folder setup made. Pass `dry_run` true to see the command without running it.
- `data.mcp.e55f2ab2`: The first `setup` call is a dry run. It returns every step with the exact command and a plan id, and runs nothing.
- `data.mcp.e8aa2d73`: Check this machine for what SETTLE needs (rustc, cargo, git, node) by running only version commands. Shows each command it ran.
- `data.mcp.ecc3ce03`: A build you already have
- `data.mcp.f1319356`: `list_examples` lists the tested programs from the SETTLE docs; `get_example` shows one with the exact output the interpreter is tested to print. Each is also a resource, `settle://examples/`.
- `data.mcp.fea7e25b`: Run SETTLE programs, store and recall with a sparse distributed memory, run KANERVA.
- `data.mcp.ff90d739`: Report a setup that is still running in the background, step by step, or the last setup this server ran.

- `docs.top.count.examples.what`: example programs in docs/examples/, each run by cargo test --release
- `docs.top.count.frames.what`: the Muybridge horse, M5 Max, high power, one thread, load 13 to 70
- `docs.top.count.tests.what`: #[test] functions in src/ and tests/
- `docs.top.counts`: {examples} example programs in docs/examples/, every one run and compared by cargo test --release; {tests} test functions in the crate. Recount: {re1} and {re2}.
- `docs.top.knife1`: Every answer is a count over samples, so it is an estimate. The same seed gives the same estimate every run.
- `docs.top.knife2`: A failing line prints one message and exits with status 2, and the lines before it print nothing.
- `docs.top.knife3`: anneal keeps the calmest arrangement it visits, which is a search, not a proof. On a 9x9 sudoku with 30 givens it reaches a valid grid in 35% of 50 seeds at 2,000 sweeps and 94% at 50,000.
- `docs.top.knife4`: The debug build runs the same coin flips many times slower; only the release binary is measured anywhere.
- `docs.top.knife5`: The command line has no options. Seeds, temperatures and file paths are written in the program, or they do not exist.
- `docs.top.knives.h`: Where it breaks is written down
- `docs.top.order`: Read it in this order: the tour, the statements by family, the cookbook, then the science. The full contents are below.
- `docs.top.sell.h`: Three leans, three pulls, and Bayes falls out of a count
- `docs.top.sell.lead`: Three things lean no. Two pulls say a burglary or an earthquake sets the alarm off; one push says the two causes compete. Hold the alarm at yes and the burglary rises to 56.5%; hold the earthquake at yes as well and it falls to 26.8%, and nobody wrote a rule for that. The whole program with all three questions is [in the cookbook](#condition-on-evidence); the crate's test runs it and compares every line (`{check}`).
- `docs.top.step1`: get it and build it
- `docs.top.step2`: stand where the examples are
- `docs.top.step3`: run one
- `docs.top.steps.h`: Three commands to a running program
- `docs.top.why.h`: SETTLE exists because we wrote the same loop twice in one morning
- `docs.top.why.p1`: On 2026-09-30 the horse film ran on a Python player with the coin, the sweep and the count written into the script (thermosim_frames.py), and the first SETTLE was 310 lines of Python beside it with the same three parts written again (settle.py). Two scripts, two coins, two counts, and no number from one could stand beside a number from the other. The Rust crate took the loop from both and left the program only what changes: the things, the leans, the pulls and the question.
- `docs.top.why.p2`: The same horse now plays at {frames}. Measured on {stamp}; the report calls that run confounded, and it is the fastest it recorded ({source}). The Python player is still in the folder. Nothing in it is wrong; it is one experiment, and this is every experiment.

- `film.fs.colour.plain`: Colour is three grids, one per channel, with no pull between channels. The same rule and read that help the grey horse help the colour clip.
- `film.fs.colour.small`: GRIDPLAYER-2's Tears of Steel clip crosses a cut after frame 6. FILMSHARP cut a new one-shot clip from 40.5 s (the player's fourth clip, with the lane's recorded outputs frame-locked beside it). The cut did not change the median. Checkerboard Metropolised Gibbs with the rb read lifts the colour clip from 35.27 to 40.12 dB at 20 sweeps.
- `film.fs.colour.title`: Colour: a one-shot Tears of Steel clip
- `film.fs.control`: control · {c}
- `film.fs.fit.plain`: TAP computes each lean from a formula. FILMSHARP instead measures what the grid actually does and corrects the leans until the measured greys match the target.
- `film.fs.fit.small`: Between J 0.38 and 0.40 the TAP formula stops holding the horse, and the grid flips toward its mirror image. The fitted leans do not collapse up to J 0.44. Where they finally degrade, the chain's slow mixing is the cause, and the leans are fine.
- `film.fs.fit.title`: Leans fitted to the grid, at strong pulls
- `film.fs.inversions`: The inversions against the exact answer on a 4x4 grid (TAP, Bethe, fits, Newton)
- `film.fs.label`: RECORDED · FILMSHARP
- `film.fs.metro.gibbs`: Gibbs, TAP J 0.2 bits
- `film.fs.metro.title`: bits at J 0.2, TAP leans: Gibbs (GRIDPLAYER-2) against Metropolised Gibbs (FILMSHARP)
- `film.fs.mix.bits`: bits 80, J 0.2, TAP, warm (dB) by update rule
- `film.fs.mix.rb`: rb 80, J 0.2 (dB) by update rule
- `film.fs.rb.j01`: J 0.1, TAP leans: dB against sweeps (random-order Gibbs)
- `film.fs.rb.j02`: J 0.2, TAP leans: dB against sweeps (random-order Gibbs)
- `film.fs.rb.plain`: A bit carries two kinds of noise: the coin's own chance, and the motion of its neighbours. The rb read removes the first kind.
- `film.fs.rb.small`: The rb read averages the coin's probability in place of its result. With no pulls the coin is the only source of noise, so soft and rb both reach 98.75 dB at every budget. With pulls the neighbours' motion remains. In random order a pixel drawn late in one sweep and early in the next gives two nearly equal values, so rb sits under soft in the charts below.
- `film.fs.rb.title`: The rb read and the update rules
- `film.fs.tau.small`: 2 tau is how many sweeps one independent sample costs. Metropolised Gibbs makes successive bits anti-correlated (2 tau under 1), which beats the coin law. Near the critical pull (J 0.4, fitted) 2 tau is about 6, and 41% of a bit's variance is the neighbourhood's slow motion, which no read can remove. Swendsen-Wang clusters do not help here, because the picture's leans pin most pixels.
- `film.g1.label`: RECORDED · GRIDPLAYER
- `film.g1.plain`: A yes-or-no pixel is a coin, and the average of S tosses of a coin has a noise floor. More sweeps per frame lower that floor at a fixed rate, which these curves show.
- `film.g1.small`: This is the coin-noise law; g is a pixel's grey in [0, 1]. The Python player is a smooth analogue circuit, so drift limits it instead of noise, and it pulls ahead after about 10 sweeps. From a cold start the p-bits do better, because they forget their starting state in about one sweep.
- `film.g1.title`: The budget curves: sweeps per frame against picture quality
- `film.g2.label`: RECORDED · GRIDPLAYER-2
- `film.g2.plain`: Pulls between neighbours smooth the picture but also push every pixel away from its target grey. A lean correction subtracts that push. The better the correction, the stronger the pull the picture survives.
- `film.g2.small`: With no correction the neighbours' pull lands on top of each pixel's lean. Mean-field subtracts the pull but over-shoots, and above J = 0.25 the grid flips to its mirror image. TAP adds the Onsager term, the last term above: part of each neighbour's pull is this pixel's own echo. TAP holds the picture to J 0.35.
- `film.g2.title`: TAP leans against mean-field: PSNR as the pull J grows
- `film.how.lede.a`: Three things set the result. The leans aim each pixel at its grey. The pulls join each pixel to its neighbours. The read turns the answers back into a picture by averaging.
- `film.how.lede.b`: The seven panels above show these stages in order, from the target frame to the error of the chosen read. The recorded sections below give the numbers the lanes measured in Rust.
- `film.how.plain`: A grey level can be written as a rate. The player gives each pixel one p-bit; a pixel that should be 70% bright says yes 70% of the time, and the average of its answers recovers the grey.
- `film.inv.mean`: mean-field
- `film.inv.no`: no
- `film.live.chart.title`: live PSNR per played frame (dB)
- `film.live.chart.x`: frame played

- `film.loading`: loading frames …

- `film.rules.checker.cap`: Checkerboard order: the shaded squares first, then the others, the same way every sweep.
- `film.rules.plain`: The four rules differ only in how one pixel is redrawn. They all settle to the same picture, and they differ in how much noise the average of their answers carries.
- `film.rules.random.cap`: Random order: every sweep visits the pixels in a fresh shuffle (the step numbers above).
- `film.rules.small`: Gibbs draws a fresh coin each time. Metropolised Gibbs proposes the other state, so it flips more often and successive bits disagree more; their average is less noisy. FILMSHARP measured bits 80 on the horse at J 0.2 with TAP leans at 26.71 dB with Gibbs and 29.68 with checkerboard Metropolised Gibbs. The rb read averages tanh I at the moment each pixel draws instead of the coin's result, so the coin's own noise drops out. The same report measured rb 80 at J 0.2 at 35.44 dB with random-order Gibbs and 39.88 with checkerboard Metropolised Gibbs. In checkerboard order rb and soft read the same neighbour states, so they almost agree. In random order rb sits 1.25 to 1.6 dB below soft. The player starts on checkerboard Metropolised Gibbs for that reason.
- `film.rules.summary`: Update rules and the rb read · default: checkerboard Metropolised Gibbs (since FILMSHARP) · now: {now}

The chord moves from a cluster to a major chord as the picture forms. When the schedule holds the picture still, the bells ring. Only one thing sounds at a time on this page. - `hero.eq.eq-crossentropy.note`: cross-entropy: the nats a code built for q spends on data from p
- `hero.eq.eq-detailed.note`: detailed balance: at equilibrium each move is as frequent as its reverse
- `hero.eq.eq-elbo.note`: the evidence lower bound: what variational inference raises
- `hero.eq.eq-entropy.note`: the Gibbs entropy: how many ways, weighted
- `hero.eq.eq-free.note`: free energy: the average energy less temperature times entropy
- `hero.eq.eq-gradient.note`: gradient descent: a step of size η down the slope of the loss
- `hero.eq.eq-hamming.note`: the Hamming distance: the bits two words differ in
- `hero.eq.eq-hebb.note`: the Hebbian rule: each stored pattern ξ adds the product of its two ends
- `hero.eq.eq-hopfield.note`: the Hopfield energy: stored patterns sit at its minima
- `hero.eq.eq-importance.note`: importance sampling: average under p using samples from q
- `hero.eq.eq-ising.note`: the Ising energy: pulls J between spins, leans h on each
- `hero.eq.eq-jarzynski.note`: the Jarzynski equality: the free energy difference from the work of many fast pulls
- `hero.eq.eq-kl.note`: the KL divergence: what the wrong code costs over the right one
- `hero.eq.eq-landauer.note`: Landauer: erasing one bit costs at least kT ln 2
- `hero.eq.eq-langevin.note`: Langevin dynamics: a gradient step plus noise of the right size samples e^(-E/T)
- `hero.eq.eq-magnetisation.note`: the magnetisation: the average spin
- `hero.eq.eq-metropolis.note`: the Metropolis rule: always go downhill, go uphill with probability e^(-ΔE/T)
- `hero.eq.eq-partition.note`: the partition function: every state's weight, summed
- `hero.eq.eq-pbit.note`: the p-bit rule: a coin whose lean I sets the chance of yes
- `hero.eq.eq-perplexity.note`: perplexity: e to the cross-entropy, in nats
- `hero.eq.eq-sdmread.note`: an SDM read is a vote: the woken hard-locations sum their bit-counters, and each bit is the sign
- `hero.eq.eq-softmax.note`: softmax: the Boltzmann weights of the scores z at temperature T
- `hero.expand`: Expand the hero on this page
- `hero.film.anneal.label`: annealing
- `hero.film.anneal.note`: cooled from T 5 to T 1 out of noise: the domains grow
- `hero.film.dollar-of-mexico.label`: the dollar of Mexico
- `hero.film.dollar-of-mexico.note`: two records bound and bundled; their product maps one onto the other, and the dollar comes out as the peso
- `hero.film.domain-wall.label`: two domains and a wall
- `hero.film.domain-wall.note`: an Ising field below its critical temperature: the wall wanders, the domains hold
- `hero.film.flock.label`: a flock
- `hero.film.flock.note`: 48 birds, each steering by its neighbours alone: separation, alignment, cohesion
- `hero.film.hopfield-complete.label`: a memory completes a letter
- `hero.film.hopfield-complete.note`: a net storing four letters is shown an S with its lower half erased, and fills it in
- `hero.film.hopfield.label`: a Hopfield recall
- `hero.film.hopfield.note`: a noisy ring falls back into the ring the net stored
- `hero.film.horse.label`: HORSE
- `hero.film.horse.note`: a horse at the gallop: Muybridge, 1878, public domain
- `hero.film.ising-critical.label`: the critical point
- `hero.film.ising-critical.note`: an Ising field at T 2.27, where order and disorder balance: clusters of every size
- `hero.film.isted-drawn.label`: ISTED?
- `hero.film.isted-drawn.note`: a rider pedalling over a jump, drawn in code
- `hero.film.magnet-flip.label`: a magnet flips
- `hero.film.magnet-flip.note`: the field leans up, then the lean is reversed: a down domain is born and spreads
- `hero.film.nonogram.label`: a nonogram solving
- `hero.film.nonogram.note`: each line placed by logic alone: a cell is filled or ruled out only when every way the clues fit agrees
- `hero.film.purkinje-grow.label`: a Purkinje cell growing
- `hero.film.purkinje-grow.note`: its dendrites spread as one flat fan
- `hero.film.sdm-heal.label`: a vote heals a letter
- `hero.film.sdm-heal.note`: a noisy A read from a real SDM of six letters comes back clean
- `hero.film.sdm-read.label`: a read
- `hero.film.sdm-read.note`: a real SDM: the woken hard locations vote on every bit, and the sign is the answer
- `hero.film.sdm-wake.label`: a read waking hard locations
- `hero.film.sdm-wake.note`: a read-address walks from one address to another; the hard locations inside its activation radius wake and go back to sleep
- `hero.film.sdm-write.label`: a write
- `hero.film.sdm-write.note`: the address wakes the hard locations inside its activation radius; each adds the word to its bit-counters
- `hero.film.softness.label`: a softness dial
- `hero.film.softness.note`: the tanh rule and a field at the same temperature, T 0.3 to 3 and back
- `hero.film.sudoku-fill.label`: a sudoku filling
- `hero.film.sudoku-fill.note`: every digit is placed only when it is the one digit its row, column and box allow
- `hero.film.sudoku.label`: a sudoku settling
- `hero.film.sudoku.note`: row swaps under the Metropolis rule while the temperature falls
- `hero.film.wave.label`: two waves
- `hero.film.wave.note`: two sources ripple the same pond: where crest meets trough the water stays still

- `hero.light.hint`: The light changes nothing about the sound.
- `hero.light.reduced`: Your system asks for reduced motion, so the 40 Hz light stays off.
- `hero.light.sitewide`: One mode for the whole site: every settling picture flickers together, the footer included. The bright 40 Hz OFF at the top right, or Escape, ends it.

- `hero.light.turnon`: turn the 40 Hz light on
- `hero.liveeq.live-actprob.label`: the activation-probability, live
- `hero.liveeq.live-actprob.note`: the activation-radius H sweeps from 400 to 500 bits of 1,000; the share of addresses within H is computed exactly at each step
- `hero.liveeq.live-anneal.label`: annealing, live
- `hero.liveeq.live-anneal.note`: a 24 by 14 Ising lattice cooled from T 3.5 to 0.8 by Gibbs sweeps; its energy E is computed every sweep and falls
- `hero.liveeq.live-boltzmann.label`: two levels cooling, live
- `hero.liveeq.live-boltzmann.note`: two states with energies 0 and 1; as T falls, the Boltzmann weights move to the lower one
- `hero.liveeq.live-hdc.label`: the dollar of Mexico, live
- `hero.liveeq.live-hdc.note`: two country records bundled from role-filler XORs; the dollar is unbound into the peso, and noise rises while the clean-up still names it
- `hero.liveeq.live-metropolis.label`: the Metropolis rule, live
- `hero.liveeq.live-metropolis.note`: a walker proposes a step left or right and accepts it with probability min(1, e^(-ΔE/T)); the running acceptance rate is counted
- `hero.liveeq.live-pbit.label`: the tanh rule, live
- `hero.liveeq.live-pbit.note`: the lean I sweeps from −3 to 3; the chance of yes is computed as it moves
- `hero.liveeq.live-softmax.label`: softmax and temperature, live
- `hero.liveeq.live-softmax.note`: five fixed scores; as T rises the probabilities flatten, as it falls the top score takes almost all
- `hero.pause`: ❚❚ pause
- `hero.pic.pause`: Pause the picture
- `hero.pic.play`: Play the picture

- `hero.plate.babbage-number-card.note`: Babbage's number card for the Analytical Engine, after Passages from the Life of a Philosopher (Freeman, Automatic Mechanical Punching ... Machines, 1915)
- `hero.plate.cajal-climbing-fibre.label`: a climbing fibre
- `hero.plate.cajal-climbing-fibre.note`: Ramón y Cajal's climbing fibre of the adult human cerebellum (Manual de histología normal, 1921)
- `hero.plate.cajal-purkinje-cell.label`: a Purkinje cell
- `hero.plate.cajal-purkinje-cell.note`: Ramón y Cajal's Purkinje cells of the human cerebellum, Golgi method (Manual de histología normal, 1921)
- `hero.plate.darcy-sunfish-grid.label`: Sunfish transformation grid
- `hero.plate.darcy-sunfish-grid.note`: The porcupine-fish grid deformed into the sunfish, Fig. 382 (D'Arcy Thompson, On growth and form, 1917)
- `hero.plate.dircks-weighted-wheel.label`: Overbalanced weight wheel
- `hero.plate.dircks-weighted-wheel.note`: A perpetual motion wheel with weighted levers, Fig. 52 (Dircks, Perpetuum Mobile, 1861)
- `hero.plate.ewing-magnet-domains.label`: magnets in groups
- `hero.plate.ewing-magnet-domains.note`: Ewing's model of molecular magnets falling into groups (Magnetic Induction in Iron and Other Metals, 1900)
- `hero.plate.galileo-moon.label`: Galileo's moon
- `hero.plate.galileo-moon.note`: Galileo's drawing of the moon at first quarter (Sidereus nuncius, 1610)
- `hero.plate.galton-quincunx.label`: the quincunx
- `hero.plate.galton-quincunx.note`: Galton's quincunx: shot falls through pins into a bell curve (Natural Inheritance, 1889)
- `hero.plate.galton-tumbling-slab.label`: the tumbling slab
- `hero.plate.galton-tumbling-slab.note`: Galton's polygonal slab model of primary and subordinate stability (Natural Inheritance, 1889)
- `hero.plate.ganot-crookes-radiometer.label`: Crookes radiometer
- `hero.plate.ganot-crookes-radiometer.note`: Crookes's radiometer, Fig. 651 (Ganot, Elementary Treatise on Physics, 1910)
- `hero.plate.ganot-gyroscope.label`: Gyroscope on stand

Totals across the lanes that list their predictions one by one: {hit} hits, {miss} misses, {split} split (partly right). Each lane’s page lists its missed predictions with the rest.

- `home.go.docs`: The programming language, every statement
- `home.go.what`: What SETTLE is, step by step

- `home.lane.tally`: {hit} hit · {miss} missed · {split} split
- `home.recorded`: the lane reports and experiments/thermosim/SETTLE_CAMPAIGN_2026-09-30.md
- `home.running`: what those lines do, running
- `home.sci`: Settling is sampling: each thing is a p-bit, a coin that comes up +1 (yes) or −1 (no), and the machine keeps re-tossing one thing at a time, so that in the long run every arrangement s turns up with probability proportional to e^(−β E(s)), with β = 1/T. Each toss sets a thing to yes with probability P(yes) = (1 + tanh(β I)) / 2, where I = lean + Σ pull × neighbour is the sum of its lean and its pulls times its neighbours’ values, and the arrangement drifts toward low energy E = −Σ lean·s − Σ pull·s·s′, the quantity Settling lowers.
- `home.start.label`: GETTING STARTED
- `home.start.lede`: Four steps from a clone of the SETTLE repository to a question answered with evidence. The two programs run live in your browser under their code.
- `home.start.title`: Build it, write a program, run it
- `home.step1`: 1 · build it
- `home.step2`: 2 · write a first program
- `home.step2.note`: One thing, named :coin, leaning toward yes with strength 1. Settle it 40,000 times and ask how often it came up yes.
- `home.step3`: 3 · run it
- `home.step3.note`: The real output of that program (recorded from src/how/01_one_thing.settle). The exact answer is (1 + tanh 1) / 2 = 88.08%.
- `home.step4`: 4 · ask a question with evidence
- `home.step4.note`: The grass is wet: did it rain? Hold the wet-grass light on and count the rain light. The release binary says {wet}% with the grass held wet, {none}% with nothing held and {dry}% with it held dry.
- `home.surprise`: Also built on a settling machine, outside the statement families: SURPRISE, a small first-person game whose agent acts to keep its observations unsurprising (Friston’s free-energy principle, in toy form).
- `home.weather`: rain, sprinkler and wet grass, settling with the grass held wet

## kanerva

- `kanerva.analogies.d1.precise`: Each word is {D} random bits. Dollar and peso agree on {pct} of them: unrelated words agree on about half.
- `kanerva.analogies.d1.title`: Every word is a long row of random dots.
- `kanerva.analogies.d2.precise`: bind: c = a XOR b, bit by bit. Tying again with b gives back a, so a tie can be undone.
- `kanerva.analogies.d2.title`: Tie a role to its value: a dot lights where the two rows differ.
- `kanerva.analogies.d3.precise`: bundle: each bit of USA is the majority of the three ties. USA still agrees with MONEY tied to dollar on {pct} of its bits.
- `kanerva.analogies.d3.title`: A country is a vote of its three ties.
- `kanerva.analogies.d4.precise`: USA XOR MEXICO keeps a trace of dollar XOR peso, because MONEY XOR MONEY cancels.
- `kanerva.analogies.d4.title`: Tie the two countries together. The result maps each of one country's values to the other's.
- `kanerva.analogies.d5.precise`: dollar XOR (USA XOR MEXICO): a noisy copy of the word that plays dollar's part in MEXICO.
- `kanerva.analogies.d5.title`: Push dollar through the map.
- `kanerva.analogies.d6.precise`: similarity = 1 - 2 x (differing bits) / {D}. Peso scores {top}, the next word {next}; chance spreads about 0.010.
- `kanerva.analogies.d6.title`: Ask the memory which word the answer looks like. Peso lights up.
- `kanerva.analogies.d7.iq.aria`: the IQ-test form of the dollar of Mexico
- `kanerva.analogies.d7.precise`: MEXICO XOR USA XOR dollar is the word from step 5 again. Cleaned up, it is {name} at {sim}; the next word scores {next}.
- `kanerva.analogies.d7.title`: The same question, as an IQ test.
- `kanerva.analogies.d8.fewer`: fewer than 100%
- `kanerva.analogies.d8.precise`: (SWEDEN XOR USA) XOR (USA XOR MEXICO) agrees with SWEDEN XOR MEXICO on {share} of its bits: the USA in the middle cancels exactly. Krona pushed through it comes back as {answer} at {sim}.
- `kanerva.analogies.d8.title`: Go through a third country. Sweden to the United States, then on to Mexico.
- `kanerva.analogies.d9.precise`: The roles NAME, CAPITAL and MONEY cancel out of the map (MONEY XOR MONEY is all zeros). What is left pairs usa with mexico, washington with mexico city, and dollar with peso.
- `kanerva.analogies.d9.quote`: “The mapping vector has the same form as the holistic record H introduced earlier, except that in place of abstract variables we have an exemplar: the particulars for the United States, USA, WDC, and DOL, play the role of the variables in terms of which the Mexican data are interpreted. This agrees with our common use of language when we refer to the peso as the Mexican dollar, for example. The ‘Mexican dollar’ is immediately understood even if there is no such a thing, literally speaking, and we know that it does not exist.”
- `kanerva.analogies.d9.title`: Why Kanerva calls this a prototype.
- `kanerva.analogies.h.dollar`: The dollar of Mexico, step by step
- `kanerva.analogies.h.king`: King is to queen as man is to woman
- `kanerva.analogies.h.more`: Three more from the same paper
- `kanerva.analogies.k1.precise`: KING = majority(KIND tied to person, RANK tied to royal, SEX tied to male); QUEEN, MAN and WOMAN are built the same way.
- `kanerva.analogies.k1.title`: A person is a vote of three ties: what kind, what rank, what sex.
- `kanerva.analogies.k2.precise`: KING XOR MAN cancels the person and male ties and keeps royal XOR common.
- `kanerva.analogies.k2.title`: Tie KING to MAN. What they share cancels; what makes a king more than a man is left.
- `kanerva.analogies.k3.precise`: KING XOR MAN XOR WOMAN: a woman given what a king has more than a man, that is, a noisy QUEEN.
- `kanerva.analogies.k3.title`: Tie that difference to WOMAN.
- `kanerva.analogies.k4.precise`: The three words we asked with also score high, because the answer is made from them; as in every analogy test they are set aside. Queen scores {top}, the best other word {next}.
- `kanerva.analogies.k4.title`: Ask the memory which word the answer looks like. Queen lights up.
- `kanerva.analogies.king.note`: This one is not in Kanerva’s paper. It is the classic word analogy, built here with the same two moves and roles we chose: KIND, RANK and SEX.
- `kanerva.analogies.label`: THE DOLLAR OF MEXICO, AND KANERVA'S OTHER EXAMPLES
- `kanerva.analogies.lede`: The tie and the vote from the first steps are enough to ask this question and get the answer back. A country is a bundle of three ties. Tie two countries together and you get a map between them. Push dollar through the map and peso comes out. Each card shows one step on the first 40 of the 10,000 bits.
- `kanerva.analogies.live`: 10,000-bit words, seed {seed}
- `kanerva.analogies.redraw`: draw new random words
- `kanerva.analogies.source`: Source for cards 1 to 9: P. Kanerva, “What We Mean When We Say ‘What’s the Dollar of Mexico?’: Prototypes and Mapping in Concept Space”, AAAI Fall Symposium on Quantum Informatics for Cognitive, Social, and Semantic Processes, 2010 (Technical Report FS-10-08, pp. 2-6; the paper). The paper writes USTATES, MEXICO and SWEDEN with the roles NAM, CAP and MON; the cards spell them out. It also says what a word like this is for: “D can later be retrieved by addressing the memory with A or with a ‘noisy’ version of it that is similar to A. The address A is also called a memory cue.” On this site the word is address, and a damaged one is a noisy address.
- `kanerva.analogies.title`: What is the dollar of Mexico?

- `kanerva.page.how.eq.read`: A read from the address z: the woken locations vote, bit by bit; repeat until z stops changing.
- `kanerva.page.how.eq.wake`: The wake set: every hard location whose address a_i is within r bits of the word z.
- `kanerva.page.how.eq.write`: A write adds the word x (as +1 and −1) to the counters of every woken location.
- `kanerva.page.how.explainer`: The simplest version, five steps in Kanerva’s own words with pictures, is at the top of SDM EXPLORE. This section is the same memory in more detail.
- `kanerva.page.how.intro`: A sparse distributed memory stores long words of bits. It owns a few thousand hard locations. Each hard location has a fixed random address, as long as a word, and a row of bit-counters, one per bit. To write a word, the memory wakes every hard location whose address is close to the word and adds the word to their bit-counters. To read, you give the memory a read-address: a word, or a noisy copy of one, which is then a read-address with address-noise. The hard locations close to the read-address are activated, their bit-counters are added up bit by bit, and each bit of the answer is the sign of its sum. Kanerva calls the read-address the retrieval address, and also the retrieval cue; the older lane reports say cue.
- `kanerva.page.how.label`: HOW AN SDM WORKS
- `kanerva.page.how.name`: The memory is called sparse because its locations are a tiny sample of all possible addresses, and distributed because every word is spread over many hard locations and every hard location holds a blend of many words.
- `kanerva.page.how.sketch.aria`: the memory, drawn as a sketch
- `kanerva.page.how.sources`: Sources: P. Kanerva, {book}, MIT Press, 1988. The equations are the ones the SDMSCALE lane states in its report (section 2). The same memory, drawn as a machine you can run, is on the SDM explore page; the three memories side by side are on the memory page.
- `kanerva.page.how.title`: A memory is a few thousand hard locations that vote
- `kanerva.page.how.why`: Why it works: a noisy address near a stored word wakes most of the hard locations that word was written to. Their bit-counters agree with each other and outvote the other words, which were written to other hard locations. Reading the answer again moves it closer still. Below, the whole thing on a memory of 1,200 hard locations: write a word, make a noisy copy of it, read from that.
- `kanerva.page.results.label`: RECORDED RESULTS
- `kanerva.page.results.note`: Every result is a seeded recall count from a simulation on an M5; the lane reports make no timing claim. Each quote above is copied from its report, and the site’s tests fail if one is not found there word for word. The reports say “cue” where this page says noisy address. More on the memory page and in each lane’s report on the results page.

Both read a word back from an address that is partly wrong, and the live one shows the bits still wrong when a read fails.
- `kanerva.pitch.install.title`: add KANERVA to a Rust project
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.clamp.body`: Store uses one byte per counter, clamps at ±127, and counts every clamp in overflow.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.clamp.head`: The byte store clamps.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.keys.body`: The key is hashed to 64 bits with FNV-1a and a guessed key can be checked offline against the padding.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.keys.head`: A keyed note is not cryptography.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.noise.body`: At 30% and 40% address-noise the address read does not grow with M, because a 40%-noisy read-address shares about one hard location with its pattern at every M under that activation radius.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.noise.head`: Noise above a third of the bits does not get better with a bigger memory.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.small.body`: 128 hard locations (32,768 bit-counters) hold 5 / 0 / 0 / 0 against 25 / 25 / 20 / 0 for a 256-unit Hopfield net with 32,640 pulls. The order reverses at a million locations: 70,000 / 30,000 / 10,000 / 10 against 100 / 70 / 30 / 3.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.small.head`: A small memory loses to a Hopfield net.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.threads.body`: smap::Lazy memoises through RefCell, so one Lazy cannot be shared between threads. store::threads() reads the environment variable SDMSCALE_THREADS (default 8), a name from the SETTLE lane that wrote it.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.threads.head`: Two of its parts are not thread-safe or thread-clean.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.unstored.body`: At light load every never-stored read-address lands on a stored pattern (500/500), so no signal read off the final state can refuse it. The travel rule refuses it; in crowded stores its refusal falls to 0.044 until it is calibrated on the memory’s own random probes.
- `kanerva.pitch.knife.unstored.head`: A never-stored address lands on something anyway.
- `kanerva.pitch.knives.label`: SHARP KNIVES
- `kanerva.pitch.knives.lede`: A sparse distributed memory is a sharp tool. These are the edges, stated as the lane reports measured them, and the crate keeps them as they are rather than hiding them.

- `kanerva.pitch.manifesto`: Nothing is kept in one place. Everything is kept a little everywhere.
- `kanerva.pitch.manifesto.plain`: No single hard location holds a word. Every word is spread over hundreds of them, and every location holds pieces of many words. That is the “distributed” in the name, and it is why a wrong address still finds the right word: the locations it reaches outvote the ones it misses.

- `kanerva.pitch.why`: We built SETTLE’s first memories as Hopfield nets, and a Hopfield net is a pull between every pair of bits: the memory grows as the square of the word, and a 256-unit net held 25 words at 10% address-noise and none at 30%. We wanted a memory that grows with the number of hard locations instead of the word, holds thousands of words, and answers a read-address it has never seen with the nearest word it has. Kanerva described that memory in 1988. Six SETTLE lanes wrote it inside the interpreter, measured it against the Hopfield baseline at equal memory, and lane SDMKIT lifted the pieces into one crate with every output kept identical. The numbers are in the README and under measured results below.

- `learning.draw.sweep`: sweep {t} of {total}. Your strokes are not MNIST's scans, so the machine can fail here on a digit a person reads easily; the measured accuracy is on the test set below.
- `learning.explain.classic`: The classic route. A second machine learns only the pixels (no labels). Its hidden things' yes-rates become 500 features, and an ordinary logistic regression reads the digit from them. That is how Boltzmann machines were first used on MNIST.
- `learning.explain.coins`: Given the pixels and labels, each hidden thing flips its own coin; given the hidden things, each label does. Doing all hidden then all visible is one exact sweep of the sampler.
- `learning.explain.kinds`: The machine has three kinds of things, each yes or no. 784 pixel things (a pixel is yes when its grey value is at least 128 of 255), ten label things (one per digit), and a layer of hidden things the machine uses however helps it. Every hidden thing pulls on every pixel and every label; nothing else is connected. That shape is a restricted Boltzmann machine.
- `learning.explain.learning`: Learning. Show the machine a digit with its label held on. Let it take one step on its own (settle the hidden things, rebuild the picture, settle the hidden things again). Then move every pull toward what the example did and away from what the machine did by itself.
- `learning.explain.likely`: An arrangement is likely when things agree with their leans and when pulled pairs agree.
- `learning.explain.plain`: The machine is an energy over pixels, labels and hidden things. Learning lowers the energy of real digits with their labels, and reading a digit lets the labels settle against held pixels.
- `learning.explain.reading`: Reading a digit. Hold a new digit's pixels, let the hidden and label things shake, and take the label that is yes most often. That is the settled readout. The exact readout computes, for each of the ten labels, how likely the machine finds that label with these pixels, and takes the best. It draws no coins.
- `learning.explain.rule`: Raise a pull when the examples agree on that pair more often than the machine does after a short settle (contrastive divergence, one step); the last term keeps pulls small. η starts at 0.005 and falls to a tenth over 20 passes.

- `llm.chat.label`: LIVE · THE CHAT

- `llm.how.features.now`: The model reads the context through a small set of features: the last 8 token embeddings and five decaying averages of everything so far, each normalised (the small model uses the last 4 and two averages). A linear map turns these features into a working vector x of 512 numbers (256 in the small model). The store is then read in two hops. At each hop a query of 256 numbers scores the key of every location; the top 64 locations are kept, they fire through a soft threshold centred on the 32nd best score, and their values are added to x. A small readout MLP follows, and the shared embedding table (129,280 rows) serves as the output layer. Training is next-token cross-entropy with AdamW.
- `llm.how.features.wide768`: SDM read, wide 768 and SDM read, wide 768, chat-tuned work the same way, with a working vector of 768 numbers and a readout MLP of 2,064; their query is still 256 numbers.
- `llm.how.label`: HOW IT WORKS

- `llm.plan.note`: This table is a plan from the report. None of these stages has been run. Training compute is 6 N D; the H100 figures assume 400 TFLOP/s and the Spark figures assume 50 TFLOP/s, neither measured. S1 could run on the Spark at 20 tokens per parameter in about 3 days after the HEADCLIMB lane ends; S2 and the 4B shape need an approved rental.
- `llm.plan.title`: Planned larger stages and their estimated cost
- `llm.pred.label`: RECORDED · PREDICTIONS
- `llm.pred.title`: Predictions written before the run: {v}
- `llm.run.how`: The checkpoint is exported by : the token table (129,280 rows, 88 to 92% of each model) as int8 with one scale per row, every other tensor float32, and the store keys already normalised. The forward pass is hand-written in JavaScript in a Web Worker, so every internal the panel draws is a value the model computed. The model keeps no state between tokens except the last 256 token ids, so a long prompt costs nothing extra. The DeepSeek V4 tokenizer (129,280 ids, 127,741 merges) is ported too; the site's tests check its token ids against the Python tokenizer on 19 strings and the forward pass against PyTorch on fixed contexts.
- `llm.run.line`: {label} · {mb} MB · same top token as float32 PyTorch on {pct}% of {n} held-out TEST positions · bits per byte on those positions {f32} (float32) and {i8} (as run here) · mean KL {kl} nats
- `llm.run.measured`: Measured by the exporter on the first 48 TEST windows. The agreement is below 100% because the int8 table moves near-tied logits; the bits per byte shows what that costs. Speed depends on your machine: the panel shows tokens per second as they are measured.
- `llm.run.notbuilt`: {label} · not built here (run {cmd})
- `llm.run.reading`: {label} · reading its export …
- `llm.run.tag`: live model in your browser
- `llm.run.tag.title`: This model runs in this browser tab; nothing is sent anywhere.
- `llm.s0.control`: control · {c}
- `llm.s0.label`: RECORDED · SDMLLM S0
- `llm.s0.note`: Bits per byte: the average number of bits a model needs per byte of text, which does not depend on the tokenizer. The differences are paired over the identical 3,873 TEST windows, with the error from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of windows. The learned store costs 0.017 to 0.025 bpb, far outside both the bootstrap error and the SDM seed spread. A dense MLP of the same size and a store of frozen random values both do better, and the trained model ignores the frozen store. This matches the earlier track4_245 result, here with no teacher model involved: the address and the readout carry the model, and the learned store does not.
- `llm.s0.title`: Result: the no-store control scores better in every seed
- `llm.s0.use`: Location use ({use}): the sealed read touches under half of its 3,600 locations. Softness 2.0 recovers most of the gap. This suggests the cause is noisy, sparse gradients reaching the store, and not the read design itself. 92% of every model's parameters sit in the embedding table, so S0 measures the table more than the body.
- `llm.sdm.intro.lead`: The default model here reads one twice per token, addressed by the context, to help choose the next token.
- `llm.seeds.aria`: TEST bits per byte per arm and seed
- `llm.seeds.dot`: {arm} seed {seed}: {v}
- `llm.seeds.title`: TEST bits per byte by arm: one dot per seed, a bar at the mean (lower is better)
- `llm.soft.s05`: softness 0.5 (the sealed arm)
- `llm.soft.s2`: softness 2.0
- `llm.soft.title`: how strongly a location fires against its score minus the threshold (from the equation)
- `llm.store.cause`: S0's store cost came from its gradient path, not from the read: the hard cut-off sent a large gradient back through the query into the shared features, and the global clip then shrank every update. Stopping that gradient (alpha 0) leaves the keys, values and query map training and removes the whole cost. The store is then heavily used (zeroing its read costs +0.045 bpb) but adds nothing net: the readout learns the same thing without it. Softness stops mattering once the gradient path is fixed.
- `llm.store.label`: RECORDED · SDMLLMSTORE
- `llm.store.sealed`: Sealed predictions: {v}
- `llm.store.title`: A properly trained store ties the control; only a per-token table wins
- `llm.store.winner`: The only consistent winner, -0.008 bpb in all three seeds, is a hashed table keyed on the current token. It works as an untied input embedding: the tied 129,280-row table is also the output layer, and a free per-token input vector helps. It is a finding about the tied embedding, not about memory. {rerun}
- `llm.sweep.aria`: delta against the no-store control by softness
- `llm.sweep.axis`: softness
- `llm.sweep.note`: Each delta's bootstrap SE is 0.00021 to 0.00022; a fixed-seed rerun moved 0.0026, so the whole sweep sits inside rerun noise.
- `llm.sweep.title`: storeopt_qstop, seed 0: bpb minus no-store, by softness (below zero means the store helps)
- `llm.talk.label`: WHAT YOU ARE TALKING TO
- `llm.talk.sdm.base`: It is a base model: it learned only to continue web text, and the chat is a prompt template () that it continues as if it were a document. It writes fluent-looking text that drifts off the question, it does not know facts reliably, and it does not follow instructions. Do not trust what it says.
- `llm.talk.sdm.chat.now`: The chat model answers in the template , so its replies take the shape of an answer. It is a small model: it writes fluent-looking text that drifts off the question, it does not know facts reliably, and it does not follow instructions. Do not trust what it says.
- `llm.talk.sdm.compare`: How these models compare with models that have no store: the results.
- `llm.talk.sdm.p1.now`: Every model on this page chooses its next token by reading a sparse distributed memory: a store of 3,600 locations, read twice per token and addressed by its last tokens. The chat opens on {name}. The model dropdown offers {n, plural, one {this one model} other {all # models, each with its score in bits per byte of held-out text (lower is better)}}:
- `llm.talk.title.sdm`: A small language model that reads a sparse distributed memory
- `llm.title`: SDMCHAT
- `llm.top.explore`: how an SDM works

- `magic8.honest.p2`: Its decision is a property of the words in the question, and magic-8-ball reproduces that property. The table below measures the teacher against the true answers: it is at chance, and on BoolQ it is below the score of always answering yes.
- `magic8.honest.title`: This model is not a knowledge source
- `magic8.intro.p1`: The model on this page is magic-8-ball. It answers a yes or no question with YES, UNSURE or NO. It does not run a language model to do it. It reads one vector, the {d} numbers the teacher (SDMCHAT's best model that reads an SDM) forms for the question before it does anything else, and turns them into a decision with {d} weights and one constant.
- `magic8.intro.p2a`: The SDMJEV idea. In this project JEV is a small head that predicts which experts a large model will route to next. It is trained on that model's own routing traces, so the engine can fetch the experts before the model asks ({path}).
- `magic8.intro.p2b`: SDMJEV does the same thing to SDMCHAT. We asked the teacher {rows} questions, recorded how far it leaned towards yes or no on each, and fitted a fast head to that record. The bet is that the decision is already present in the teacher's first vector, before its memory, its readout and its 129,280-way output layer run. On the {test} held-out test questions the head agrees with the teacher on {agree} of them.
- `magic8.intro.p3`: The head was taught what the teacher would say, not what is true. The teacher is a small base model and is near chance on the truth (see HOW IT WAS TRAINED), so this is a magic 8 ball, not an oracle.
- `magic8.intro.riding`: WHAT THIS IS
- `magic8.intro.title`: A decision read in one pass from SDMCHAT's vector space

- `magic8.measured.label`: WHAT WAS MEASURED
- `magic8.measured.p1a`: Chance agreement for the shipped student, from the class rates alone, is {chance}. A student trained on shuffled leans stays near it, and the same head on a random vector space of the same shape reaches {random}: token identity alone carries part of the teacher's decision, and the teacher's vector space carries the rest.
- `magic8.measured.p1b`: The reference probe on the teacher's own last hidden state reaches {reference}, which is close to the ceiling for any student, since the teacher's lean is nearly a straight line in that state.
- `magic8.measured.p2.now`: The small SDM read (width 256, 20M tokens) leans differently: the rank correlation of the two models' leans on the test split is {rho} and their three-way decisions agree on {agree}. Neither is better against the truth.
- `magic8.measured.p3`: The full teacher spends most of its time in the output layer. A teacher that computes only the 32 answer-word logits gets the same lean (largest difference {diff}) {trimmed} times faster, and against that fair comparison magic-8-ball is still about {shipped} times faster. The machine was loaded by other work during the run, so the ratios are the claim, not the milliseconds.

- `magic8.settle.n.same`: push apart less (A - tie, tie {tie}), so moves inside a group are cheap
- `magic8.settle.n.schedule`: geometric over {sweeps} sweeps, then {hold} held at {T}
- `magic8.settle.n.self`: every light wants to be on (A / 2)
- `magic8.settle.p1`: Each of the twenty answers is a light that is on or off. Its lean is the log of its group's chance divided by the group's size, shifted so the best is 0. So the ten yes answers share the yes chance, and with equal chances the yes group weighs twice what each other group weighs, as on the real ball.
- `magic8.settle.p2`: Each sweep visits the twenty lights in a random order and sets each one on with probability 1 / (1 + e-u/T), where u is its lean plus the self bias plus the pulls from the lights now on. Hot, many lights flicker. Cold, one light stays on and the rest are pushed off. The seed comes from your question, so the same question gives the same answer; SHAKE AGAIN changes the seed.

- `magic8.train.caveat`: The caveat. The teacher does not know the answers. On the templated questions with a known answer its YES or NO is right {tpl} of the time. On BoolQ it is right {bq} of the time, while always answering yes scores {always}. magic-8-ball copies that teacher closely, so it is a magic 8 ball, not an oracle.
- `magic8.train.choice`: The choice. Four one-pass students were fitted and compared on the validation split only. The rule: {rule}. The test split was used once, after the choice.
- `magic8.train.data`: The data. {templated} questions were written from small fact tables (animals, capitals, numbers, colours, everyday facts, and Magic 8 Ball questions with no answer). {boolq} came from BoolQ. Each question was put in the prompt and run through the teacher once. The label is the teacher's lean, not the true answer.
- `magic8.train.fit`: The fit. A ridge regression from x0 ({d} numbers) to the lean, on the {train} training questions. Each input is standardised first, and the penalty was chosen from {grid} by agreement on the validation split; {param} won. The result is {d} weights and a constant ({file}).
- `magic8.train.label`: HOW IT WAS TRAINED
- `magic8.train.memories`: Why the memories lost. A memory can only separate questions that reach different locations. The teacher's own address reaches {locs} of its {m} locations across every question, and two questions share {overlap} of their 64. Every prompt ends {answer}, and the teacher addresses its memory mostly from the last words. Both memory students put every test question in UNSURE.
- `magic8.train.result`: The result. On the {test} test questions magic-8-ball gives the teacher's class {agree} of the time (kappa {kappa}; rank correlation of the leans {rho}). When it disagrees it moves one band, to or from UNSURE: on the test questions where the teacher said YES or NO, it never said the opposite.

The last tokens are the same for almost every question, so the two averages carry most of what is particular to yours.

It stores a hash of what it read, and the server checks that hash when it starts and rebuilds if the site has changed. A site test fails while the generated docs are out of date.
- `mcp.truth.label`: THE SOURCE OF TRUTH
- `mcp.truth.title`: This website writes the MCP’s docs
- `mcp.why.body`: We had two READMEs, a forty-line --help and a language whose statement words live in six files. The first person to try SETTLE asked us what the read-address was, and we answered by pasting a file into the chat. That is the old way: a person reads, finds, pastes. settle-mcp does the finding. The editor asks help, the server opens the same file, and the line comes back with its path. Then the same server copies the crates, builds them, verifies them on tested programs and runs yours, so the question and the thing it was about sit in one window.
- `mcp.why.label`: WHY THIS EXISTS
- `mcp.why.title`: We pasted files at people; the server pastes them for us
