## memory

- `memory.chip.hop`: Hopfield
- `memory.chip.keys`: notes under a key
- `memory.chip.live`: live in your browser
- `memory.chip.sdm`: Kanerva SDM
- `memory.chip.soft`: soft SDM, toward attention
- `memory.equal.addr`: SDM address read, best activation radius
- `memory.equal.hop`: Hopfield (same memory)
- `memory.equal.title`: 30% address-noise, P90 at equal memory (M x 256 bit-counters), log-log
- `memory.equal.topk`: SDM top-k read
- `memory.equal.x`: budget: SDM hard locations M
- `memory.h1`: SDMMEMORY
- `memory.hop.damage`: address-noise to the start
- `memory.hop.figcap`: {k} · mirror
- `memory.hop.from`: start from
- `memory.hop.go`: add noise to the letter and settle
- `memory.hop.how.label`: HOPFIELD · HOW IT RECALLS
- `memory.hop.how.title`: A damaged letter rolls down into its valley
- `memory.hop.idle`: press a button to start the memory
- `memory.hop.label`: LIVE · HOPFIELD MEMORY
- `memory.hop.letters`: stored letters (up to 8)
- `memory.hop.mirrorof`: mirror of {k}
- `memory.hop.noise`: settle from random noise
- `memory.hop.plain`: A Hopfield memory stores each pattern as a valley in its energy. A damaged letter starts on the valley's side, and Settling rolls it down to the stored pattern.
- `memory.hop.rule`: store rule
- `memory.hop.rule.hebb`: Hebbian (memory.rs)
- `memory.hop.rule.proj`: projection
- `memory.hop.settling`: settling …
- `memory.hop.small.letters`: The letters show the limit of the simplest rule. With the Hebbian rule and the letters S, E, T and L, recall falls into one blend, because the letters overlap and their backgrounds agree. The projection rule makes each letter an exact fixed point.
- `memory.hop.small.mirror`: The pulls record only which pixels agree with which, so the mirror image of a stored pattern, with every pixel reversed, is a valley as well: E(-s) = E(s). A settle begun from noise often ends in a mirror or in a fake valley; SDMKEYS measured 22.3% fake for 5 random patterns.
- `memory.hop.state`: the memory's current state
- `memory.hop.stored`: stored {k}
- `memory.hop.temp`: temperature
- `memory.hop.title`: Recall a noisy letter
- `memory.how.label`: HOW THESE MEMORIES WORK
- `memory.how.p1`: Every memory on this page works on one principle. A pattern is stored by carving a valley into the energy landscape, and it is recalled by starting nearby and letting the machine settle into that valley.
- `memory.how.p2`: Three memories are shown, and all three run live. In Hopfield's memory the patterns are held in the pulls. In Kanerva's sparse distributed memory they are held in the counters of random hard locations, which are drawn here as lights. The soft version of Kanerva's memory becomes, in its limit, attention.
- `memory.how.title`: One principle, four memories
- `memory.keys.accepted`: ACCEPTED: the padding checks out
- `memory.keys.forced`: forced read: “{text}”
- `memory.keys.how.label`: KEYS · WHAT A KEY HIDES
- `memory.keys.how.title`: The text is hidden, the note is not
- `memory.keys.label`: LIVE · KEYS
- `memory.keys.landed`: landed in the note's valley: overlap {q} · note bits right when read with the true key {p}%
- `memory.keys.note`: the note (up to 59 bytes)
- `memory.keys.plain`: A key turns the note before it is stored, so only an address turned by the same key starts near the note's valley. The key hides what the note says. It does not hide that a note is there.
- `memory.keys.pub`: public memories beside it
- `memory.keys.readwith`: read with the key
- `memory.keys.recall`: recall with this key
- `memory.keys.refused`: REFUSED: the padding does not check out
- `memory.keys.saved`: saved under the key
- `memory.keys.small.stranger`: A stranger who lands in the note's valley holds the turned pattern, and this reads as about 50% of bits right, which is chance. The key protects the text of the note and leaves its existence visible. It is not cryptography.
- `memory.keys.small.turn`: A key is a rotation of the cube: a mask of sign flips together with a shuffle of positions. The note is stored in its turned form, and the holder of the key reads the memory from the turned all-yes padding, which the holder knows. A wrong key turns the result into noise.
- `memory.keys.state`: the memory state, 512 things
- `memory.keys.stranger`: read without the key, starting from noise
- `memory.keys.title`: Store a note under a key
- `memory.lights.default`: a pattern of lights
- `memory.llm.label`: RECORDED · SDM LANGUAGE MODEL
- `memory.llm.lede`: An SDM can also be the whole language model. The model uses the context as an address, reads the store, emits the next token and appends it to the context. SDMLLM trained one at the DeepSeek V4 vocabulary; its own page is THE SDM LANGUAGE MODEL.
- `memory.locM`: hard locations M
- `memory.noise`: noise in the address
- `memory.noisefmt`: {p}% of bits flipped
- `memory.obars.aria`: overlap with each stored pattern
- `memory.of`: {a} of {b}
- `memory.picker.aria`: stored patterns
- `memory.pulls.h`: Content-based reads: the pulls read and top-k
- `memory.pulls.small`: The pulls read wakes a location when its stored counters agree with the current state; the address plays no part. The sealed threshold scaled to the store's density failed, because rows holding one other pattern wake together. Waking exactly the k = p M rows with the largest agreement worked everywhere.
- `memory.race.aria`: the address shares 3 hard locations with its target and 4 with a rival; the rival wins the read
- `memory.race.bars`: reads that failed, by the target's shared hard locations minus the best rival's (M 1e5, r 107, T 5)
- `memory.race.cap`: The stored pattern whose wake set shares the most hard locations with the address wins every bit where it differs.
- `memory.race.ring`: dashed: the address's wake ring
- `memory.race.rival`: rival: shares 4
- `memory.race.smap`: Every S-map variant treats the other patterns as fresh noise on every bit and predicts about 0.1% failure. The RACE predictor, built after the data, treats them as whole patterns and lands close to the measured failures.
- `memory.race.subtitle`: a drawing of the mechanism, not a measurement
- `memory.race.target`: target: shares 3
- `memory.race.title`: The race between whole patterns
- `memory.radius.cap30`: 30% address-noise: P90 capacity against hard locations M, log-log
- `memory.radius.cap40`: 40% address-noise: P90 capacity against hard locations M (cd0.4 activation radius)
- `memory.radius.cd03`: cd0.3 activation radius
- `memory.radius.cd04`: cd0.4 activation radius
- `memory.radius.control`: control · {c}
- `memory.radius.failed`: {a} of {b} failed ({p}%)
- `memory.radius.front10`: P90 at 10% address-noise against the activation radius, log y
- `memory.radius.front30`: P90 at 30% address-noise against the activation radius, log y (zeros left out)
- `memory.radius.full`: Capacity at every activation radius and M (the full tables)
- `memory.radius.h.front`: Capacity against the activation radius, at 10% and 30% address-noise
- `memory.radius.h.race`: Why capacity at 40% address-noise stays near 2: competing stored patterns (post-hoc analysis)
- `memory.radius.label`: RECORDED · SDMRADIUS
- `memory.radius.marks`: The report scores predictions as right, wrong or split; the site's marks read right as hit and wrong as miss.
- `memory.radius.peaks`: The 10% peak sits at the SNR activation radius and the 30% peak at the cd0.3 activation radius, plus or minus 1, at every M. No activation radius lifts 40% above 3.
- `memory.radius.plain`: The activation radius decides how many hard locations a read wakes. A very noisy address needs a wider activation radius to reach its pattern, and a wider radius lets the other patterns' noise in.
- `memory.radius.rx`: activation radius r (bits of 256)
- `memory.radius.small`: A small radius keeps a read clean but wakes few locations; a wide one wakes enough locations to reach an address that is far from its pattern, at the price of more noise from the others. SDMSCALE used one activation radius for every address-noise. SDMRADIUS picks the activation radius that keeps an address D x 256 bits away inside the critical distance and compares it with SDMSCALE's SNR radius.
- `memory.radius.snr`: SNR activation radius (SDMSCALE's)
- `memory.rcoded.label`: RECORDED · SDMCODED
- `memory.rcoded.plain`: A note is stored as bits, so fewer bits per character means more text per memory. The tables measure the compression and how many bytes of text come back from each note.
- `memory.rkeys.label`: RECORDED · SDMKEYS
- `memory.rkeys.plain`: Both memories were filled with random patterns and read from noisy addresses, and the tables count how often a read lands on the right pattern. The rows are the lane's own lines, copied from its report and checked against it by the site's tests.
- `memory.room.aria`: {M} hard locations; {n} are activated
- `memory.rscale.eqsrc`: The equations are the report's own (Bricken and Pehlevan 2021, Eq. 25), from REPORT_SDMSCALE.md.
- `memory.rscale.label`: RECORDED · SDMSCALE
- `memory.rscale.plain`: Capacity here is P90, the largest stored count at which 90% of reads recall. The chart follows it as the memory grows, and the equations are the prediction the lane tested against it.
- `memory.rsoft.bars`: largest stored count with recall >= 50% at 10% address-noise (first number of each row)
- `memory.rsoft.label`: RECORDED · SOFTSDM
- `memory.rsoft.plain`: Each bar gives the largest number of stored patterns a memory still recalls at least half the time from a 10% noisy address. A longer bar holds more.
- `memory.scale.measured`: measured P90 (SNR policy)
- `memory.scale.smap`: S-map prediction
- `memory.scale.thumb`: 0.1 M (Kanerva's thumb rule)
- `memory.scale.title`: capacity at 10% address-noise (P90) against hard locations M, log-log
- `memory.sdm.M`: hard locations M
- `memory.sdm.fire`: activation probability
- `memory.sdm.firefmt`: {p}% (activation radius {r} bits)
- `memory.sdm.how.label`: KANERVA SDM · HOW A READ WORKS
- `memory.sdm.how.title`: The nearby hard locations vote
- `memory.sdm.idle`: read from a noisy address
- `memory.sdm.intro.lead.above`: The lab above is one of these, with 256-bit words.
- `memory.sdm.label`: LIVE · KANERVA SDM
- `memory.sdm.letters`: letters
- `memory.sdm.live`: read {i} · {n} of {M} locations awake (expected about {e} at radius {r})
- `memory.sdm.other`: landed on a different pattern, {name}
- `memory.sdm.patterns`: patterns
- `memory.sdm.plain`: Kanerva's memory scatters many fixed random addresses through the space of patterns. A pattern is written into every address near it. To read, you give an address, and the hard locations near it vote. A stored pattern with some bits flipped is a read-address with address-noise. Kanerva calls it a retrieval address, or a retrieval cue, and the noise in it simply noise.
- `memory.sdm.random`: random (the lanes' setting)
- `memory.sdm.read`: the read
- `memory.sdm.readbtn`: read from a noisy address
- `memory.sdm.recalled`: recalled the pattern the address came from
- `memory.sdm.small`: Each hard location has a fixed random 256-bit address. A write wakes every hard location within the activation radius r of the pattern and adds the pattern to the bit-counters of those hard locations. A read wakes the hard locations near the address and lets them vote, bit by bit. Here there are no mirror images: the bit-counters record the signs of the bits, and they keep no record of how pairs of bits agree.
- `memory.sdm.title`: Hard locations and their bit-counters, drawn as lights
- `memory.sdm.verdict`: {what} · overlap with that pattern {q}
- `memory.sdm.voting`: the woken hard locations vote …
- `memory.soft.T`: stored random patterns
- `memory.soft.busy`: reading …
- `memory.soft.dist`: distance d
- `memory.soft.firing`: activation probability against distance from the address (bits)
- `memory.soft.how.label`: SOFT SDM · HOW THE DIAL WORKS
- `memory.soft.how.title`: A softer edge, and the read becomes attention
- `memory.soft.kernel`: shared activation K(d)/K(0) of two points d bits apart (log)
- `memory.soft.kseries`: kernel · fitted inverse temperature {b}
- `memory.soft.label`: LIVE · SOFT SDM
- `memory.soft.live`: t re-fitted to {t} so the expected firing stays at 5% of 2,000
- `memory.soft.plain`: A soft memory wakes each hard location with a probability that falls smoothly with distance. In the limit its read is a softmax vote over the stored patterns, which is attention.
- `memory.soft.run`: run 10 noisy addresses through both reads
- `memory.soft.series`: softness {s}
- `memory.soft.small`: The dial turns the hard cut-off, which wakes a hard location if it lies within the activation radius, into a logistic one. As the cut-off softens, the kernel between two points flattens, and the read becomes a softmax-weighted vote over the stored patterns (Bricken and Pehlevan 2021). SOFTSDM measured a limit to the correspondence: at softness 1 the two reads agree on 99.2% of bits and both recall 0%, because the matching inverse temperature is too low to pick out one pattern.
- `memory.soft.soft`: softness (units of sqrt(n)/2 bits)
- `memory.soft.stat.agree`: bits the two reads agree on
- `memory.soft.stat.att`: attention read with the fitted temperature
- `memory.soft.stat.sdm`: soft SDM read recalls (overlap >= 0.95)
- `memory.soft.title`: From hard SDM to attention
- `memory.sweep`: sweep {n}
- `memory.top.cap`: the stored letters S, E, T, L
- `memory.top.cap.live`: settling live
- `memory.top.explore`: how an SDM works
- `memory.top.foot`: 16 by 16 lights each · projection rule
- `memory.top.go`: recall a noisy letter
- `memory.top.here`: sdmmemory
- `memory.top.lede`: A pattern is stored by carving a valley into an energy landscape, and recalled by starting nearby and settling into it. Hopfield's memory, Kanerva's sparse distributed memory, its soft version and a note kept under a key all run in this tab.
- `memory.top.panel`: the four stored letters S, E, T and L, each settling out of noise in turn
- `memory.top.sub`: Four memories you can operate, each one settling live.
- `memory.verdict.fake`: a FAKE VALLEY: stable, but no stored pattern (best overlap {q} with {name})
- `memory.verdict.mirror`: landed on the MIRROR IMAGE of {name} (overlap {q})
- `memory.verdict.stored`: landed on {name} (overlap {q})

Press gradient descent (T = 0) and drop the swarm again: every walker stays left. Press anneal: the dial falls to 0 slowly and most walkers end in the deeper well.

- `numbers.gradhow.eq.dist`: Above 0 the walkers settle into this distribution. At T = 1 it is the posterior, exp(-U); hotter flattens it, colder sharpens it. With minibatches this is stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (Welling and Teh 2011).
- `numbers.gradhow.eq.doubt`: Doubt: how much the members disagree. It is the entropy of the averaged prediction minus the average entropy of each member's. One set of parameters has none.
- `numbers.gradhow.eq.energy`: The energy is the loss of every example plus a prior that keeps parameters small. Lower energy means the parameters fit the data better.
- `numbers.gradhow.eq.predict`: A cloud predicts by averaging its members' predictions, not their parameters.
- `numbers.gradhow.eq.step`: The Settling step: move downhill by the step h times the slope, then take a random kick. The temperature T sets the kick's size.
- `numbers.gradhow.eq.t0`: At T = 0 the kick is gone and the step is gradient descent. With a minibatch of B of N examples the slope is estimated and scaled by N/B: stochastic gradient descent.
- `numbers.gradhow.label`: HOW GRADIENT DESCENT IS SETTLING
- `numbers.gradhow.lede1`: Training a model is finding parameters that make its loss small. Call the loss an energy and the parameters numbers on springs, and training is Settling: every parameter slides downhill, and a temperature shakes it.
- `numbers.gradhow.lede2`: At temperature 0 nothing shakes, and the slide is gradient descent: it stops in the nearest valley. Above 0 the walkers keep moving, and over time they visit each set of parameters as often as the evidence supports. That cloud is the Bayesian posterior. Where the cloud's members disagree, the model is unsure, and it can say so.
- `numbers.gradrec.label`: RECORDED · GRADSETTLE
- `numbers.h1`: Numbers
- `numbers.how.label`: HOW THE SPRINGS SOLVE A x = b
- `numbers.how.lede1`: A thing in a settling machine need not be yes or no. It may be a number which slides on a spring. The springs are the matrix A, the pull is the right-hand side b, and the calm point of the whole arrangement is the solution of A x = b.
- `numbers.how.lede2`: Noise of temperature T keeps the numbers moving about the calm point. Their average is then the answer, and their spread gives the inverse of A. The cloud above shows both for the first two numbers.
- `numbers.how.lede3`: Every walker starts at 0, so the first steps are a burn-in for the softest spring, and the averages start after it. The page sets the burn-in to 3 / (h lambda_min) steps, where lambda_min is the smallest eigenvalue of A.
- `numbers.how.plain`: Each number slides on a spring. Settling with a little noise, the springs gather around the solution of A x = b. The average of the cloud gives x, and the spread of the cloud gives the inverse of A.
- `numbers.how.title`: The energy, the step and the two reads

## paper

- `paper.abstract`: Abstract. “We put the lime in the coconut and shake it all about.” The sentence is exact, and this paper does no more than say so at length, which is to say briefly. The coconut is a set of pulls between things that are each yes or no; the lime is a set of leans upon them; to shake is to let each thing in turn take a side with the odds its neighbours give it. What remains when the shaking has gone on long enough is the Boltzmann distribution. Without the lime the coconut has no up, and a tumble lands as readily in the mirror as in the memory; with it, one valley is chosen.

- `paper.s1.h`: The coconut and the lime
- `paper.s1.p1`: The first noticeable fact about a settling machine is that it applies to everything: to horses and to sudoku, to memories and to parity checks, to limes and to coconuts. The nature of the things is perfectly indifferent. Each is a yes or a no, si ∈ '{'−1, +1'}', for i = 1, …, n; and between things there are two relations, and only two. A thing may lean, by hi; a pair may pull, by Jij = Jji, with Jii = 0. We call the leans the lime and the pulls the coconut. The coconut is the structure, and it holds; the lime is the particular, and it tilts. Their conjunction is an energy,
- `paper.s1.p2`: which is low where things agree with their leans and pulled pairs agree with each other. The machine prefers the low places, at temperature T, in exactly the proportion
- `paper.s1.p3`: Z has 2n terms and is never computed. That is the whole reason for shaking.
- `paper.s2.h`: Shaking it all about
- `paper.s2.p1`: It is a profoundly erroneous truism that a machine should think before it answers. The precise opposite is the case. Each thing consults only its local field, the lean it has and the pull it feels,
- `paper.s2.p2`: and takes the side +1 with probability
- `paper.s2.p3`: A sweep redraws every free thing once, in a fresh random order; a held thing is merely left out. Rule (4) is the exact conditional of (2), so (2) is left invariant; and since at T > 0 every arrangement can reach every other, (2) is where the shaking ends [1]. The physicist calls this a heat bath and the engineer a p-bit; it is the same coin. On the three-thing weather model the machine agrees with exact enumeration to 0.0008 in a yes-rate and 0.0005 in a pair average ({n}). To anneal is to shake while cooling [2],
- `paper.s2.p4`: from ten times the temperature to a twentieth of it, keeping the calmest arrangement met on the way. To ask is to count: after a tenth of the sweeps is thrown away, the yes-rate of thing i over K recorded sweeps is
- `paper.s2.p5`: Where there are no pulls the K draws are independent coins, and
- `paper.s2.p6`: so that a picture read in this way has a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 10 log10(K / ⟨g(1 − g)⟩), gaining 3.01 dB at each doubling of K. The law and the machine agree to 0.08 dB (Fig. 2).
- `paper.s3.h`: The tumble, and what stops it
- `paper.s3.p1`: First the general symmetry. Put h = 0. Then
- `paper.s3.p2`: for a pull asks only whether two things agree, and an arrangement turned head over heels agrees with itself exactly as before. The empty coconut has no up. A walk that tumbles lands in a valley exactly as calm as the one it left, and in the long run every thing is yes exactly half the time.
- `paper.s3.p3`: Now the instance which breaks it. Restore the lime: E(−s) − E(s) = 2 Σi hi si, so of each pair of mirror valleys one is lower, and the stumbling walk falls into that one. It does not look; it is held. But a lime is small and a coconut large. In the mean-field reading at T = 1, mi = tanh(hi + Σj Jij mj), on a square grid of z = 4 neighbours, the chosen state is stable only while
- `paper.s3.p4`: Beyond it the neighbours alone hold a region either way up, and the lime is outvoted. The film player shows it: with pulls of 0.4 and 0.6 every arm plays the horse at {value}, its mirror image, where the same frames with no pulls reach 15.60 to 27.71 dB. The memory shows it too.
- `paper.s4.h`: Memory, and the size of the house
- `paper.s4.p1`: A Hopfield memory [3] is a coconut with no lime. It stores a pattern ξ by
- `paper.s4.p2`: recalls by rule (4) with no leans, and holds about 0.138 n patterns [4], which is 35 when n = 256: a small place holds only so many houses. Since (−ξ)(−ξ)T = ξ ξT, every memory is stored with its mirror, and from noise the machine finds the mirror more often than the memory: {value} ({n}).

- `paper.s4.p4`: a write adds the pattern to the counters of every woken location, Cm ← f Cm + ξ, and a read is their vote,
- `paper.s4.p5`: The mirror of a cue wakes other locations, so the mirror is not recalled: {value}, from the same noise. Let a location wake with probability 1/(1 + e−(t − dm)/w) instead, and in the soft limit the read becomes
- `paper.s4.p6`: which is attention [6, 7]. At the inverse temperature this machine affords, it is too flat to separate one pattern from another: {value} ({n}).
- `paper.s5.h`: The lime and the coconut, learned
- `paper.s5.p1`: The lime and the coconut need not be given; they may be grown [8]. The log-likelihood of examples under (2) has gradient
- `paper.s5.p2`: and likewise for hi with ⟨si⟩. The fit is finished when the shaken machine agrees with the world on every thing and every pair. A machine with 64 hidden things, so grown (by contrastive divergence, which estimates the second average by a short shake), reads binarised digits at 93.8%, against 91.2% for logistic regression and 7.8% when the labels are shuffled ({n}).

- `poem.page.exp.label`: THE POEM LAB · EXPERIMENTS
- `poem.page.exp.lede`: Each card builds its own small memory from an excerpt of the poem (the card says which) and measures one thing. They run one after another in a second worker once this grid comes into view, so the first results take a few seconds and the last a minute or two.
- `poem.page.exp.title`: Sixteen ways to remember a poem, each run live in this tab
- `poem.page.film.label`: THE POEM LAB · THE FILM
- `poem.page.film.title`: A memory remembering the poem, as a silent picture of settles
- `poem.page.how.bind`: Multiplying by the address before storing binds the character to its context. A write made at the same address reads back as its code; writes made far away read back as noise, which sums toward zero. Without that binding a frequent character such as the space drowned every other one.
- `poem.page.how.errdriven`: The memory writes a character only when it would read it back wrong (error-driven), and passes over the poem up to {passes} times. Experiment 4 compares this with writing everything.
- `poem.page.how.greedy`: The recital is greedy: each recalled character joins the context for the next. One error makes a context the memory never saw, so the recital is only as good as its weakest step. The rollout section measures exactly that.
- `poem.page.how.hybrid`: The settle hybrid holds the next six characters at once and resamples them with a Gibbs schedule whose temperature falls, scoring each choice by how confidently the memory reads the characters after it.
- `poem.page.how.label`: HOW THE MEMORY WORKS
- `poem.page.how.lede1`: The memory holds {m} hard locations, each a random 256-bit address with 256 counters. To store the poem it walks through it one character at a time.
- `poem.page.how.lede2`: The 48 characters before each position are hashed into a 256-bit address. Every location within Hamming distance {radius} of that address (about 80 of them) adds the next character's random code of +1 and -1 to its counters, multiplied entry by entry by the address read as +1 and -1.
- `poem.page.how.lede3`: To recall, the memory forms the address of the context it has, sums the counters of the locations near it, multiplies by the same address again, and picks the character whose code the sum resembles most.
- `poem.page.how.title`: Kanerva's sparse distributed memory, used as a recitation machine

- `puzzles.colouring.caption`: Each node takes one of three colours, and no edge may join two nodes of the same colour. An edge that breaks this rule is drawn in red. SETTLEZOO measured n=40 at 10,000 sweeps coloured in 98% of seeds and n=80 in 62%.

- `puzzles.factor.caption1`: Column k of the long multiplication p x q, counted from the right, shows the bit products that land in it, the carry bits that leave it (rose when yes) and the carry bits that arrive. A column must equal N's bit plus twice what it carries on.
- `puzzles.factor.caption2`: Every answer is checked by multiplying, never by the energy. ZOOHARD found that nearly all the successes come from the calmest-so-far record: the warm walk passes through the answer and then freezes into another valley. A prime can never be factored, so the two prime controls must always fail.
- `puzzles.factor.chart`: energy while cooling: now and calmest so far

- `puzzles.how.check`: A low energy is not a proof that an answer is right, so the decoded answer is always checked by the puzzle's own rules. Each puzzle writes its rules as costs, with y = (1 + s) / 2 a thing that is 1 when yes:
- `puzzles.how.constants`: In the factoring cost z_ij stands for the product p_i q_j and λ = 2. Sudoku, the nonogram, colouring and n queens use A = B = C = 1; the given reward G is a slider on the sudoku bench. Factoring cools with ZOOHARD's temperature rule, T = the largest lean or pull / 10.
- `puzzles.how.intro`: Every broken rule costs energy, so the arrangement that breaks no rule is the calmest one. The machine is cooled slowly, and the calmest arrangement it passes is read back and checked in plain code.
- `puzzles.how.label`: HOW A PUZZLE IS SOLVED
- `puzzles.how.labels`: On the colouring board the three node colours are only labels for the puzzle's three colours.

- `puzzles.nonohow.h`: The nonogram: why the encoding decides it
- `puzzles.nonohow.p1`: A nonogram gives each row and column its runs: "3 1" means a run of 3, a gap, then a run of 1. The machine has a thing per cell, and a few more things per run that say where the run starts.
- `puzzles.nonohow.p1b`: The first way to write a start is one thing per possible start, with exactly one of them yes. Moving a run one cell then takes two flips, the old start off and the new one on, and the step between them costs energy, so the cooling machine freezes with runs in the wrong places.
- `puzzles.nonohow.p2`: The domain wall writes a start as a row of "past here" bits that read 1 1 0 0 0: the start is where the ones stop. Moving a run one cell is one flip, and every rule stays a sum over pairs. On the survey's 50 seeds the 10x10 duck went from 0 of 50 solved to 50 of 50 at the same 4,000 sweeps.

- `puzzles.sudoku.notes.p1`: The puzzle is written as n x n x n yes-or-no things (4,096 for 16x16), one for each combination of row, column and digit. Each cell, and each digit in each row, column and box, is pushed toward exactly one yes, and each given earns a reward G. The machine is then cooled, and the calmest arrangement it passes is read back as a grid and checked by the rules in plain code.
- `puzzles.sudoku.notes.p2`: The 4x4 and 9x9 puzzles are the ones in settle-rs/examples/sudoku.settle. For example, SETTLEZOO measured the 9x9 easy puzzle solved in 94% of 50 seeds at 50,000 sweeps, and in 32% at 10,000. The larger puzzles are made here: a solved grid by the standard pattern, relabelled and shuffled by the puzzle seed, then emptied down to the chosen share of givens. They are not checked for a single solution, so a puzzle may have several, and the check accepts any grid that keeps every rule and every given.

- `relax.lede`: Every picture on this page is a field of p-bits settling out of noise into two cartoon figures: Richard Simmons, the aerobics instructor, and David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH), the creator of Ruby on Rails. Nothing is drawn as a vector; each figure appears because thousands of lights lean toward it and pull on their neighbours. The workout is noise, the cool-down is annealing (lowering the temperature on a schedule), and relaxing is Settling.

The right one drops to 0.45 at once. In this picture the pose is the only valley, so both arrive; watch how differently they get there.

- `relax.script.again.dhh.1`: Same four moves, new pose. That is a convention.
- `relax.script.again.m.1`: The heat climbs from {from} back to {to} over {frames} sweeps, the hold is released, and the next pose is stored. The home room reheats from 0.45 to 3.0 over 20 frames the same way.
- `relax.script.again.rich.1`: And when the song ends? We warm up and we do it AGAIN, with a new pose. Every class the same four moves: jiggle, work, cool, settle.
- `relax.script.again.rich.2`: I love you all. Drink some water. Settle petal.
- `relax.script.again.term`: the reheat
- `relax.script.ask.dhh.1`: So the answer is a rate, not a yes. I can live with that.
- `relax.script.ask.m.1`: ask :rain reports the share of recorded samples with rain yes. Held wet grass, 40,000 samples at temperature 1: rain 63.9%, rain and sprinkler 31.6%, rain or sprinkler 95.7%.
- `relax.script.ask.m.2`: The live class asks the lights the pose wants off, in the row beside the held band and in a row far from it, and counts how often each says yes over the stretch's sweeps.
- `relax.script.ask.m.3`: An asked answer carries sampling noise that shrinks with more sweeps; the exact answer is shown beside the live one for the weather model.
- `relax.script.ask.rich.1`: Last stretch, and it's a QUESTION. You don't ask a class "are you tired?" ONCE. You watch them for a whole song and you COUNT.
- `relax.script.ask.rich.2`: How many counts was that light on? Out of how many? THAT'S your answer. Not yes, not no, honey: HOW OFTEN.
- `relax.script.ask.rich.3`: The row next to the held ones says yes more often than the row way over there. Nobody told them to. They felt it.
- `relax.script.ask.term`: reading a marginal
- `relax.script.cooldown.dhh.1`: I like a slow cool-down. Fewer surprises at the end.
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.1`: The live class cools geometrically from T = {hot} to {calm} over {frames} sweeps, the same ratio every sweep. The home room does the same over about eight seconds.
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.2`: settle-rs anneal: T(t) = 10 T x 0.005t/(S-1). "The core anneal cools from 10T to T/20 and keeps the calmest arrangement visited; the range is fixed at 200x."
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.3`: Slow cool-downs solve more. 4x4 sudoku, share of 50 anneals that found a valid grid: 28% at 100 sweeps, 88% at 500, 100% at 2,000; random guessing 0%. 9x9 easy: 4% / 32% / 94% at 2,000 / 10,000 / 50,000 sweeps.
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.4`: For decoding codes the lane found the schedule itself is the lever: "What seems to matter is the schedule of the effective odd-check price: soft while hot, hard while cold."
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.5`: Honest note: in this little class the picture is the only valley, so dropping the heat at once also settles (the page's tests check it). A slow cool-down pays where there are many valleys, as in sudoku.
- `relax.script.cooldown.rich.1`: Okay. Okay, babies. Now we come down. Not all at once! You never stop a class dead, you'll CRASH. We bring the heat down a little... and a little... and a little. Every count a bit cooler than the one before.
- `relax.script.cooldown.rich.2`: Three... two and a half... two... one and a half... Let the picture come up out of the noise. Don't grab it. Let it come to you, honey.
- `relax.script.cooldown.rich.3`: You know why I take my time here? Because the people who rush the cool-down end up in the wrong position and they STAY there. The slow ones find the right one. Every time I have ever watched.
- `relax.script.cooldown.term`: annealing
- `relax.script.head.instructor`: THE INSTRUCTOR AND DHH
- `relax.script.head.machine`: THE MACHINE
- `relax.script.hold.dhh.1`: Holding a row is like pinning a version. Everything else moves around it.
- `relax.script.hold.m.1`: hold :wet_grass, :yes fixes a thing. A held thing is left out of the sweep's list of free things, so it never moves.
- `relax.script.hold.m.2`: The live class holds a two-row band yes and raises the heat to T = {T}, so the free lights visibly move and the held ones cannot.
- `relax.script.hold.m.3`: Holding changes the answers: in the weather model, rain is yes 9.0% of the time with nothing held and 63.8% with wet grass held yes.
- `relax.script.hold.rich.1`: Stretch time!! Partners!! You two rows in the middle: somebody HOLDS you. You are ON and you STAY on, no matter what. Everybody else, warm up a touch and feel who's being held.
- `relax.script.hold.rich.2`: See that? The held ones don't twitch. Not once. And everybody near them leans in a little. That's what holding does, honey: you don't move the held ones, the held ones move the ROOM.
- `relax.script.hold.rich.3`: And it works on a question too! You see the grass is wet? HOLD that. Now ask the room about the rain.
- `relax.script.hold.term`: clamping
- `relax.script.nowtag`:  · the class is here
- `relax.script.relax.dhh.1`: It settled. Ship it.
- `relax.script.relax.m.1`: Temperature T = {calm}, beta = {b}. The same fully agreeing light now says yes with chance {p}.
- `relax.script.relax.m.2`: Overlap q = (1/n) sum of ti si: +1 is the picture exactly, -1 its mirror, 0 unrelated. It is the live percentage above.
- `relax.script.relax.m.3`: A valley is an arrangement where every single flip costs energy: dEi = 2 si (hi + sumj Jij sj) > 0 for every i.
- `relax.script.relax.m.4`: Settled is not frozen. The machine keeps sampling; a light still flips now and then, and that is what the next stretch reads.
- `relax.script.relax.rich.1`: ...and here we are. Temperature under a half. Nobody's pushing anybody.
- `relax.script.relax.rich.2`: Every light is doing what its lean says and what its neighbours say, and for once they all say the SAME thing, so it just... stays. Look at the two of us, babies. Nobody switched those lights on by hand. You settled into it.
- `relax.script.relax.rich.3`: You can still wiggle a toe. Once in a while somebody wiggles. That's fine. That's alive. Breathe in, breathe out. Settle petal.
- `relax.script.relax.term`: settling

- `relax.script.warmup.dhh.1`: I start wherever the room starts. Convention over configuration.
- `relax.script.warmup.m.1`: In the live class the warm-up runs at beta 0 (infinite temperature), so every light says yes with chance {p} whatever its lean and neighbours say.
- `relax.script.warmup.m.2`: settle-rs starts every free thing at a coin flip.
- `relax.script.warmup.m.3`: A settle burns in a tenth of its sweeps and records nothing from them: "Burn in a tenth of sweeps, then record one arrangement per sweep."
- `relax.script.warmup.m.4`: The start hardly matters: "a p-bit forgets its start in about one sweep", and a warm start bought at most about 1.4 dB on the film grid.
- `relax.script.warmup.rich.1`: OKAY BABIES, ON YOUR FEET!! Nobody knows the routine yet and THAT IS FINE, honey!! Every one of you is a little light going on, off, on, off, like a coin in a tumble dryer!! Flip! Flop! Flip!
- `relax.script.warmup.rich.2`: And listen to me, sweetheart: I do NOT care where you start. Start on, start off, start in the wrong corner of the room. One good sweep and your body forgets it anyway!!
- `relax.script.warmup.rich.3`: And the first few reps DON'T COUNT!! We are loosening up!! Nobody is keeping score in the warm-up, not even me, and I keep score of EVERYTHING!!
- `relax.script.warmup.term`: every light a fair coin
- `relax.script.who.dhh`: DHH:
- `relax.script.who.richard`: RICHARD:
- `relax.script.workout.dhh.1`: Lean 0.9, pull 0.3. Sensible defaults, Richard. I would not change them.
- `relax.script.workout.m.1`: Temperature T = {T}, so beta = 1/T = {b}. The home room's hot phase uses the same {T}.
- `relax.script.workout.m.2`: The update rule: P(si = yes) = (1 + tanh(beta Ii)) / 2, with Ii = hi + J times the sum of the neighbours. Lean h = {lean} toward the picture, pull J = {pull} to four neighbours.
- `relax.script.workout.m.3`: One sweep updates every free light once, in a fresh random order. That is exact Gibbs sampling.
- `relax.script.workout.m.4`: A light whose lean and all four neighbours agree has input {agree}; at T {T} it says yes with chance {p}.
- `relax.script.workout.m.5`: Counting reps: with no pulls, each doubling of sweeps buys 3.01 dB. Measured on the Muybridge horse, 150x100: 15.60 / 18.59 / 21.68 / 24.72 / 27.71 dB at 5 / 10 / 20 / 40 / 80 sweeps.
- `relax.script.workout.m.6`: Form check: the film grid is stable only while J z (1 - m2) < 1; with z = 4, that is J < 0.25 at m = 0. Above it the grid flipped to its mirror image, scoring 1.9 to 4.1 dB.
- `relax.script.workout.rich.1`: NOW WE MOVE!! Temperature THREE, babies!! AND ONE, two, three, four, five, six, seven, EIGHT!!
- `relax.script.workout.rich.2`: Every light gets two voices in its ear: its own lean, "I think I belong in the picture," and its four NEIGHBOURS, "come with us, honey!" At this heat the voices are small and the jiggle is BIG. Do you see the two of us in there? A little? A LITTLE!! That's a workout!!
- `relax.script.workout.rich.3`: Count your reps!! Every time you DOUBLE the reps you get three more decibels of picture. Three! Every time! I have never had a class that consistent in my LIFE!!
- `relax.script.workout.rich.4`: And form check, sweetheart: hold your neighbour's hand, don't CRUSH it!! Pull too hard and the whole row flips into the MIRROR, everybody doing the move backwards, very committed, very wrong!!
- `relax.script.workout.term`: sweeps at T = {T}

## repo

- `repo.kanerva.head`: It’s like Redis! But for Sparse Distributed Memory!
- `repo.kanerva.install`: test KANERVA from its repository
- `repo.kanerva.kicker`: KANERVA · SPARSE DISTRIBUTED MEMORY
- `repo.kanerva.line`: Sparse Distributed Memory: write patterns, read them back from a read-address, a copy with some of its bits flipped.
- `repo.kanerva.note`: A Rust crate with no dependencies. Its home is the {label} .
- `repo.kanerva.para`: KANERVA is the toolbox for Sparse Distributed Memory that SETTLE uses. You write long patterns of bits into a few thousand hard locations, each pattern spread over the hard locations whose addresses lie near it, then read one back from a read-address, a copy of it with some of its bits flipped: the nearby hard locations vote, bit by bit, and the stored pattern comes back. It is named for Pentti Kanerva, who described the memory in 1988.
- `repo.kanerva.sub`: It’s so awesome!! Wow!
- `repo.kanerva.who`: the navigator, on KANERVA
- `repo.mcp.head`: This is absurd! People will need an MCP to explain or use this nonsense!
- `repo.mcp.install`: install settle-mcp and add it to Claude Code
- `repo.mcp.kicker`: MCP · THE SETTLE MCP SERVER
- `repo.mcp.line`: A Model Context Protocol server: docs and help, setup, and tools for SETTLE and KANERVA.
- `repo.mcp.note`: Node 18 or newer, two dependencies, MIT. Its home is the {label} .
- `repo.mcp.para`: settle-mcp lets an assistant work with SETTLE and KANERVA. It has three parts. Docs and help: what everything is named and how it works, with nothing installed. Setup: check the machine, then fetch, build and verify SETTLE and KANERVA in a folder you choose, showing every command before it runs. Usage: run SETTLE programs, store and recall with a sparse distributed memory, and run KANERVA. Its docs are built from this website.
- `repo.mcp.sub`: Imagine we want to use it from scratch.
- `repo.mcp.who`: the navigator, on settle-mcp
- `repo.note.access`: While it is private, a clone needs access: ask for it.
- `repo.private`: private repository
- `repo.public`: public repository
- `repo.settle.head`: It’s like Ruby on Rails! But for Settling - p‑bits annealing downhill!
- `repo.settle.install`: build SETTLE from its repository
- `repo.settle.kicker`: SETTLE · THE PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE
- `repo.settle.line`: A small language for settling machines.
- `repo.settle.note`: The binary is target/release/settle. The code is the {label} .
- `repo.settle.para`: SETTLE is a small language for settling machines. You name a few yes-or-no things, say how much each one leans toward yes and how much pairs of them pull toward agreeing, then let the machine settle: every thing keeps flipping like a weighted coin until the whole arrangement calms down. You ask a question by counting how often a thing came up yes. The same few words answer probability questions, clean up pictures, recall memories, solve puzzles and learn from examples.
- `repo.settle.sub`: It’s awesome!
- `repo.settle.who`: the navigator, on SETTLE
- `repo.settletext.head`: Let people not give a whit about the theory and just render text, and render backgrounds, using this effect.
- `repo.settletext.install`: test settle-text from its repository
- `repo.settletext.kicker`: SETTLE TEXT · THE REACT COMPONENT LIBRARY
- `repo.settletext.line`: React components that render text, images and vectors as a live settle of lights. You supply the words and the font.
- `repo.settletext.note`: React 18 or newer as a peer, settle-see as its one dependency, no licence chosen yet. Its home is the {label} .
- `repo.settletext.para`: settle-text is four React components. SettleText takes your words and your font and renders them as a grid of neon lights that comes out of noise, rests, and breathes now and then. SettleImage does the same for a picture, by brightness, with a dither for photos and the picture’s own colours per light if you want them. SettleVector takes an SVG, by ink. SettleBackground puts any of them behind your content, drawn once and then costing nothing. You choose the colour, the size, the resolution and the glow; the physics is settle-see’s and you never meet it.
- `repo.settletext.sub`: This is a way in for the visual designers, or programmers who do not care about theory.
- `repo.settletext.who`: the navigator, on settle-text

## sdmexplore

- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.aria`: Test bits per byte of every recorded arm, one dot per seed. Lower is better.

- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.qwen5`: transformer (qwen), 5 seeds

- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.s0`: SDM model, S0 store
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.subtitle`: TEST bits per byte, one dot per seed; lower is better
- `sdmexplore.chat.dots.title`: Every arm the two lanes measured
- `sdmexplore.chat.loop.aria`: The SDM language model's loop: context, features, query, store, soft read, update, readout, next token, appended to the context.
- `sdmexplore.chat.loop.foot`: the sampled token joins the context, and the loop runs again
- `sdmexplore.chat.loop.mem`: the memory: keys say where, values say what
- `sdmexplore.chat.loop.subtitle`: each sampled token joins the context and the pass runs again
- `sdmexplore.chat.loop.title`: The loop, one token at a time
- `sdmexplore.chat.p.how`: SDMCHAT is a language model in which a Kanerva-style memory takes the place of attention. At each step it turns the recent text into a query, the query wakes a few of 3,600 stored locations, and the woken locations' values are added into a working vector. That vector becomes a score for each of the 129,280 tokens of the DeepSeek V4 vocabulary; one token is sampled, joins the text, and the loop runs again.
- `sdmexplore.chat.p.lede`: SDMCHAT is a language model whose attention is replaced by a learned Kanerva-style memory. Two lanes measured it, and the memory added nothing net to the model.
- `sdmexplore.chat.p.read`: The memory's read is the soft read of the experiments below, with one change: instead of a fixed radius it wakes the 64 locations whose keys score highest and lets each fire with a sigmoid of its score above the 32nd best. A key says where a memory sits; a value says what it holds. Both are learned by gradient descent, with the rest of the model.
- `sdmexplore.chat.p.result`: The store first cost the model 0.017 to 0.025 bits per byte against the same model with the store removed. Once the query's gradient was stopped, the store tied the control. It was heavily used and added nothing net.
- `sdmexplore.chat.precise.from`: From {src} §4, verbatim:
- `sdmexplore.chat.precise.p`: n is RMS normalisation, BN a batch norm on the query, k_m_hat a unit-length key, v_m a value row, k = 32. The working vector x then passes a SwiGLU block, and the logits are n(x) against the tied embedding E, one row per token. Bits per byte is the summed negative log probability of each next token, in bits, divided by the bytes of text: it does not depend on the tokenizer. The vocabulary, from the model's own file: {vocab} The embedding table holds {embed}
- `sdmexplore.chat.precise.tag`: THE PRECISE VERSION
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.context.name`: the context
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.context.sub`: tokens so far
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.features.name`: features
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.features.sub`: last 4 + 2 averages
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.next.name`: next token
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.next.sub`: one of 129,280
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.query.name`: the query
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.read.name`: the soft read
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.read.sub`: top 64, 32nd = theta
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.readout.name`: readout
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.readout.sub`: SwiGLU, then E^T
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.store.name`: the store
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.store.sub`: 3,600 keys, values
- `sdmexplore.chat.stage.update.sub`: twice: 2 hops
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.aria`: The soft top-k read on 128 illustrative scores: the best 64 are kept and fire with weight sigmoid((s - theta) / {soft}).
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.below`: below here: not considered
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.cap`: An illustration of the rule, computed here on made-up scores. A small softness makes the read a hard top 32; a large one gives all 64 nearly weight one half. The model itself runs on SDMCHAT.
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.scores`: SCORES s_m, sorted (illustration: 128 random scores, not the model's)
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.softness`: softness
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.subtitle`: the store's activation rule, drawn on 128 random scores
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.sum`: sum of weights {sum}, divided by k = 32 in the update
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.theta`: theta = the 32nd best score
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.title`: The soft top-k read
- `sdmexplore.chat.topk.weight`: FIRING WEIGHT w_m = sigmoid((s_m - theta) / softness)
- `sdmexplore.chip.exp`: six live experiments
- `sdmexplore.chip.locations`: 64 hard locations
- `sdmexplore.chip.radius`: activation radius 12
- `sdmexplore.chip.words`: 32-bit words
- `sdmexplore.ex.close.p`: Kanerva’s two comparisons. A computer’s random access memory: one address wakes one location; here one address wakes several, and the several share what they hold. And the cerebellum: he reads its granule cells as the hard locations and the synapses on its Purkinje cells as the bit-counters, a memory nature built. The machine below is this memory with every part drawn and every control live.
- `sdmexplore.ex.kicker`: the explainer · in Kanerva’s words
- `sdmexplore.ex.lede`: Pentti Kanerva published this memory in 1988. {n}-bit words, {M} hard locations, three stored patterns, :cat :dog :owl.
- `sdmexplore.ex.quote.ref`: Kanerva, lecture {id} at {time}
- `sdmexplore.ex.s1.p`: Everything the memory stores or reads is a pattern of bits, here the {n} bits of :cat, drawn as lights: lit for +1, dark for -1. Kanerva’s own examples use a thousand or ten thousand bits. A thousand-bit word has 2 to the power 1,000 possible values, far too many for a memory to keep one location for each.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s1.title`: A word is a long row of bits
- `sdmexplore.ex.s2.p`: An ordinary memory has one location for every address. This one has {M} hard locations. Each has a random {n}-bit address, chosen once and kept, and a row of {n} bit-counters that start at zero. The stars are the three stored patterns; each dot is one hard location, drawn near the patterns its address resembles.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s2.title`: The memory builds a few hard locations, at random addresses, and never moves them
- `sdmexplore.ex.s3.p`: No hard location has exactly the word’s address. So the word wakes every hard location within the activation radius, {r} bits here, and is added to their bit-counters: +1 where the word has a lit bit, -1 where it has a dark one. Writing :cat woke {k} of the {M}; the other patterns went to other hard locations.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s3.title`: A write spreads the word over the hard locations near it
- `sdmexplore.ex.s4.p`: Give the memory an address. The hard locations within {r} bits of it wake, their rows of bit-counters are added up bit by bit, and each bit of the answer is the sign of its column. Shown: the {k} rows woken by a noisy copy of :cat (rose +, indigo -), the column sums, and the answer underneath.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s4.title`: A read lets the nearby hard locations vote
- `sdmexplore.ex.s5.p`: That copy of :cat had {flipped} of {n} bits flipped. It woke {shared} of the {k} hard locations :cat was written to, and their votes outweighed the rest: one read left {off} bits wrong, and reading again from each answer reached :cat in {rounds} reads and then stopped changing. The chart counts the bits that differ from :cat after each read. An address far from every stored word wakes hard locations that agree on nothing, and the answer is noise, which is the memory’s way of saying it does not know.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s5.title`: A noisy address still finds the word, read by read
- `sdmexplore.ex.src`: Every quote is a line of YouTube’s auto-caption, verbatim and unpunctuated, with the lecture and the time it was said. The condensed version of the lectures, with every quote, is {doc}; the transcripts themselves stay in the research vault and are not shipped.
- `sdmexplore.ex.title`: What a sparse distributed memory is

- `sdmexplore.exp.keys.before.legend`: length byte (amber) · the text's bits · padding, all +1 (ice): before the key turns it

- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.again`: START THE COUNT AGAIN
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.aria`: How far each read travels from its address. Noisy addresses of stored patterns travel little; never-stored addresses travel far. The travel rule refuses anything past {h} bits.
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.axis`: bits the read travelled from its address
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.counting`: counting
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.h`: h = {h}: an answer farther than this from its address is refused
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.never`: never-stored random addresses: land on one {land}, accepted {acc} (the rule allows 1%)
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.reads`: {n} reads
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.rule`: h(T) is the largest h with 1 - (1 - P[Bin(32, 1/2) <= h])^3 <= 0.01, so h = {h}.
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.stored`: 10% noisy addresses of stored patterns: land on one {land}, accepted {acc}
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.subtitle`: violet: noisy addresses of stored patterns · red: addresses never stored · dashed: the refusal distance h
- `sdmexplore.exp.refuse.title`: How far each read travels from its address
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.aria`: The chance a hard location is activated against its distance from the address, at softness {soft}. Expected hard locations activated for this address: {e}.
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.axis`: distance d from the address (bars: where the 64 locations sit for a 10% noisy :cat)
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.exact`: exact, computed here
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.expected`: expected firing for this address {e} (hard: {h})
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.hard`: softness 0 is the hard ball: {n} hard locations wake
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.radius`: activation radius 12, hard
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.softness`: softness s
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.subtitle`: the soft ball of one hard location, at the chosen softness
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.title`: Firing chance against distance
- `sdmexplore.exp.soft.tw`: t {tv} · w {wv} · temperature 2w {tw}
- `sdmexplore.exp.still`: still, reduced motion
- `sdmexplore.page.chat.title`: How the SDM language model works, from its reports
- `sdmexplore.page.exp.label`: EXPERIMENTS · SETTLE x KANERVA
- `sdmexplore.page.exp.p`: Each experiment runs the memory in this tab and sets the result beside a recorded or sealed number. Together they show where the memory holds, where it melts, and how a key or a refusal rule changes what a read returns.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp.title`: Six experiments on the memory, run in this tab
- `sdmexplore.page.exp1.p`: Start from a 10% noisy address, read 30 times at one temperature, and count how many of the last ten reads sit on the pattern. A tied bit (sum exactly 0) is a fair coin at any heat. With a self-pull of 0.5 it leans to keep its value, which is the T = 0 tie rule written as a lean.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp1.title`: The memory melts as it warms
- `sdmexplore.page.exp2.p`: Kanerva's size: 256 bits, 2,000 locations, radius 112. Random patterns are written one at a time. After each, 48 stored patterns are read back from noisy addresses. The S-map (Bricken and Pehlevan's signal-to-noise map, ported from KANERVA) predicts the largest count that still converges. The lanes recorded where recall first fell under 90%.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp2.title`: How many patterns fit, against the S-map's prediction
- `sdmexplore.page.exp3.p`: In the small memory almost every address falls into some stored pattern, so landing on one proves nothing. The travel rule asks how far the answer moved from its address. A stored pattern within h bits of a random address is unlikely, so an answer farther than h is refused.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp3.title`: Refusing an address that was never stored
- `sdmexplore.page.exp4.p`: settle-rs keeps the bit-counters as pulls between 64 hard location things and 32 data things. Settle that model and each hard location is itself a p-bit: it switches on when the data agree with what it holds, and the data take the vote of the hard locations that are on. At temperature 0 this is the {via} read.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp4.title`: The hard locations as settling p-bits
- `sdmexplore.page.exp5.p`: A soft SDM lets a hard location fire with a chance that falls with its distance d. That chance is the p-bit rule with lean t minus d at temperature 2w. As the softness grows the edge of the ball blurs, and t is re-fitted so the expected number activation stays the same. At the soft end the read approaches attention.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp5.title`: In a soft SDM a hard location is a p-bit leaning by its distance
- `sdmexplore.page.exp6.p`: A key names a turn of the cube: a sign flip on every bit and a shuffle of positions. The note, its length byte and a padding of +1s are turned and stored; nothing else of the text is kept. The key's address is the turned all-+1 list, which agrees with the note on the padding only. So a short note is found, and a long one leaves the address too far away for an SDM's narrow basins.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp6.title`: A note only its key can find
- `sdmexplore.page.hero.aria`: the three stored 32-bit patterns, :cat :dog :owl, settling out of noise one after another
- `sdmexplore.page.how.label`: HOW IT WORKS · ONE IDEA AT A TIME
- `sdmexplore.page.how.title`: Who wakes, how they vote, and a warm read
- `sdmexplore.page.machine.label`: 1 · LIVE · THE MACHINE
- `sdmexplore.page.machine.line`: Each hard location has a fixed random 32-bit address and 32 bit-counters. The three stars are the stored patterns, :cat :dog :owl, drawn at their distance from the address.
- `sdmexplore.page.machine.p`: Pick a start on the left: a stored pattern with some of its bits flipped (a noisy address), a word that was never stored, or pure noise. The hard locations within 12 bits of the address wake and vote, and the answer appears on the right. Press RUN and the answer becomes the next address, until the read gives back what it was given. Press an address bit to flip it, or hold it.
- `sdmexplore.page.machine.title`: The machine: an address, 64 hard locations, an answer
- `sdmexplore.page.output.line`: The page's JavaScript machine prints these six lines byte for byte ({test}, X1), and the test re-runs the binary when it is present.
- `sdmexplore.page.output.p`: Recorded with {bin}. Read the last two lines: an address that was never written (:zebra) and pure noise both come back as :cat. A memory this small has basins that cover most of the cube. Experiment 3 below is the remedy.
- `sdmexplore.page.output.title`: What the release binary printed
- `sdmexplore.page.prog.label`: THE PROGRAM · SETTLE
- `sdmexplore.page.prog.title`: Sixteen lines, and what the binary printed
- `sdmexplore.page.program.line`: The addresses come from the memory's name and seed (FNV-1a of {name}), each pattern from its name, and each noisy address from its seed. So the drawing above holds the same 64 addresses, the same three patterns and the same bit-counters.
- `sdmexplore.page.program.p`: Sixteen lines build the machine on this page. The program's word for the address you read from is {ra}. Kanerva calls it the retrieval address, or the retrieval cue. {an} flips a tenth of its bits, which Kanerva calls noise in the address.
- `sdmexplore.page.program.title`: The same memory, as a SETTLE program
- `sdmexplore.page.vote.line`: A write adds the pattern, as +1 and -1, to every woken hard location's bit-counters. A read adds the woken bit-counters bit by bit; a sum of exactly 0 keeps the bit it had.
- `sdmexplore.page.vote.p`: THE VOTE panel under the diagram shows it. Each woken hard location is a row of 32 bit-counters, rose for positive and indigo for negative. The sums are the bars; the sign of each bar is one bit of the answer. The amber ring marks a tie.
- `sdmexplore.page.vote.title`: The vote: add the bit-counters, keep the sign
- `sdmexplore.page.wake.line`: The dashed circle in the diagram is this set. Move the address and the circle keeps its size while the hard locations slide in and out of it.
- `sdmexplore.page.wake.p`: The distance between two words is the number of bits where they differ. A hard location wakes when its address is within the activation radius. With 64 random addresses and activation radius 12, about five wake for any address.
- `sdmexplore.page.wake.title`: Who wakes: every hard location within 12 bits
- `sdmexplore.page.warm.line`: Given the address, the 32 bits are independent, so the exact chance that one read lands on a pattern is the product of the 32 chances; the diagram prints it and counts 400 reads beside it. This read picks hard locations by address and votes with bit-counters, so it is not a settle of one energy; experiment 4 shows the version that is.
- `sdmexplore.page.warm.p`: Turn the temperature up in the diagram. At T = 0 a bit takes the sign of its sum. Warm, it is a weighted coin, SETTLE's p-bit: a big sum still almost always wins, a small sum is a near toss-up. The memory holds its pattern when warm and melts when hot.
- `sdmexplore.page.warm.title`: A warm read: each bit becomes a p-bit

## sdmintro

- `sdmintro.p`: A sparse distributed memory is Kanerva’s memory for long words of bits. It has a few thousand hard locations, each at a fixed random address with a row of bit-counters. A write adds a word to the hard locations near its address. A read wakes the hard locations near the read-address and lets their bit-counters vote, bit by bit, so a noisy address still finds the stored word. The five-step explainer, with pictures, is at the top of SDM EXPLORE.

## settletext

- `settletext.claim`: Your words, your font, as a settle of lights. One line of React.
- `settletext.code.note`: That is the whole call. The words come out of noise in about a second and a half, rest, and breathe now and then.
- `settletext.code.words`: What?
- `settletext.contents.label`: ON THIS PAGE
- `settletext.contents.title`: What this page holds
- `settletext.cost.body`: The README’s Performance table is measured with settle-see’s own meter on this machine, headless, at the three presets: the physics is under a fifth of a millisecond a frame at every preset, the draw one to two and a half, and a still picture drew zero frames in five seconds. A settled picture rests until a breath or a page event wakes it, so the cost is the settling, not the sitting.
- `settletext.cost.label`: WHAT IT COSTS
- `settletext.cost.title`: A few milliseconds a frame while it settles, nothing once it has
- `settletext.fit`: SETTLE is the language, KANERVA its memory, the MCP the door from an editor, and settle-text is the look of all of it, handed to anyone with a React page.

- `settletext.toc.cost`: what it costs

- `settletext.toc.show`: five live recipes
- `settletext.why.body`: Everything on this site is a settle, and until now the only way to have one was to read how it works. A visual designer wants the look: a title in their own font that settles out of noise and sits there glowing, a photo as lights behind a page, a logo drawn in dots. They should get that from a component with a text prop and a font prop, and never meet a lean, a pull or a temperature unless they go looking. settle-text wraps settle-see, the drawing library every picture here runs on, and shows four components with plain names and sensible defaults: the measured tuning of this site’s own titles.

The neons colour the lights, the charts and the KEY’s dots; headings, numbers in text and the HIT, SPLIT and MISS words are chrome and use the red shades above. Every page carries the key, small and collapsed, in its bottom-right corner, listing only the neons that page uses.

The SETTLE pictures keep the ten neons of the code, each meaning one thing in the physics. Every value on this page is read from the same lists the stylesheet declares.
- `style.mark.badges`: The language chips wear a tiny badge each, every colour a site variable: EN a prime-red star and a KANERVA-cyan stripe {en}, JA a pale disc with a hyper-pink sun {ja}.

One constant, {name} in {file}, is the source for the header, the favicon and this page. The five candidates below are drawn the same way at 64, 32 and 16 px; the chosen one is {glyph} ({reading}: {meaning}).
- `style.mark.title`: A kanji drawn in lights
- `style.red.label`: THE RED-LIGHT RULE
- `style.red.p1`: Grounds, text, rules, buttons, menus, headings, links, code, tables, the KEY panel and the footer use colours whose blue channel is at most 0x{blue} and whose green is at most {green} of their red: light from orange (about 600 nm) to deep red. Body text is warm amber on the ground, and every text colour meets WCAG AA (4.5:1) on the ground, the panel and the room.
- `style.red.p2`: Purple, {hi}, is the prime red’s highlight and nothing else: the hover rule on a menu item or a button, the keyboard focus ring, the bar under the active menu item. It reaches 3.60:1, enough for a graphic, and it is never a text colour. A neon appears only in a picture, a chart or a key dot.

- `surprise.control.label`: SURPRISE · SDM OR SETTLE?
- `surprise.control.note`: All six numbers are live, from the model and the step on screen now. In LEARNING mode the leans and pulls move, so ln Z moves too.
- `surprise.control.p1`: The agent's control is SETTLE-based. Its model is a settling machine: a chain Ising model (a Boltzmann machine whose links form a chain) over the {n} p-bits it senses, with a lean on every bit and pulls between linked bits. Because the links form a chain, ln Z is summed exactly by a transfer matrix, so the surprise of any observation, −ln p(o) = E(o) + ln Z, is exact. To act, the agent steps an imagined copy of the game forward under each of {plans} plans of {horizon} steps, scores every predicted observation by its surprise under the machine, and takes the first move of the plan with the lowest total. Surprise here means how unlikely a sight is under a model fitted to calm wandering: an enemy in view, a hit, a bump or the alarm all make it rise.
- `surprise.control.p2`: It is not SDM. A sparse distributed memory stores patterns at random hard addresses and recalls them by Hamming distance; this agent has no hard locations, no addresses, no counters and no recall. Nothing on this page uses the Kanerva memory. The settle-drawn picture above is SETTLE too: the same p-bit rule, run on the picture's lights.
- `surprise.control.stat.e`: E(o) of what it sees now
- `surprise.control.stat.g`: chosen plan's G (nats)
- `surprise.control.stat.g.before`: before the first step
- `surprise.control.stat.g.first`: first move: {move}
- `surprise.control.stat.lnz`: ln Z now (exact)
- `surprise.control.stat.model`: model
- `surprise.control.stat.model.note`: {p} parameters (leans and pulls) over {n} bits
- `surprise.control.stat.model.value`: chain Ising, exact
- `surprise.control.stat.plans`: plans scored this step
- `surprise.control.stat.plans.note`: {h} steps each, plan time {ms} ms
- `surprise.control.stat.s`: surprise = E + ln Z (nats)
- `surprise.control.title`: The control is SETTLE-based, not SDM
- `surprise.controls.help.basics`: A new level is generated from the next seed. Switching the model or starting a new level resets the model to the comfort prior. Nothing here is saved; reloading starts again. The share of one core is the frame time times the frame rate plus the planning time times the step rate. The game stops while the view is off screen.
- `surprise.controls.help.picture`: EVERY FRAME A SETTLE: every frame the raycaster draws a small picture, and a grid of p-bits takes a few sweeps of the SETTLE rule toward it. NEON BY CLASS: each light shines in a neon chosen by what its pixel shows (sky, sun, cloud, skyline, wall, neon trim, floor, enemy, rain), four tones per class from dark to bright. THE PIXEL'S OWN: each light shines in its pixel's colour. THREE: three grids (red, green, blue) settle each colour on its own. SOFT READ draws each light's running average; RAW BITS draws every light fully on or off. A DAY LASTS sets the length of the day; HOLD stops the sky at the time of day chosen. WEATHER: CYCLE brings rain and night sparks on their own clocks.
- `surprise.controls.help.truetime`: TRUE TIME SETTLE: the game films a frame on a fixed grid and keeps the last {ring}; the settle works toward the frame it was given as fast as this machine allows, and once the lights that frame asked to change agree with it to the threshold, it takes the frame the game is at now. The strip under the view marks each filmed frame SHOWN, SKIPPED, NOW (being settled toward) or FILMED (not yet aimed at). MACHINE SPEED: 60 or 15 SWEEPS/S hold the settle to that rate, to show what a slower machine does; the game keeps its time either way.

- `surprise.enemies.label`: SURPRISE · THE ENEMIES
- `surprise.enemies.live`: live, this level: {alive} alive · {killed} killed · {hits} hits on the player
- `surprise.enemies.note`: The level holds six enemies at a time: a spiker, a runner, a brute and a swarm of three mites. A killed enemy comes back 120 to 239 steps later. All of them follow fixed rules with no learning, and the agent's imagined copies of the world run the same rules. Each type has its own neon and four frames: two that alternate while it moves, one while it attacks, one when it is hit.
- `surprise.enemies.title`: Four kinds of enemy, each with its own look and rules
- `surprise.fep.choice`: Plans are chosen with probability falling with their expected free energy; γ, the precision, sets how strongly. E(π) is a prior over plans, which in active inference carries habits.
- `surprise.fep.expected`: Expected free energy of a plan π: how far the outcomes the plan is predicted to bring are from the preferred outcomes p̃ (risk), plus how uncertain those outcomes are (ambiguity).
- `surprise.fep.free`: Free energy is surprise plus how far the beliefs q about hidden causes x are from the correct ones. It is never smaller than surprise, and equals it when the beliefs are exact.
- `surprise.fep.intro1`: Karl Friston's free-energy principle says that a living system stays in the small set of states that keep it alive, and that it does this by minimising surprise: how unlikely its sensations are under its own model of the world. Surprise itself cannot be computed directly by the system, so the principle uses an upper bound on it, variational free energy, which can be computed.
- `surprise.fep.intro2`: Perception lowers free energy by changing beliefs. Action lowers it by changing the sensations. Learning lowers it over a longer time by changing the model. Active inference is the name for the action half: the agent chooses actions whose predicted outcomes have low expected free energy.
- `surprise.fep.label`: SURPRISE · THE FREE-ENERGY PRINCIPLE
- `surprise.fep.surprise`: Surprise is the negative log probability of an observation o under the model. Rare observations have high surprise.
- `surprise.fep.title`: Friston's free-energy principle and active inference

- `surprise.map.aria`: The level from above: rooms, doors (amber), the route the agent is following (dashed), the player and its twelve sense rays, each enemy (a dot in its type's colour, labelled with its type and tactic) and where the agent believes it is (a ring).
- `surprise.map.enemy`: {type} {mode}
- `surprise.measured.arms`: FIXED: the prior never changes. LEARNING: one Boltzmann step per observation at rate 0.02, body preferences held. LEARNING-ALL: the same, with the body preferences learning too. WANDER: the route every step, with no planning: the habit alone. UNTRAINED: the planner with an untrained model, whose every plan predicts the same surprise, so only the habit separates them. RANDOM: a uniformly random move of the nine each step. "enemies" counts every enemy that appeared, including the six present at the start; "seen" counts those the player saw.

- `surprise.measured.intro`: Measured headless in Node with the same engine: {n} seeds ({first} to {last}), each its own level, {steps} steps each, planning over {horizon} steps with {plans} plans, habit {habit} nats per route step and alarm tail {tail}. Every run is deterministic from its seed; the site's tests re-run seed 1 of FIXED and compare. Measured {date} UTC by {cmd} (file: {file}).
- `surprise.measured.label`: SURPRISE · MEASURED
- `surprise.measured.mixed`: the MIXED roster (a spiker, a runner, a brute and three mites): totals over all seeds per arm; fractions are means over the runs
- `surprise.measured.onsets`: the mixed roster: surprise at the first sight of the k-th enemy, mean over seeds (n = seeds that reached that enemy)

- `surprise.mode.duck`: duck
- `surprise.mode.hunt`: hunt
- `surprise.mode.lunge`: lunge
- `surprise.mode.recoil`: recoil
- `surprise.mode.retreat`: retreat
- `surprise.mode.wander`: wander
- `surprise.model.fixed`: FIXED
- `surprise.model.learning`: LEARNING
- `surprise.modes.closer`: Which is closer to Friston. LEARNING with the body preferences held. In active inference the parameters of the generative model are learned by the same free-energy minimisation that drives perception and action, on a slower time scale, while the prior preferences over outcomes belong to the kind of creature the agent is and are not rewritten by experience. FIXED is the special case with a learning rate of zero. Letting the preferences learn is the version the principle warns about: an agent that learns to prefer whatever happens to it stops acting to change anything.
- `surprise.modes.fixed`: FIXED. The prior is set once and never changes. An enemy stays exactly as surprising the hundredth time as the first, so the agent reacts to every enemy the same way. Surprise drives action only.
- `surprise.modes.label`: SURPRISE · THE TWO MODES
- `surprise.modes.learning`: LEARNING. After every step the model takes one Boltzmann learning step on what it saw. Views of enemies can become more expected, so the first sight of later enemies can become less surprising (habituation; the measured table shows how much). With the body preferences held (the default), habituation touches only what views look like; being hurt and being alarmed stay exactly as unwelcome. With the checkbox on, the preferences learn too, and the agent learns to expect being hurt and alarmed; the table measures what that does.
- `surprise.modes.title`: FIXED and LEARNING, and which is closer to Friston
- `surprise.pad.aria`: move buttons
- `surprise.pad.help`: Click the view first, then use the arrow keys or W A S D, space to shoot, E to follow the route, F to face the nearest known enemy, C to take cover. Each button takes one step.
- `surprise.page.label`: SURPRISE · WHAT THIS PAGE SHOWS
- `surprise.page.p1a`: The view above is a small first-person game. Its level is generated from a seed: rooms of different styles joined by doors and two-cell corridors, lit by neon trim. The whole level is open to the sky: over the walls lies a painted outside, a sun or a moon on its arc, drifting clouds, a skyline of hills and lit towers, and weather.
- `surprise.page.p1b`: Six enemies of four kinds move about the level: a spiker that keeps its distance and fires, a runner that lunges, a swarm of three mites, and a slow brute that fires orbs in a fan. By default the picture is drawn as a settle in true time: the game runs at its own pace, and a grid of p-bits catches up with it, frame by frame, as fast as this machine allows.
- `surprise.page.p2a`: The player is a settling machine with one goal: keep what it senses unsurprising. Its model was fitted to calm wandering through other levels. It has no score and no reward. It has a habit, which is to follow its route from room to room, so wandering is what it does when nothing happens.
- `surprise.page.p2b`: Seeing an enemy, being hurt and being alarmed are all surprising under its model, so in a fight it picks the moves it predicts will lead back to calm, and a dead enemy ends the alarm. You can take the controls at any time; the meter keeps measuring the surprise of what you see.
- `surprise.page.title`: A game agent that acts to keep its observations unsurprising

It still killed {kps} of the enemies it saw ({ckps} on the classic roster), and it took {wratio} times fewer hits than WANDER and {rratio} times fewer than RANDOM on the same levels.

- `surprise.reading.fewer`: fewer
- `surprise.reading.fixed`: FIXED spent {explore} of its steps on the route and visited {rooms} of each level's rooms. It saw {seen} enemies and killed {killed}, {tokill} steps after first sight on average, and took {hits} hits ({hpk} per 1,000 steps) with {deaths} deaths. WANDER, the same route with no planning, took {whits} hits and died {wdeaths} times; RANDOM took {rhits} and died {rdeaths} times.
- `surprise.reading.learning`: LEARNING (preferences held) took {hits} hits ({more} than FIXED), killed {killed} and died {deaths} times. Its first sight of the first enemy measured {l1} nats against FIXED's {f1}, and of the fifth {l5} against {f5}; its mean surprise over the run was {ls} against {fs}.
- `surprise.reading.learningall`: LEARNING-ALL (preferences learning too) had a mean surprise of {s} nats, took {hits} hits, killed {killed} and died {deaths} times. Low surprise is not good play: a model that learns to expect being hurt no longer prefers any outcome.
