- `surprise.reading.nocost`: The new enemies did not cost the agent more hits.
- `surprise.reading.notsame`: did not match WANDER on every seed
- `surprise.reading.same`: made exactly the same moves as WANDER on every seed (the per-seed counts are identical)
- `surprise.reading.untrained`: UNTRAINED {verb}: with no model, active inference reduces to its habit. Its mean surprise is {s} nats, {n} times ln 2, the same for every observation.
- `surprise.related.cl1`: Neurons and DOOM. News reports in 2026 describe Cortical Labs' CL1, a computer built on living human neurons, being shown running DOOM: TechSpot, 28 February 2026 and Military.com, March 2026. The Military.com report says the neurons "spin in circles, wander through levels and often die quickly" and that the demo "has not yet appeared in a peer-reviewed scientific paper". We cite these as reports, not as results.
- `surprise.related.darkroom`: The dark room problem. Friston, Thornton and Clark (2012), "Free-energy minimization and the dark-room problem", Frontiers in Psychology 3. {doi}.
- `surprise.related.dishbrain`: DishBrain and Pong. Kagan et al. (2022), "In vitro neurons learn and exhibit sentience when embodied in a simulated game-world", Neuron. {doi}. Cultured neurons, in a system the paper calls DishBrain, played Pong. The abstract says: "Applying implications from the theory of active inference via the free energy principle, we find apparent learning within five minutes of real-time gameplay not observed in control conditions." The feedback followed the principle: when the paddle hit the ball, "a predictable stimulus was delivered across all electrodes simultaneously"; when it missed, "an unpredictable stimulus was delivered". The paper gives the reasoning: "it should be possible to shape BNN behavior by simply presenting unpredictable feedback following 'incorrect' behavior." The alarm in this game follows the same logic: a live enemy keeps the input unpredictable, and removing it makes the input calm again.
- `surprise.related.gym`: Active inference and Doom. Cullen, Davey, Friston and Moran (2018), "Active Inference in OpenAI Gym: A Paradigm for Computational Investigations Into Psychiatric Illness", Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging 3(9):809-818. {doi}. The abstract names Doom among the OpenAI Gym tasks used.
- `surprise.related.habits`: Habits as a prior over plans. Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, O'Doherty and Pezzulo (2016), "Active inference and learning", Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 68:862-879. {doi}.
- `surprise.related.label`: SURPRISE · RELATED WORK
- `surprise.related.principle`: The principle. Friston (2010), "The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory?", Nature Reviews Neuroscience 11(2):127-138. {doi1}. Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck and Pezzulo (2017), "Active Inference: A Process Theory", Neural Computation 29(1):1-49. {doi2}. Parr, Pezzulo and Friston (2022), "Active Inference: The Free Energy Principle in Mind, Brain, and Behavior", The MIT Press, open access. {doi3}.
- `surprise.related.response`: A response to it. Balci et al. (2023), "A response to claims of emergent intelligence and sentience in a dish", Neuron 111(5):604-605. {doi}. A letter from many researchers responding to the paper's claims, as its title says.
- `surprise.related.title`: Related work: DishBrain, DOOM and active inference
- `surprise.related.vizdoom`: The research platform. Kempka et al. (2016), "ViZDoom: A Doom-based AI Research Platform for Visual Reinforcement Learning", IEEE CIG 2016. {arxiv}.
- `surprise.rules.brute`: Slow (0.055 cells a step) and takes four hits, twice a spiker. It walks in to 4 cells and keeps coming slowly, and fires three slow orbs in a fan every 40 steps from up to 10 cells. It never ducks or retreats; with 2 points left it rages, 1.7 times faster, firing every 26 steps.
- `surprise.rules.mite`: Comes in a swarm of three. One hit kills a mite, and it is small, so it is a narrow target. While wandering it follows the swarm's first mite. Seeing you, it calls every mite within 8 cells, closes in, and weaves from side to side for the last 3 cells. A dead mite returns beside a live one.
- `surprise.rules.runner`: Chases along the shortest walk at 0.15 cells a step (two thirds of your speed). From 1.4 cells it lunges straight in at 0.24 for up to 8 steps; after a bite or a spent lunge it springs back for 14 steps, then comes again. Sees 13 cells.
- `surprise.rules.spiker`: Wanders between rooms until it sees you (11 cells, a 140 degree view). Then it approaches beyond 6 cells, backs off inside 2.5, strafes between, and fires a shot every 22 steps. After a shot it ducks round a corner; at its last point of health it retreats to cover and comes back. The original enemy, unchanged.
- `surprise.scope.choices`: The alarm-tail term in G, the plan family (one move for 8 steps, or one move for 1, 2 or 4 steps and then another), the fast "face" turn and the habit's size are engineering choices of ours, made to keep planning cheap and to let a fight finish inside an 8-step horizon. The enemy types' numbers (speeds, health, ranges) are ours too; the brute's four hit points were set so it can be shot down inside one plan.
- `surprise.scope.darkroom`: The dark room problem is real here. Without the habit and the "closer" preference, this agent found the most typical views it could, which are open rooms seen from the middle, and rocked forward and back there instead of passing through doors and corridors, whose views are rarer. The habit and the preference make it wander; they do not remove the problem. Friston, Thornton and Clark (2012) discuss it.
- `surprise.scope.forward`: The agent's forward model is the game's own rules, except that it holds only the enemies the agent knows of, where it believes they are, and runs each in the tactic it was last in. Real active inference agents have to learn how their actions change the world. Here that part is given.
- `surprise.scope.hidden`: The agent has no inferred hidden states. The alarm and the believed enemy positions are set by fixed rules, so the free-energy bound is tight and free energy equals surprise. The meter shows surprise, exactly.
- `surprise.scope.kinds`: The agent's senses do not tell the enemy kinds apart: an enemy is an enemy bit, whatever its kind. Its model and its comfort prior are exactly as before the new enemies; only its imagined copies of the world run the new rules.
- `surprise.scope.label`: SURPRISE · SCOPE
- `surprise.scope.shows`: It shows an agent that chooses moves by predicted surprise and a habit, with no reward, wandering a level and dealing with enemies, and that its behaviour depends on what its model counts as comfortable.
- `surprise.scope.title`: What this demo shows and what it does not
- `surprise.scope.toy`: It is a toy. It is not a model of a brain and not a claim about how cells or animals work. The levels, the enemies' rules, the bits, the habit and every number in the prior were chosen by us.
- `surprise.settle.body`: The body (6 bits). hurt this step; walked forward this step; bumped a wall; fresh (stepped into a cell not stood in for 40 steps); closer (nearer the end of its route than before the step); alarm. The alarm is a belief bit: on while an enemy is seen or heard (within 2.5 cells) or the player is hurt, off when the agent sees the last enemy it knows of die, and it fades after 40 quiet steps. Being hit by a shot tells the agent where the shooter is.
- `surprise.settle.exact`: Surprise is the energy of what the agent sees plus one constant, ln Z. The pulls link each ray to its neighbours and the body to the centre ray, which makes a chain, so Z is summed exactly by a transfer matrix (8 states per ray, 64 body states). The surprise on the meter is exact.
- `surprise.settle.label`: SURPRISE · HOW IT MAPS ONTO SETTLE
- `surprise.settle.learning`: The learning rule (Boltzmann learning): move each lean and pull so that what was just seen becomes more expected. The averages ⟨·⟩ under the model are computed exactly on the chain. Each step is one gradient step on −ln p(o), so learning lowers the surprise of what is seen often.
- `surprise.settle.machine`: The model is a SETTLE machine over the {n} sense bits: every bit has a lean h, and linked pairs have a pull J. Comfortable arrangements have low energy.
- `surprise.settle.moves`: The moves. wait; turn left; turn right (22.5 degrees); forward; back; shoot (a shot hits an enemy inside the crosshair and in sight; two hits kill); explore (one step along the route); face (turn up to 67.5 degrees toward the nearest enemy it knows of); cover (one step toward the nearest cell that enemy cannot see from where the agent believes it is).
- `surprise.settle.pbit`: The p-bit rule that SETTLE uses to shake a machine is also each bit's own prediction of itself given the others. The "local surprise" row is that prediction's error, bit by bit. The "dreamed" row is the same rule running freely: the machine settling into what it expects.
- `surprise.settle.plan`: In this game the agent predicts each plan's observations ô by stepping a copy of the world that holds only the enemies it knows of, at the places it believes them to be. The predictions are certain, so the ambiguity term is zero and the risk term is the surprise of each predicted observation. The second term charges an alarm still on at the end of the plan as if it lasted {tail} more steps; without it, a fight that ends after the plan's eight steps earns nothing for ending it. The third term is ln E(π), the habit: {habit} nats for each step of the plan spent following the route. The second term is our engineering addition; the third has its place in active inference, and its size is our choice.
- `surprise.settle.prior`: The comfort prior. The body leans are set by hand and never learned in the default setting: the agent expects to walk (lean {walked}), to find fresh ground ({fresh}), to get closer to where it is going ({closer}), not to be hurt ({hurt}), not to bump ({bumped}) and not to be alarmed ({alarm}). These are Friston's prior preferences. Everything else, what comfortable views look like, is fitted by maximum likelihood to {steps} steps of wandering with no enemy on levels {levels}, which no measured run uses. The mean surprise on that walk is {mean} nats (the dashed line).
- `surprise.settle.senses`: The senses (36 bits). 12 rays across a 66 degree view. Each ray has three bits: an enemy in its direction, a wall nearer than 1.6 cells, a door panel as the first thing it hits.

- `surprise.view.aria`: The game view. Focus it and use the arrow keys or W A S D to move, space to shoot, E to follow the route, F to face the nearest known enemy, C to take cover.
- `surprise.view.canvas`: First-person view of a neon level of rooms and corridors. Surprise now {s} nats. {n} enemies in the level.
- `surprise.world.enemies`: Enemies and their tactics. Four kinds, six at a time; their rules are in the section on the enemies above. Every enemy sees across a 140 degree view; lost from sight, it goes to where it last saw the player and gives up after 80 steps. All of this is fixed rules, with no learning and no randomness inside a step, so the agent's imagined copies of the world run exactly the same rules.
- `surprise.world.label`: SURPRISE · THE WORLD
- `surprise.world.level`: The level. A 44 by 32 grid. Up to nine rectangular rooms are placed at random; a minimum spanning tree over their centres, plus the two shortest extra edges, says which rooms are joined, so there are loops. Each joining corridor runs from a door on one room's wall to a door on the other's, carved by an A* search that may not cross a room, and is then widened to two cells. A level is rebuilt from the next seed until every floor cell can be reached. Doors are panels that slide open while anyone is within 1.6 cells.
- `surprise.world.outside`: The outside. Every pixel above the horizon is painted from the time of day ({file}). Eight keyframes, from dawn through noon and dusk to midnight, hold the colours of the sky, the sun, the clouds, the skyline and the fog, and the sky blends between the two around the moment. The sun runs from east to west along an arc, with stripes cut across its lower half; at night a moon takes the same arc and stars come out. Clouds are a noise map seen on a plane above, drifting with the wind and drawn in three flat tones with a bright rim. A skyline of rolling hills and seven clusters of towers stands on the horizon in every direction; their windows are lit by a fixed hash, so they never flicker. The fog takes a colour near the horizon's, so the far floor fades into the haze. By day the rows near the horizon shimmer sideways with the heat, at under one cycle a second. Rain is a field of slanted streaks and sparks are rising embers; both are closed formulas in time, so a frame drawn twice at the same moment is identical. The light on walls and floors follows the day.
- `surprise.world.pathfinding`: Pathfinding. A* over the grid with eight neighbours, cost 1 for a straight step and √2 for a diagonal, the octile distance as its heuristic, and no corner cutting. The tests check its path length against an independent Dijkstra search on 63 levels, and check that it reports no path on a map split by a wall.
- `surprise.world.picture`: The picture. A textured raycaster: one ray per picture column through the same grid the agent senses, walls and door panels with neon trim, the floor drawn row by row, light pooling under the lamps, distance fog that the neon shows through, and sprites sorted far to near. Beside each pixel's colour the renderer writes what the pixel shows (its class), which the settle can use to choose a light's colour. Every frame is written into one array of pixels and drawn at the chosen width. The figures under the view are this tab's own timings.
- `surprise.world.roof`: The open roof. No room and no corridor has a ceiling. The roof was taken off without a draw from the level's random number generator, so no wall, door, lamp or pickup moved, and the comfort prior still fits these levels exactly. The sky is only a picture: nothing the agent senses changed, and the test that re-runs a recorded seed still matches the measured table.
- `surprise.world.settle`: The picture drawn as a settle. In this mode the raycaster draws a small frame, one pixel per light (up to 128, 192 or 256 lights across). The frame is first brightened (g' = 1.5 g^0.8, capped at 1), because the dark neon scene would otherwise light only a few lights. Each light is a p-bit with the lean h = atanh(2g − 1) for its grey g, and a pull J to its four neighbours. With J = 0 a light says yes a fraction g of the time, so grey becomes a rate. By default there is one light per pixel: its grey is the pixel's brightness and a lit light shines in the pixel's own colour, so the settle decides how bright each light is and the frame decides its colour. The other option gives each pixel three lights, one per colour. Every frame the lights take a few Gibbs sweeps in checkerboard order, starting from where they ended the frame before, and the picture is drawn from each light's running average (the soft read) or from the raw bits. The lights keep fizzing because each is a coin. The caption reports the settle's own time and the PSNR of the soft read against the brightness it aims at.
- `surprise.world.title`: Level, pathfinding, enemies and the picture
- `surprise.world.truetime`: True time. In this mode (the default) the game and the picture keep separate clocks. The game steps at its own rate and is filmed on a fixed grid, one frame every 500 ms unless the control says otherwise, into a ring of the last {ring} frames. The settle in front works toward the frame it was given, as many sweeps per animation frame as fit in {budget} ms. A frame counts as shown when 80% of the lights it asked to change agree with it: a light agrees when its soft read sits within 0.05 plus two standard deviations of a coin of its target rate, which is where a settled light stays. Counting only the lights a frame changed matters: frames half a second apart differ in a few percent of the lights, so a share of the whole frame would pass before anything had moved. When a frame is shown, the settle takes the frame the game is at at that moment, not the next one in order. A fast machine shows every frame and holds each, still fizzing, until the game moves on; a slow one skips frames and is never far behind. The clock is settle-see's TRUE TIME ({fn}, lane PERFLADDER), which {file} re-exports, so its frames turn on the page's one master beat.
- `surprise.world.wandering`: Wandering. The route: walk the A* path to a room, look round for six steps on arrival while strolling, then choose the next room, one of the three least recently entered, at random.

## valleys

- `valleys.chip.exact`: every arrangement enumerated
- `valleys.chip.grid`: 16x16 grid survey
- `valleys.chip.lane`: VALLEYMAP, recorded
- `valleys.chip.n`: 6 to 16 things live
- `valleys.how.lede1`: On a small machine the valleys are counted exactly, by enumerating all 2^n arrangements. Random pulls with no leans make every valley come with its mirror image, so the valleys pair up. On a large machine the valleys can only be surveyed, by Settling from many random starts. The recorded section below also asks what the shape of the landscape is good for.
- `valleys.how.lede2`: The shuffled line is the control. Give the same 2^n energies to the arrangements in a random order, and each arrangement is the lowest of itself and its n neighbours with chance 1 / (n + 1). The grid survey Settles a 16x16 wrapped grid with every pull equal to 1, by Gibbs draws P(s_i = yes) = (1 + tanh(β Σ_nb s_j)) / 2 at T = 1 / β = 0.05.
- `valleys.how.plain`: Every settling machine defines a landscape of energy over its arrangements. A valley is a place where the machine can come to rest, and its basin is the share of the landscape that drains into it.
- `valleys.kind.other`: other
- `valleys.kind.stripes`: stripes
- `valleys.kind.uniform`: uniform
- `valleys.lab.basins.title`: Basin share of the valleys: calmest first, a valley and its mirror come in pairs
- `valleys.lab.card.aria`: arrangement {bits}
- `valleys.lab.live`: {count} valleys among {N} arrangements
- `valleys.lab.n`: things n (2^n arrangements, all enumerated)
- `valleys.lab.note`: The strip plots energy with the calmest arrangements at the top. The arrangements are laid out in Gray-code order, so two neighbours on the strip differ by a single flip. Each lime circle marks a valley, and its size shows the size of the valley's basin.

- `what.dat.coin.cap`: a lean and a pull feed one input, from
- `what.dat.coin.p`: The temperature T divides the input: the rule is really (1 + tanh(I / T)) / 2. Hot means every coin is nearly fair; cold means every coin follows its input. A p-bit is a device that does exactly this rule in hardware.
- `what.dat.coin.say`: Every draw is the same coin. Add up a thing's lean and its pulls times what its neighbours say now; that sum is the input I. The chance of yes is (1 + tanh I) / 2. At I = 0 it is a fair coin; at I = 2 it is 98% yes.
- `what.dat.coin.word`: the coin rule
- `what.dat.cool.p`: The schedule is geometric: it starts at ten times T and ends at a twentieth of it. Every puzzle on the puzzles page is solved by this one word.
- `what.dat.cool.say`: Anneal is a settle while the temperature falls. Hot first, so every thing moves freely and nothing gets stuck; cold last, so only the calmest arrangement survives. The calmest arrangement seen is kept.
- `what.dat.cool.word`: cooling
- `what.dat.count.p`: For a picture the count is per pixel: how often each light was on is that pixel's grey. One sample is black and white; forty samples bring back the greys. That is the next section.
- `what.dat.count.say`: An answer is a fraction of samples. The count wobbles by about one over the square root of the number of samples, so 40,000 samples give an answer good to about half a percent.
- `what.dat.count.word`: counting
- `what.dat.intro`: Four mechanisms do all the work. Each is one line of mathematics, and each has a live block here so you can watch it happen.
- `what.dat.sweep.cap`: the same word in every run, from
- `what.dat.sweep.field`: sixty fair coins, each drawn once per sweep
- `what.dat.sweep.out`: three runs
- `what.dat.sweep.p`: The samples a settle keeps are one arrangement per sweep. Because each sweep starts from the one before, early sweeps still remember the coin flips they began with; the burn-in throws those away.
- `what.dat.sweep.say`: One sweep visits every free thing once, in a fresh random order, and tosses it with the coin rule. A settle is thousands of sweeps. Held things are skipped.
- `what.dat.sweep.word`: a sweep
- `what.dat.title`: The coin rule, sweeps, cooling, counting
- `what.dec.caption`: How likely was rain? The three runs.
- `what.dec.label`: WAT DAT · DECISIONS AND STATE MACHINES
- `what.dec.opt.dry`: held dry
- `what.dec.opt.none`: not looked at
- `what.dec.opt.wet`: held wet
- `what.dec.out`: three runs, one after another
- `what.dec.p1`: Rain and a sprinkler can each wet the grass. Rain is unusual, the sprinkler a little less so, and nobody waters in the rain. You look outside and see that the grass is wet. How likely is it that it rained?
- `what.dec.p2`: SETTLE answers by letting the three lights flip until they agree with each other, with the wet-grass light held on, and counting how often the rain light was on. A decision is a settle with a hold in it. Choose what you saw:
- `what.dec.p3`: Holding the grass wet changes what calm looks like. The pull of 1.5 between rain and wet grass now rewards rain being on, and the pull of 1 does the same for the sprinkler. Both still lean toward off, so neither is certain. Either one explains the wet grass, so each ends up on about 64% of the time, and the push between them makes both at once less likely than it would be without it. With the grass held dry, rain almost never happens.
- `what.dec.row.dry`: grass held dry
- `what.dec.row.none`: nothing held
- `what.dec.row.wet`: grass held wet
- `what.dec.seg`: the grass is
- `what.dec.sm.p1`: A state machine is the same Settling run over and over. The state is held, the machine settles, the answer is read, and that answer is held as the next state. Every step is one settle, so the machine can be as unsure as its coins are.
- `what.dec.sm.p2`: SDM EXPLORE draws Kanerva's memory as exactly this: every read is a step, and you can watch the state walk to a stored pattern, or refuse. SDMJEV, the magic 8 ball, is one pass of the same loop settled into an answer.
- `what.dec.sm.word`: a state machine
- `what.dec.th.rain`: rain was yes
- `what.dec.th.saw`: what you saw
- `what.dec.title`: A question with evidence
- `what.dis.ask.out`: every ask in the three runs
- `what.dis.ask.p`: An ask can count a joint event too: {code} counts the samples in which both were yes. The language reference lists every form.
- `what.dis.ask.say`: An ask counts. How often was this thing yes in the kept samples? That fraction is the answer: a probability, a grey level, a remembered bit.
- `what.dis.ask.word`: an ask
- `what.dis.hold.cap`: hold the grass wet, then ask about rain, from
- `what.dis.hold.out`: the second run
- `what.dis.hold.p`: Rain leans toward no, so on its own it is yes {a}% of the time. Hold the grass wet and rain becomes yes {b}% of the time. The whole of decisions, further down, is this one word.
- `what.dis.hold.say`: A hold pins a thing to what you saw. A held thing never flips, and everything pulled to it rearranges itself around that fact.
- `what.dis.hold.word`: a hold
- `what.dis.intro`: Using these six words one constructs a {settle} program.
- `what.dis.lean.cap`: the whole one-thing program, from
- `what.dis.lean.p`: The light was on in 88.0% of 40,000 samples. For a lean of 1 the exact answer is (1 + tanh 1) / 2 = 88.08%, so the count is right to within the noise of counting. Move the slider to see the rule for any lean.
- `what.dis.lean.say`: A lean tilts the coin. A thing that leans toward yes by 1 comes up yes about 88% of the time; by 3, nearly always. A lean toward no works the same way down.
- `what.dis.lean.word`: a lean
- `what.dis.pull.cap`: three pulls, one of them a push, from
- `what.dis.pull.p`: A pull of 1 makes two things agree about 88% of the time, the same number as a lean of 1 makes one thing say yes, and for the same reason: the rule inside is one rule. Pulls are also how news travels. Hold one light and its pulls carry what you saw to the others.
- `what.dis.pull.say`: A pull joins two things and makes them want to agree. A push is a negative pull: it makes them want to differ. Neither light below has a lean, so each alone is a fair coin, yet together they agree most of the time.
- `what.dis.pull.word`: a pull
- `what.dis.settle.field`: sixty copies of the one-thing program, each a light leaning yes by 1
- `what.dis.settle.p`: A settle first burns in a tenth of its sweeps and throws them away, then keeps one sample per sweep. The seed makes the run repeatable: the same seed gives the same samples every time.
- `what.dis.settle.say`: A settle shakes everything. Each sweep draws every free thing once, in a fresh random order, each one a weighted coin that watches its neighbours. Forty thousand sweeps is a few milliseconds of Rust.
- `what.dis.settle.word`: a settle
- `what.dis.thing.cap1`: a thing with no lean, from
- `what.dis.thing.cap2`: six things in one line, from
- `what.dis.thing.p`: A program names its things in a {model} block. Yes is +1 and no is -1 underneath, and every answer SETTLE gives is a count of how often a thing was yes.
- `what.dis.thing.say`: A thing is a light. It is yes (on) or no (off), and it never stays still: the machine keeps tossing it. With no lean it is a fair coin.
- `what.dis.thing.word`: a thing
- `what.dis.title`: A thing, a lean, a pull, a hold, a settle, an ask

- `what.horse.label`: WAT DAT · THE HORSE, IN TRUE TIME
- `what.horse.ml`: In machine-learning words the movie is a data stream on a fixed clock and the field is an anytime estimate, read out when it passes a quality bar and then re-aimed at the newest frame rather than the backlog. The clock is settle-see's {tt}. The film player page takes the per-frame Settling apart stage by stage, and the two strongest frame rows and three retraining runs are folded further down.
- `what.horse.p1`: The film player does the picture trick for every frame of a film: {play}. Here it runs under TRUE TIME RENDER. A movie runs behind at its real pace, one frame every 500 ms, whatever this machine can do.
- `what.horse.p2`: The field of 15,000 p-bits in front Settles toward the frame it was given. When its picture agrees with that frame 80%, it snaps to whatever frame the movie is at now. A fast machine draws many in-between pictures of each frame; a slow one draws few and skips frames; on both, the movie keeps time.
- `what.horse.title`: A film plays behind; the field in front keeps up as best it can

- `what.mem.label`: MEMORY
- `what.mem.p1`: A memory stores patterns in the pulls themselves. Remembering a pattern adds a small pull between every pair of things that agree in it and a small push between every pair that differ, so each stored pattern becomes a calm arrangement. Start from a copy with 30% of its lights flipped, settle at a low temperature, and the lights roll back into the stored pattern.
- `what.mem.p2`: The drawing stores a letter S so you can see it; the program beside it stores random patterns named :cat and :dog, and a line of text, in 512 things. The mechanism is the same.
- `what.mem.p3`: Each recall lists how far the settled lights are from every stored pattern. +1.00 means they match :cat exactly; numbers near 0 mean unrelated. The text comes back letter for letter from a copy with 30% of its bits flipped. The SDMMEMORY page goes further, into Kanerva's sparse distributed memory.
- `what.mem.title`: Save a pattern, add noise to it, get it back

- `what.pic.files`: These two pictures are the files the Rust run wrote. One sample scores 7.27 dB; forty samples score 22.39 dB.
- `what.pic.forty`: {file}, written by the Rust run: the yes-rate over 40 samples
- `what.pic.one`: {file}, written by the Rust run: one sample, black and white
- `what.pic.p`: A picture is a grid of things, one per pixel. Each pixel leans toward the brightness of the photograph (a light pixel leans yes, a dark one no) and pulls gently on its four neighbours so that nearby pixels agree. One sample is a speckled black-and-white picture. Counting how often each pixel was on over many samples gives back the greys.
- `what.pic.title`: A grid of things makes a picture
- `what.plain`: You describe a few yes-or-no lights: how much each one wants to be on, and how much pairs of them want to agree. Then the machine shakes them. Every light keeps flipping like a weighted coin while it watches its neighbours, until the whole picture calms down. That is Settling. To get an answer, you count how often a light was on.
- `what.plain.label`: WHAT · IN PLAIN WORDS
- `what.plain.title`: Lights, a shake and a count
- `what.precise.anneal`: {anneal} is simulated annealing: the same sampler while the temperature falls geometrically from 10 T to T/20 over the sweeps, keeping the lowest-energy arrangement it passes through.
- `what.precise.ask`: {ask} is a Monte Carlo estimate of a marginal: the fraction of the N kept samples in which the thing was yes. With {and}, {or} and {andNot} it counts a joint event the same way. {hold} is conditioning: a held spin is clamped and never updated, so the samples come from p(free | held).
- `what.precise.energy`: Energy. A thing that agrees with its lean lowers the energy; two things joined by a pull lower it by agreeing, and two joined by a push lower it by differing.
- `what.precise.gibbs`: {settle} is Gibbs sampling, the heat-bath rule of Glauber dynamics. In a fresh random order each free thing is set to yes with this chance: its lean plus its neighbours' current pull, pushed through tanh. A p-bit is a device that does exactly this. A settle burns in a tenth of its sweeps, then keeps one sample per sweep.
- `what.precise.h`: What a SETTLE program is, in the standard terms
- `what.precise.learn`: {learn} is Boltzmann-machine learning: a pull grows when two things agree more often in the examples than in the machine's own samples, and shrinks when they agree less. The model term is estimated by contrastive divergence (a short settle from each example) or avoided by pseudo-likelihood.
- `what.precise.memory`: {memory} is a Hopfield network: each stored pattern xi adds 1/N to the pull between two things that agree in it and -1/N between two that differ, so every pattern becomes a low-energy arrangement. {recall} samples from a noisy address at a low temperature (0.1 by default). {sdm} and {softsdm} are Kanerva's sparse distributed memory, with its bit-counters held in pulls.
- `what.precise.p`: A SETTLE model is an Ising-type energy function over binary spins. Each thing is a spin si in {set}, with +1 read as yes. A lean is a field hi and a pull is a coupling Jij: {lean} adds +b to hi (and -b for {no}), {pull} adds +w to Jab, and {push} adds -w.
- `what.precise.tag`: THE PRECISE VERSION · for the technical reader
- `what.precise.target`: The target. Every arrangement can come up, and calmer ones come up more often. The temperature T sets how much more; Z makes the chances add to one. This is the Boltzmann distribution.
- `what.puzzle.p1`: Six guests, two tables. Three pairs are old rivals and must sit apart; three pairs are friends and would like to sit together; and there is one small grudge. A guest is a thing: yes is table A, no is table B. Rivals push hard, friends pull gently, and the best seating is the calmest arrangement.
- `what.puzzle.p2`: {anneal} finds it by starting hot, where every guest moves freely, then cooling slowly and keeping the calmest seating it passes through.
- `what.puzzle.p3`: Energy -11: all three rival pairs are apart and so are the two with a grudge, while bo and eli, who are friends, sit at different tables. No seating does better; checking all 64 gives the same lowest energy. The puzzles page solves sudoku, graph colouring, max-cut and factoring the same way.
- `what.puzzle.title`: Solve a puzzle by cooling

- `what.runs.temp.anneal`: anneal T {from} to {to} over {over} sweeps
- `what.runs.temperature`: temperature

- `what.sdm.addr.cap`: the memory, its word size and its hard locations, from
- `what.sdm.addr.p`: In SETTLE a memory is a thing in the model: {code} makes 256 address things and 2,000 hidden hard locations. A stored pattern is its own address: the memory is addressed by what it holds.
- `what.sdm.addr.say`: An address is a pattern of bits: 256 of them here. Every pattern is a corner of a 256-dimensional cube, and two patterns are near when few of their bits differ. That count is the Hamming distance.
- `what.sdm.addr.word`: an address
- `what.sdm.again.out`: reads that took three rounds
- `what.sdm.again.p`: Pure noise walked three rounds and fell into :cat: with nothing written near a random address, whichever stored pattern has the most hard locations in reach wins the vote, and the next round pulls the answer the rest of the way in.
- `what.sdm.again.say`: The read is an address too, so it can be read again. Each round the answer moves closer to the stored pattern, until it stops moving: a fixed point. The program reads in rounds until the answer repeats.
- `what.sdm.again.word`: reading again
- `what.sdm.ball.cap`: the activation radius, from
- `what.sdm.ball.p`: The activation radius sets how many hard locations two patterns share. Two random patterns differ in about 128 bits, far outside the ball, so their hard locations barely overlap and the two writes do not mix. A noisy copy differs in fewer, so it still shares most of them.
- `what.sdm.ball.say`: The hard locations that wake for an address are the ones within Hamming distance r of it: a ball in the cube. With 256 bits and r = 112 about 2% of the hard locations fall inside, so a write touches about 40 of 2,000 and a read hears from about 40.
- `what.sdm.ball.word`: the Hamming ball
- `what.sdm.crit.out`: two reads that landed outside it
- `what.sdm.crit.p`: The :owl read at 40% noise and the :zebra read (never written, so there is nothing to converge to) both stop outside the critical distance, and the program says so rather than naming a pattern. SDM EXPLORE draws this distance live.
- `what.sdm.crit.say`: There is a distance from a stored pattern inside which reading again converges to it and outside which it wanders off. Kanerva's critical distance is sharp: a little nearer and you get the pattern whole, a little farther and you get nothing.
- `what.sdm.crit.word`: the critical distance
- `what.sdm.dat.intro`: Five mechanisms do all the work. Each is one line of arithmetic on bits, and each has its drawing and its lines of code here.
- `what.sdm.dat.label`: HOW DAT · FOR SDM
- `what.sdm.dat.title`: The Hamming ball, the vote, reading again, the critical distance, the soft read
- `what.sdm.dis.intro`: Kanerva's memory stores long patterns of bits in a few thousand hard locations, each sitting at a random address in the space of all patterns. Five words make it, in the same shape as the six above. Each has its drawing, the lines of SETTLE's own {sdm} program that use it, and what the Rust {settle} binary printed when it ran.
- `what.sdm.dis.label`: WAT DIS · FOR SDM
- `what.sdm.dis.title`: An address, a hard location, a write, a read, a noisy address
- `what.sdm.far.cap`: a pattern never written, and pure noise, from
- `what.sdm.far.out`: what came back
- `what.sdm.far.p`: Pure noise falls into the nearest valley (:cat), and that is honest too: the program reports which pattern it fell into and how far it was. SDM REFUSE, on the results page, measured how often each case is told apart.
- `what.sdm.far.say`: A memory that answers every question is lying about some of them. Kanerva's answers nothing clear when the address is too far from anything stored, and it cannot invent a pattern it never took.
- `what.sdm.far.word`: too far, never written
- `what.sdm.hard.cap`: two thousand hard locations, from
- `what.sdm.hard.p`: Each hard location keeps 256 small bit-counters, one per bit. The bit-counters live in the pulls between the hard location and the data things, so a hard location is a hidden thing in the settling machine and its bit-counters are weights.
- `what.sdm.hard.say`: A hard location is one of a few thousand addresses chosen at random in the space of 2^256 corners. Nearly every pattern you could store has no hard location of its own; the ones near it stand in.
- `what.sdm.hard.word`: a hard location
- `what.sdm.heal.out`: the text read
- `what.sdm.heal.p`: The same mechanism brings a text back letter for letter from a copy with 15% of its bits flipped. The SDMMEMORY page runs this on words you type: SDMMEMORY.
- `what.sdm.heal.say`: Three letters are written below. A noisy address, the letter S with 30% of its bits flipped, wakes the hard locations near it; their vote brings S back. Then E, then T.
- `what.sdm.heal.word`: letters healed
- `what.sdm.keys.cap`: a text written and read, from
- `what.sdm.keys.p`: SDMCHAT is that model, live in your browser; the poem lab has it recite a whole poem; SDMJEV reads one answer out of its vector space. KANERVA is the toolbox, with the dollar of Mexico and king and queen in plain words.
- `what.sdm.keys.say`: A note stored under a key is written at an address made from the key, so only a reader who turns the same key lands near it. Store every next word of a text under the address of the words before it, and reading becomes a language model.
- `what.sdm.keys.word`: keys and a language model
- `what.sdm.meets.cap`: the same memory read by the pulls alone, from
- `what.sdm.meets.hop`: SETTLE's Hopfield memory, the same words, from
- `what.sdm.meets.label`: HOW IT MEETS SETTLE
- `what.sdm.meets.out`: the read by the pulls
- `what.sdm.meets.p`: Three readings of one memory. Kanerva's read is a vote; the read by the pulls is a settle of the data things with the locations held; the soft read warms the coins. All three are the tanh rule at a different temperature, which is why one language holds them. SDM EXPLORE draws the memory as a state diagram you operate.
- `what.sdm.meets.say`: In SETTLE a stored pattern is a calm arrangement: recall is a settle from a noisy address at a low temperature, and the lights roll down into the pattern. The hard locations' bit-counters live in the pulls between the hard locations and the data things, so the same memory can be read by Kanerva's vote or by the pulls alone, and the two agree.
- `what.sdm.meets.title`: A memory the machine can settle into
- `what.sdm.meets.word`: an SDM in SETTLE
- `what.sdm.noisy.cap`: two amounts of noise, from
- `what.sdm.noisy.out`: a read from too far
- `what.sdm.noisy.p`: At 40% noise the address wakes the wrong hard locations too, and the vote comes back with nothing clear: the closest name is :note at +0.62, which the program refuses to call a recall. The next section says where that line is.
- `what.sdm.noisy.say`: A noisy address is a stored pattern with some of its bits flipped (20% here). Kanerva calls the address you read at the retrieval address, or the retrieval cue; SETTLE says read-address. If it is still inside the activation radius of enough of the right hard locations, the vote brings the whole pattern back.
- `what.sdm.noisy.word`: a noisy address
- `what.sdm.read.cap`: a read, from
- `what.sdm.read.out`: the first read
- `what.sdm.read.p`: 48 of 2,000 hard locations woke, two rounds of reading walked to a fixed point, and the answer matched :cat at +1.00. The numbers beside the other names are how far the answer is from them: near zero means unrelated.
- `what.sdm.read.say`: A read starts from an address, wakes the hard locations near it, and lets them vote bit by bit: the sign of the summed bit-counters is the read. The vote is the stored pattern, and reading again from the answer walks closer still.
- `what.sdm.read.word`: a read
- `what.sdm.soft.cap`: a hard and a soft memory, and the attention read, from
- `what.sdm.soft.out`: the soft memory's reads
- `what.sdm.soft.p`: {softness} blurs the cut-off of the ball and {fire} sets what fraction of locations wake; {attend} computes the attention limit outside the sampler, so the two can be compared. The soft memory is the one that settles: its hard locations are p-bits like everything else.
- `what.sdm.soft.say`: At temperature 0 the vote is a hard majority. At a higher temperature each bit is a coin weighted by the tally, the same tanh rule as everywhere on this page, and the edge of each hard location's ball blurs too: a hard location near the edge counts a little, one at the centre counts fully. The read becomes attention.
- `what.sdm.soft.word`: the soft read
- `what.sdm.vote.out`: two reads, two rounds each
- `what.sdm.vote.p`: A vote is a majority, and a majority is a hard cut. In SETTLE's terms the tally is the input I to a coin that is cold enough to follow it every time. Warm it up and the read becomes the soft read below.
- `what.sdm.vote.say`: Every woken hard location adds its 256 bit-counters to a tally. Where the tally is positive the read bit is one, where negative it is zero. Each hard location holds a mix of every pattern it ever took, so the bits of the other patterns cancel as noise while the bits of the one you asked for add up.
- `what.sdm.vote.word`: the vote
- `what.sdm.wat.label`: WAT DAT · FOR SDM
- `what.sdm.wat.title`: Letters healed, a text back, too far, never written, keys
- `what.sdm.who.label`: WHO DIS · FOR SDM
- `what.sdm.who.p`: Sparse distributed memory is Pentti Kanerva's (1988). It stands between Hopfield's network, where every pattern is a calm arrangement of the whole machine, and attention, where every stored row is weighted by how near it is. The credits page has the papers.
- `what.sdm.who.title`: Kanerva, and the two his memory stands between
- `what.sdm.write.cap`: four writes, one of them a text, from
- `what.sdm.write.p`: Four patterns are written: three random ones named :cat, :dog and :owl, and a line of text. A text is written as its bits, so the same memory holds words and pictures. Nothing is stored whole anywhere; every pattern is spread over the locations it woke.
- `what.sdm.write.say`: A write wakes every hard location within the activation radius of the pattern's address (112 bits of 256 here: about 2% of the hard locations) and adds the pattern to each one's bit-counters: +1 for a one, -1 for a zero.
- `what.sdm.write.word`: a write

- `what.tt.dia.fast`: A FAST FRONT: settles, hits 80%, snaps to the frame the movie is at, again and again

- `what.tt.dia.movie`: THE MOVIE BEHIND, 500 ms a frame, whatever the machine does

- `what.tt.note`: One sweep of checkerboard Metropolised Gibbs per picture, pull {J}, TAP leans, warm across every switch. The movie's pace is {ms} ms a frame and no control changes it. {clip}.

- `what.tt.playing`: playing, on the clock

- `what.uses.anneal.line`: Cool slowly and keep the calmest arrangement: the rules a puzzle breaks are pushes.
- `what.uses.anneal.name`: Puzzles
- `what.uses.anneal.pitch`: Every rule of a puzzle is a push between the lights that must not agree, and every wish is a pull. Anneal starts hot, where every light moves freely, then cools slowly and keeps the calmest arrangement it passes through. The calmest arrangement is the answer.
- `what.uses.film.line`: Every pixel is a light. Counting how often each one was on gives back the greys.
- `what.uses.film.name`: Pictures
- `what.uses.film.pitch`: A picture is a grid of lights, one per pixel, each leaning toward the brightness of the photograph and pulling gently on its neighbours. One sample is black and white speckle. Counting how often each light was on over many samples gives back the greys, and a film is that trick once per frame.
- `what.uses.hold.line`: Hold what you saw, settle the rest, and count how likely each cause is.
- `what.uses.hold.name`: Decisions
- `what.uses.hold.pitch`: Hold the light you saw, so it never flips, and let every other light settle around that fact. Then count how often each possible cause was on. The grass is wet; held wet, rain comes up about 64% of the time.
- `what.uses.pull.line`: Pulls grow where the examples agree more often than the machine does.
- `what.uses.pull.name`: Learning
- `what.uses.pull.pitch`: Show the machine examples. A pull between two lights grows when they agree more often in the examples than in the machine's own samples, and shrinks when they agree less. After enough examples the machine settles into arrangements that look like the examples.
- `what.uses.recall.line`: A stored pattern is a calm arrangement, so a noisy copy rolls back to it.
- `what.uses.recall.name`: Memory
- `what.uses.recall.pitch`: Remembering a pattern adds a small pull between every pair of lights that agree in it and a small push between every pair that differ, so the pattern becomes a calm arrangement of the whole machine. Start from a copy with some lights flipped and settle at a low temperature, and the lights roll back into what was stored.
- `what.vocab.anneal`: Settle while cooling; keep the calmest arrangement.
- `what.vocab.ask`: Count how often a thing was yes.
- `what.vocab.hold`: Pin a thing to what you saw. It never flips.
- `what.vocab.lean`: How much a thing wants to be yes (or no).
- `what.vocab.pull`: How much two things want to agree.
- `what.vocab.push`: How much two things want to differ.
- `what.vocab.recall`: Settle from a noisy address back to what was stored.
- `what.vocab.save`: Store a pattern or a text in the pulls.
- `what.vocab.settle`: Flip every free thing, again and again, keeping samples.
- `what.vocab.thing`: A yes-or-no light.

- `what.who.p`: SETTLE invents no physics. Each card names a person, what SETTLE took from them, and where it lives in the language. The credits page has the papers.
- `what.who.title`: The people this rests on
- `what.why`: The same few words (thing, lean, pull, hold, settle, ask) answer probability questions, clean up pictures, play films, recall memories, solve puzzles and learn from examples. The shaking is the one thing a chip of p-bits, tiny random switches, does natively, so the same programs could run in hardware.
- `what.words.label`: THE WHOLE LANGUAGE, IN WORDS
- `what.words.p`: Go deeper: the programming language (every statement, with the real output), the film player, memory, puzzles, learning and every result. The second half of this page, KANERVA, is the memory SETTLE remembers with.
- `what.words.title`: All the words on one screen

## wlg

- `wlg.chat.absent`: His weights are not on this machine ({error}). They are dev only and never committed, so a clean checkout has none. Where his checkpoint exists ({ckpt}, gitignored), run {exp} and reload. The paper below needs no weights.
- `wlg.chat.empty`: Say anything. He will turn it into a question about how anybody knows anything, or draw you something.
- `wlg.chat.endofturn`: his end of turn

- `wlg.chat.name`: the guy

- `wlg.chat.status.run`: your own post-trained run {name} · live in your browser · the template is {tpl}
- `wlg.chat.title`: Talk to him
- `wlg.chip.dev`: dev only
- `wlg.chip.mem`: 3,600 memory locations
- `wlg.chip.net`: the SDMCHAT network
- `wlg.chip.searle`: not John Searle
- `wlg.credits.c10`: computer-10. The inspiration: {model} by {author}, a model with a personality of its own. From its model card (read {read}):
- `wlg.credits.c10.where`: It posts as {bot} and talks at {door}. Our guy is a small SDM model trained for minutes; computer-10 is a 70B model ten generations deep. We borrowed its idea, not its weights or its words.
- `wlg.credits.h`: Credits
- `wlg.credits.lectures.meta`: ({channel}, uploaded {date})
- `wlg.credits.lectures.summary`: the {n} lectures and talks, by title
- `wlg.credits.searle`: John Searle, the style source. These {n} recorded talks were read as subtitles for research and are not stored in this repository:
- `wlg.devonly.note`: He runs in the local build only. His training text was written in the style of John Searle’s lectures, so his weights stay on the machine that made them until the navigator rules otherwise. Run the site with {run} after {exp} and he will talk to you here.
- `wlg.face.aria`: WEIRD LITTLE SDM GUY's face, drawn in ASCII
- `wlg.head.title`: WEIRD LITTLE SDM GUY
- `wlg.here`: weirdlittlesdmguy
- `wlg.hero.says`: “What do you know, and how do you know it?”
- `wlg.paper.abstract.h`: Abstract
- `wlg.paper.abstract.now`: He is an SDMCHAT language model, whose next token comes from reading a sparse distributed memory, trained on a small corpus of our own writing: about three quarters plain-worded epistemics in the style of John Searle’s lectures, about one quarter WEIRD LITTLE SDM GUY material with a lot of ASCII drawings. He answers almost anything with a question about evidence, the difference between what exists and what we know, or a drawing of a snail. He is not a good model. He is a model with a character, which is the point.
- `wlg.paper.by.now`: the SETTLE campaign · numbers from {report}
- `wlg.paper.kicker`: HIS TINY PAPER
- `wlg.paper.limits.background`: Searle himself warned against a philosopher who treats life as a constant knowledge problem; most of what we do rests on a Background we take for granted. The guy cannot take anything for granted. That is the joke, and it is also his flaw.
- `wlg.paper.limits.context`: The network reads only the last 256 tokens and has no attention, so long conversations drift.
- `wlg.paper.limits.corpus`: His corpus is generated from a few hundred sentences we wrote, recombined. He learns those sentences well and little else; a held-out topic gets a familiar paragraph with the new noun in it.
- `wlg.paper.limits.h`: 4. Limits
- `wlg.paper.limits.probe`: The style probe scores words and shapes, not ideas: a reply can mention evidence and still say nothing.
- `wlg.paper.regime.missing`: The regime table is filled from the report once the run is measured.
- `wlg.paper.results.h`: 3. Results
- `wlg.paper.title`: WEIRD LITTLE SDM GUY: a small SDM language model that only cares how we know things
- `wlg.paper.trained.h.now`: 2. How he is trained
- `wlg.paper.trained.loss`: The loss counts only his own turns, as computer-10’s card describes for its last stage; the visitor’s words are context. The mix is set by tokens, so a short weird document and a long philosophy one are weighed fairly.
- `wlg.paper.what.h`: 1. What he is
- `wlg.paper.what.now`: The same network as SDMCHAT’s SDM-read models: the last eight tokens and five running averages form an address, two hops read a memory of 3,600 locations, and a small readout picks one of 129,280 tokens. Only the text it learned from is his own. He is not John Searle, does not speak for him, and was never endorsed by him; Searle’s recorded lectures taught us the manner, and the sentences are ours.
- `wlg.run.unnamed`: your run
- `wlg.studio.back`: back to the guy himself
- `wlg.studio.label`: THE LITTLE ML STUDIO · HIS PRIME USE
- `wlg.studio.title`: Train your own strange little guy
- `wlg.top.cap`: $ weirdlittlesdmguy --face
- `wlg.top.cap.listening`: listening
- `wlg.top.cap.writing`: writing
- `wlg.top.go`: talk to him
- `wlg.top.lede`: He is the SDMCHAT network, reading a sparse distributed memory of 3,600 locations, trained on our own writing about evidence. Ask him anything and he asks how you know it. He runs in a dev build only; a run you train yourself talks here in every build.
- `wlg.top.sub`: A small SDM language model with one obsession: how we know things.
- `wlg.top.train`: train your own

- `wtf.kind.keyword.line`: words you write in a SETTLE program: statements, keywords, blocks

- `wtf.kinds.all`: all
- `wtf.kinds.label`: show one kind of term
- `wtf.line`: every word on this site, what we mean by it, where it is used, and where it came from.
- `wtf.link`: link
- `wtf.none`: No term matches that. Try a shorter word, or clear the filter.
- `wtf.related`: related

- `wtf.search.placeholder`: a word, in English or Japanese
- `wtf.source`: source
- `wtf.term.access-circle.meaning`: The hard locations within the activation radius of an address: the ones a read or a write touches.
- `wtf.term.access-circle.usage`: Kanerva's 1988 book calls the set the access circle; his 1993 chapter draws it as "the set activated by x". SDM EXPLORE draws it as the dashed circle.
- `wtf.term.activation-probability.meaning`: The fraction of hard locations one address activates, Kanerva's p; SETTLE derives the activation radius from it.
- `wtf.term.activation-probability.usage`: Kanerva: "p Probability of activation (e.g., p = 0.000445 ...). This important parameter determines the number of hard locations that are activated, on the average, by an address." The keyword was `fire:`; in his words a location is activated, it does not fire.
- `wtf.term.activation-radius.meaning`: The Hamming distance within which an address activates a hard location.
- `wtf.term.activation-radius.usage`: Kanerva: "H Radius of activation (e.g., H = 447 bits)" (1993, P. 10). The keyword was `radius:`. Our wiki also said access radius; Kanerva's chapter says activation radius, so SETTLE takes his word. The hard locations inside it form the access circle.
- `wtf.term.address-matrix.meaning`: Kanerva's A: the hard locations' fixed random addresses, one row each.
- `wtf.term.address-matrix.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.address-noise.meaning`: The fraction of a read-address's bits flipped at random before the read.
- `wtf.term.address-noise.usage`: `address-noise: 0.2` flips a fifth of the bits. Kanerva never says damage; he says noise, and he says which thing is noisy: "If the memory is probed with a noisy address A', the retrieved pattern X' will usually have some noise" (2009, p. 144). The keyword was `damage:`.
- `wtf.term.address-register.meaning`: The register holding the address being written or read.
- `wtf.term.address-register.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.analogy.meaning`: X is to Y as A is to B, worked out by binding and unbinding hypervectors.
- `wtf.term.analogy.usage`: A hero word. The KANERVA page works Kanerva's analogies.
- `wtf.term.anneal-schedule.meaning`: Runs several anneals with a chosen cooling schedule; x.final judges the puzzle on the last arrangement.
- `wtf.term.anneal-schedule.usage`: The zootemp family measures how the schedule and restarts change the success rate.
- `wtf.term.anneal.meaning`: Settles while cooling, sweep by sweep, and keeps the calmest arrangement it finds.
- `wtf.term.anneal.usage`: Written `anneal 20_000, temperature: 1`. The temperature falls over the sweeps toward zero, so the machine ends in a low valley. best prints what it found. The puzzles use it.
- `wtf.term.annealing-schedule.meaning`: How the temperature falls during annealing; cooled too fast, a system freezes in a shallow valley.
- `wtf.term.annealing-schedule.usage`: A hero word. The hero's own schedule heats, cools, holds and reheats each picture.
- `wtf.term.ask.meaning`: Counts how often a thing, or a combination of things, was yes in the recorded samples.
- `wtf.term.ask.usage`: Written `ask :rain` or `ask :a, and: :b`. With a thing held, asking about another is a question with evidence: the weather program says how likely rain is once the grass is held wet. In the descend family, ask prints each parameter's mean and spread.
- `wtf.term.associative-memory.meaning`: A memory read with part of what was stored, which returns the rest.
- `wtf.term.associative-memory.usage`: A hero word, followed by a Hopfield net completing a letter.
- `wtf.term.atari-light-organ.meaning`: Eight diamonds, one per band from bass to treble, each swelling with its band.
- `wtf.term.atari-light-organ.usage`: One of the hero's eight visualisers, drawn from THE DJ's sound and shown in the slot the VISUALISERS bag holds.
- `wtf.term.attention.meaning`: Each token takes a weighted sum of the others' values, the weights a softmax of how well its query matches their keys.
- `wtf.term.attention.usage`: A hero word, followed by its equation picture.
- `wtf.term.attractor.meaning`: A state the dynamics pull back to from all around it.
- `wtf.term.attractor.usage`: A hero word, followed by a Hopfield recall film.
- `wtf.term.autoassociative.meaning`: A memory that stores each word at its own address, so a noisy copy reads it back.
- `wtf.term.autoassociative.usage`: A hero word. SETTLE's SDMs are autoassociative.
- `wtf.term.backprop.meaning`: The chain rule run backwards through a network to get the gradient of the loss for every weight.
- `wtf.term.backprop.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.base.meaning`: A house or ambient rhythm bed in our own JSON (settle-base/1): a tempo range, a meter, a tick grid, a swing, a key, and separate parts (kick, snare, hats, percussion, bass, chords, lead, texture) as events on the grid, each part with its density, syncopation and energy, the whole with a signature. The library on #/hear holds 300: 150 house, 150 ambient; 224 imported from open MIDI, 76 authored from theory. A base is named base-NNNN and carries no source; the ledger holds its source and licence.
- `wtf.term.base.usage`: The DJ asks the library for a kind, a family, a tempo and a key, scores every base, and settles one from exp(-G / T) as T cools; any part or any bar range of a base can be sliced and laid under another base when the compatibility rule (meter, tempo overlap, key or a transposition) allows it. A melody is laid over a base through the hats gate and the kick duck.
- `wtf.term.basin.meaning`: Every starting state that settles into the same attractor.
- `wtf.term.basin.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.belief-propagation.meaning`: Decoding by passing messages between bits and checks; the classic LDPC decoder, beside decoding by settling.
- `wtf.term.belief-propagation.usage`: c.decode_bp runs it, so a SETTLE decode can be compared with it on the same received word.
- `wtf.term.best-match.meaning`: Finding the stored word nearest a given word, the problem an SDM answers approximately.
- `wtf.term.best-match.usage`: Flynn, Kanerva and Bhadkamkar: "An apparently simple way in which this best-match problem could be tackled is the following" (1989, p. 7).
- `wtf.term.best.meaning`: Prints the calmest arrangement the last anneal found, with its energy.
- `wtf.term.best.usage`: Written `best` after an anneal.
- `wtf.term.binary-spatter-code.meaning`: Kanerva's binary hypervectors: XOR to bind, the bitwise majority to bundle.
- `wtf.term.binary-spatter-code.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.bit-counters.meaning`: The integer counters each hard location keeps, one per bit of the data word; a write adds +1 or -1 to each.
- `wtf.term.bit-counters.usage`: Kanerva: "C Contents matrix; U x M up-down counters with range c" (1993, P. 10). In SETTLE an sdm's counters are pulls between hard locations and data things.
- `wtf.term.bits-per-byte.meaning`: How many bits a model needs, on average, to code each byte of text; lower is better.
- `wtf.term.bits-per-byte.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.block-gibbs.meaning`: Gibbs sampling that re-tosses a whole set of variables with no pulls between them at once, as a checkerboard does on a lattice.
- `wtf.term.block-gibbs.usage`: A hero word. The film player's checkerboard rule is one.
- `wtf.term.boltzmann-constant.meaning`: k = 1.380649 × 10^-23 joules per kelvin, exact since 2019: it turns a temperature into an energy, kT.
- `wtf.term.boltzmann-constant.usage`: A hero word. SETTLE folds k into its units, so its T is kT.
- `wtf.term.boltzmann-distribution.meaning`: Each arrangement s turns up with probability proportional to e^(-E(s)/T): the distribution settling samples.
- `wtf.term.boltzmann-distribution.usage`: Named for Ludwig Boltzmann. It is the target of every settle; ask estimates it by counting.
- `wtf.term.boltzmann-machine.meaning`: A settling machine that learns: its leans and pulls are fitted so its settles reproduce a set of examples.
- `wtf.term.boltzmann-machine.usage`: The learn family and the LEARNING page. Learning compares how often pairs agree in the data and in the machine, and nudges the pulls.
- `wtf.term.brownian-motion.meaning`: The jitter of a small particle struck at random by the molecules around it.
- `wtf.term.brownian-motion.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.bundling.meaning`: Adding hypervectors bit by bit and keeping the majority: a vector that resembles each one added.
- `wtf.term.bundling.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.burn-in.meaning`: The first sweeps of a settle, thrown away because the machine has not forgotten its random start.
- `wtf.term.burn-in.usage`: settle runs max(1, N / 10) burn-in sweeps before it records.
- `wtf.term.burn.meaning`: How many early sweeps or steps are thrown away before samples are counted.
- `wtf.term.burn.usage`: The same idea as the burn-in of every settle.
- `wtf.term.burst.meaning`: A short settle-see animation that fires when the footer rises on a page change.
- `wtf.term.burst.usage`: One of 25 bursts, picked at each page change; none under reduced motion.
- `wtf.term.by.meaning`: The strength of a lean or a pull.
- `wtf.term.by.usage`: Written after `leans:` on thing and after the other thing on pulls and pushes: `a.pulls :b, by: 2`.
- `wtf.term.cerebral-cortex.meaning`: The outer layer of the brain; the footer draws a schematic of it above the cerebellar layer.
- `wtf.term.cerebral-cortex.usage`: Our own drawing of two layers of the brain, a schematic and not a measurement of any one area.
- `wtf.term.cl1.meaning`: Cortical Labs' CL1: a computer built on living human neurons, which 2026 news reports describe running DOOM.
- `wtf.term.cl1.usage`: Cited on the SURPRISE page as reports, not as results: the demo has not yet appeared in a peer-reviewed paper.
- `wtf.term.classify.meaning`: Scores a learned machine: hold an example's pixels and settle the label things.
- `wtf.term.classify.usage`: shuffle swaps labels between rows to give a chance baseline. The LEARNING page reads handwritten digits this way.
- `wtf.term.clean-up.meaning`: The last step of a hyperdimensional answer: compare the noisy result with every word in the item memory and take the word it looks most like.
- `wtf.term.clean-up.usage`: On the KANERVA page the answer to the dollar of Mexico is a noisy copy until the clean-up names it.
- `wtf.term.climbing-fibre.meaning`: In Kanerva's model of the cerebellum, the line that brings a Purkinje cell the word to be stored.
- `wtf.term.climbing-fibre.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.colour-stmt.meaning`: Declares three grids, red, green and blue, for a colour picture.
- `wtf.term.colour-stmt.usage`: The grids are named film_r, film_g and film_b.
- `wtf.term.concentration-of-measure.meaning`: In many dimensions nearly every random point lies about the same distance from any given one; for n bits, close to n/2.
- `wtf.term.concentration-of-measure.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.content-addressable.meaning`: Found by what it holds, not by where it is kept.
- `wtf.term.content-addressable.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.contents-matrix.meaning`: Kanerva's C: every hard location's bit-counters together, one row per hard location.
- `wtf.term.contents-matrix.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.contenttrack.meaning`: Predicts how well a memory's content reads will recall, without building the memory.
- `wtf.term.contenttrack.usage`: It builds nothing and does not touch the model or the run.
- `wtf.term.contrastive-divergence.meaning`: A cheap way to train a Boltzmann machine: compare the data with a few settling steps started from the data.
- `wtf.term.contrastive-divergence.usage`: The denoiser chain trains each machine this way.
- `wtf.term.critical-distance.meaning`: How far a read-address can be from a stored word and still converge to it under iterated reads.
- `wtf.term.critical-distance.usage`: Kanerva: "the distance beyond which divergence is more likely than convergence" (1988, p. 63). Inside it, each read lands closer; outside it, reads wander off. The hero draws it as one of its shapes.
- `wtf.term.critical-temperature.meaning`: The temperature at which order sets in: about 2.27 for the square-lattice Ising model.
- `wtf.term.critical-temperature.usage`: A hero word, followed by the critical-point film.
- `wtf.term.cross-entropy.meaning`: H(p, q) = −Σ p ln q: the average number of nats a code built for q spends on data drawn from p.
- `wtf.term.cross-entropy.usage`: A hero word, followed by its equation. A language model trained on text lowers it.
- `wtf.term.data-word.meaning`: The word stored and read back.
- `wtf.term.data-word.usage`: Kanerva: "Except for the lengths of the address and data words, the memory resembles ordinary computer memory." In SETTLE's autoassociative memories the data word is the pattern itself.
- `wtf.term.default-mode.meaning`: The hero's sound on load, one mix for everyone: the settle's own static loudest, then the binaural pair, then the flute.
- `wtf.term.default-mode.usage`: DEFAULT_MIX in src/heroControls.js; the console lists it first among the sound choices.
- `wtf.term.denoiser.meaning`: A chain of small machines trained to turn coin noise into examples, step by step.
- `wtf.term.denoiser.usage`: d.train fits each machine by contrastive divergence; d.generate draws samples from the chain; coins draws a baseline from pixel rates.
- `wtf.term.descend-stmt.meaning`: Gradient descent as settling: fit parameters to data on a loss, with Langevin noise above temperature 0.
- `wtf.term.descend-stmt.usage`: data reads the examples, loss names the loss, descend runs, ask prints the parameters, score predicts the test set.
- `wtf.term.detailed-balance.meaning`: At equilibrium each move is made as often as its reverse; the usual proof that a sampler has the right distribution.
- `wtf.term.detailed-balance.usage`: A hero word, followed by its equation.
- `wtf.term.diffusion.meaning`: A generative model that adds noise to data step by step and learns to take it away again, step by step.
- `wtf.term.diffusion.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.dimacs.meaning`: Two text formats for a weighted graph, the ones max-cut and colouring solvers read.
- `wtf.term.dimacs.usage`: export writes a model's pulls as a Gset or DIMACS graph, so another solver can take the same problem.
- `wtf.term.dollar-of-mexico.meaning`: Kanerva's example of computing with long random words: bind country and money, then unbind to ask what Mexico's dollar is (the peso).
- `wtf.term.dollar-of-mexico.usage`: Each word is a long random pattern; binding and adding make a record of a country, and a map between two records answers the analogy. The KANERVA page walks it step by step in rows of dots.
- `wtf.term.domain-wall.meaning`: The boundary between a region of yes and a region of no in a pulled grid; it costs energy along its length.
- `wtf.term.domain-wall.usage`: One of the hero's computed films shows a domain wall shrinking as the field settles.
- `wtf.term.drift.meaning`: Lets the numbers drift under Langevin noise; means and spread read the cloud; solve does it for A x = b.
- `wtf.term.drift.usage`: The cloud's centre is the answer to A x = b and its spread gives the inverse of A.
- `wtf.term.dropout.meaning`: Switching off random units during training, so no unit can come to rely on another.
- `wtf.term.dropout.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.elbo.meaning`: The evidence lower bound: ln p(x) minus the KL divergence from q to the posterior, so never above ln p(x).
- `wtf.term.elbo.usage`: A hero word, followed by its equation.
- `wtf.term.embedding.meaning`: A word or a thing written as a point in a space of many dimensions, so that similar things lie near each other.
- `wtf.term.embedding.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.end.meaning`: The line that closes a block; `do` ends the line that opens one.
- `wtf.term.end.usage`: A block opens with exactly three tokens (`model :m do` or `run :m do`) and closes with the one token `end`. A block still open at the end of the file is an error naming the line where it opened.
- `wtf.term.energy-based-model.meaning`: A model that gives every state an energy, low for likely states; its probabilities are e^(−E/T)/Z.
- `wtf.term.energy-based-model.usage`: A hero word. Every SETTLE program is one.
- `wtf.term.energy-landscape.meaning`: Every arrangement of a machine placed by its energy: valleys are calm arrangements, barriers lie between them.
- `wtf.term.energy-landscape.usage`: Settling rolls the machine into valleys; heat lets it climb out; annealing cools it into a deep one. The VALLEYS page draws the map; the hero draws it as a plot with a ball rolling downhill.
- `wtf.term.energy.meaning`: E = -Σ lean·s - Σ pull·s·s': a number for an arrangement that settling lowers.
- `wtf.term.energy.usage`: Low energy means things agree with their leans and their pulls. Settling visits low-energy arrangements most; annealing looks for the lowest.
- `wtf.term.entropy.meaning`: How many arrangements a machine can be in at a given energy, on a log scale; heat favours high entropy.
- `wtf.term.entropy.usage`: One of the hero's words. At high temperature entropy wins and the lights look like noise; at low temperature energy wins and the picture appears.
- `wtf.term.equilibrium.meaning`: The state where a system's probabilities stop changing; for a settle, the Boltzmann distribution.
- `wtf.term.equilibrium.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.ergodicity.meaning`: A sampler is ergodic when it can reach every state, so its long-run average equals the true average.
- `wtf.term.ergodicity.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.examples.meaning`: Reads an example set for learning; hidden declares hidden things the machine may use.
- `wtf.term.examples.usage`: The learn family fits leans and pulls so that settling reproduces the examples.
- `wtf.term.export-stmt.meaning`: Writes a model as Ising, QUBO, Gset or DIMACS; import reads an Ising file back.
- `wtf.term.export-stmt.usage`: So a SETTLE model can go to another solver and come back.
- `wtf.term.fade.meaning`: A factor every counter or pull is multiplied by before each write, so old words fade.
- `wtf.term.fade.usage`: `fade: 1` means nothing fades.
- `wtf.term.fake-valley.meaning`: A place a recall settles into that is stable but holds no stored pattern.
- `wtf.term.fake-valley.usage`: The SDMMEMORY page names each recall: a stored pattern, a mirror image, or a fake valley. SDMKEYS measured 22.3% fake for 5 random patterns in a Hopfield memory.
- `wtf.term.family-coded.meaning`: Compress and error-code text before storing it in a memory; decode it on recall.
- `wtf.term.family-coded.usage`: The coded family is number 13 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-colour.meaning`: Three grids per colour picture: PPM in and out, colour playback.
- `wtf.term.family-colour.usage`: The colour family is number 11 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-core.meaning`: Things, leans and pulls; hold, settle, anneal, show, best and ask.
- `wtf.term.family-core.usage`: The core family is number 1 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-denoise.meaning`: A chain of small machines trained to turn coin noise into examples.
- `wtf.term.family-denoise.usage`: The denoise family is number 14 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-descend.meaning`: Gradient descent as settling: parameters on a differentiable loss, Langevin noise above temperature 0, the posterior cloud.
- `wtf.term.family-descend.usage`: The descend family is number 20 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-export.meaning`: Write a model as Ising, QUBO, Gset or DIMACS; read an Ising file back.
- `wtf.term.family-export.usage`: The export family is number 10 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-grid.meaning`: One thing per pixel: read and write PGM pictures, play a folder of frames.
- `wtf.term.family-grid.usage`: The grid family is number 3 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-ldpcmoves.meaning`: Multi-bit moves and Nishimori-temperature decoding for those codes.
- `wtf.term.family-ldpcmoves.usage`: The ldpcmoves family is number 16 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-ldpcsettle.meaning`: LDPC error-correcting codes as springs; decode by settling or by belief propagation.
- `wtf.term.family-ldpcsettle.usage`: The ldpcsettle family is number 15 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-learn.meaning`: Example sets, hidden things, Boltzmann machine learning, classification by settling.
- `wtf.term.family-learn.usage`: The learn family is number 5 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-memory.meaning`: A Hopfield memory: patterns and text stored in the pulls, recalled from a damaged read-address, keyed notes.
- `wtf.term.family-memory.usage`: The memory family is number 2 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-numbers.meaning`: Real-valued things on springs, Langevin drift, solving linear systems.
- `wtf.term.family-numbers.usage`: The numbers family is number 7 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-sdm.meaning`: Kanerva sparse distributed memory with hard locations and bit-counters.
- `wtf.term.family-sdm.usage`: The sdm family is number 8 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-sdmrefuse.meaning`: When a sparse distributed memory read should refuse to answer.
- `wtf.term.family-sdmrefuse.usage`: The sdmrefuse family is number 17 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-sdmscale.meaning`: Sparse distributed memory at scale, up to a million hard locations.
- `wtf.term.family-sdmscale.usage`: The sdmscale family is number 12 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-sdmtrack.meaning`: Predicted recall of a sparse distributed memory's content reads, without building the memory.
- `wtf.term.family-sdmtrack.usage`: The sdmtrack family is number 19 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-softsdm.meaning`: Sparse distributed memory built from p-bits, with a soft cut-off.
- `wtf.term.family-softsdm.usage`: The softsdm family is number 9 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-valleys.meaning`: Test landscapes; exact enumeration and random surveys of the calm arrangements.
- `wtf.term.family-valleys.usage`: The valleys family is number 6 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-zoo.meaning`: Puzzles as models: sudoku, graph colouring, max-cut and factoring, and checking a solution.
- `wtf.term.family-zoo.usage`: The zoo family is number 4 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.family-zootemp.meaning`: An anneal with a chosen schedule and restarts; judging a puzzle on the end state.
- `wtf.term.family-zootemp.usage`: The zootemp family is number 18 in the order the interpreter offers each line to the families. Its statements and their exact output are on its page.
- `wtf.term.filesystem-menu.meaning`: The site as a tree under /settle with folders, an ls -l listing, one mark per page and a preview; the second row is the tour, the recommended order.
- `wtf.term.filesystem-menu.usage`: Derived from App.jsx's NAV by src/navtree.js, with the folders packages, language, demos, science, account, about and misc. The tour row marks the page you are on and the next one.
- `wtf.term.film.meaning`: A sequence of frames a grid settles through: the Muybridge horse, Tears of Steel, or a film computed in code.
- `wtf.term.film.usage`: The hero plays ten films at 2 frames a second; nine are computed by src/topicFilms.js and their facts are tested.
- `wtf.term.films-and-frames.meaning`: The hero's main bag: its films and still pictures, played on shuffle.
- `wtf.term.films-and-frames.usage`: The hero's rotation is two seeded bags on one slot clock: FILMS AND FRAMES take 7 slots of every 8 and a visualiser the eighth, never two visualisers in a row, each bag used up before it repeats. Every slot starts on a master bar line. THE DJ's line names the bag and the item on air.
- `wtf.term.fluctuation-dissipation.meaning`: The theorem that one coupling to the heat bath sets both a system's random fluctuations and its friction.
- `wtf.term.fluctuation-dissipation.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.fnv-1a.meaning`: The hash KANERVA uses on names and keys.
- `wtf.term.fnv-1a.usage`: A note's key is hashed to 64 bits with FNV-1a, and a guessed key can be checked offline against the padding. On SDM EXPLORE an SDM's addresses come from the memory's name and seed, through the FNV-1a of the name.
- `wtf.term.fokker-planck.meaning`: The equation that moves a probability density under drift and noise; Langevin dynamics follows it.
- `wtf.term.fokker-planck.usage`: A hero word.
- `wtf.term.footer-brain.meaning`: A live picture of two layers of the brain at the end of every page, docked as a 50 px strip until you scroll to it.
- `wtf.term.footer-brain.usage`: Mounted once beside the router, so its settle carries on across pages. OPEN scrolls to it; in a voyage view a click rides into the Purkinje forest like a game's fly-cam: the mouse looks, W A S D fly, SPACE rises and SHIFT SPACE sinks. It rises on a page change with a burst. Its depth is inspired by Yayoi Kusama's infinity mirror rooms.
- `wtf.term.forty-hz-light.meaning`: An opt-in flicker of the picture at 40 Hz, behind a warning, with a 432 Hz flute: the 40 Hz AND 432 Hz FLUTE MODE, also called the McKusker mode.
- `wtf.term.forty-hz-light.usage`: Off on load. After the warning it is a full on-off square wave at 40 Hz; a display slower than 100 frames a second flickers at the nearest rate it draws exactly and says so, while the sound stays at 40 Hz. Its name is one constant in settle-hear, FLUTE_MODE_NAME in src/tuning.js.
